namesOverTime.note: 'Densely inhabited land'. Wahunsenacawh, whom the English called Powhatan, ruled about thirty tributary communities from Werowocomoco.

namesOverTime.name: Virginia
namesOverTime.note: Named by Walter Raleigh's expedition for Elizabeth I, the unmarried queen, twenty-three years before anyone settled at Jamestown.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: The colony's land became Virginia, West Virginia (1863) and Kentucky (1792).

geoCoverage.label: Charter claims far beyond the settled tidewater
geoCoverage.change: English settlement in 1607 was a single palisade on a marshy peninsula; the charter claimed a wedge of the continent nobody had surveyed.

geoCoverage.label: East of the Proclamation Line
geoCoverage.change: The Royal Proclamation closed the land beyond the Appalachian watershed to settlers and reserved it for Indigenous nations. Virginians ignored it and Virginia never accepted it.

acquisitions.how: About 104 men and boys sent by the Virginia Company of London built a palisade on the James River inside the territory of the Powhatan paramount chiefdom, without asking permission and without the means to feed themselves.

counterparties.name: The Powhatan paramount chiefdom (Tsenacommacah)
counterparties.lost: Roughly 15,000 people under Wahunsenacawh lost first the fertile riverfront, then, after two long wars, their political independence: the treaty of 1646 made the Powhatan tributaries of the colony and fixed them behind a line.
counterparties.note: Opechancanough's attacks of 1622 and 1644 each killed several hundred colonists; the English answer was to burn cornfields, which killed far more Powhatan people than fighting did.

instrument.name: First Charter of Virginia
instrument.note: James I granted a joint-stock company the right to settle and govern; the Crown itself risked nothing.

people.name: Wahunsenacawh (Powhatan)
people.role: paramount chief who fed the starving colony in 1607-08 and then tried to contain it

people.name: Opechancanough
people.role: his successor; led the coordinated attacks of 1622 and 1644 that nearly ended the colony

people.name: John Smith
people.role: council president 1608-09 who kept the settlement alive by trading and extorting maize

people.name: Pocahontas (Matoaka)
people.role: Wahunsenacawh's daughter, taken hostage in 1613, married to John Rolfe and displayed in London as proof the colony was safe

acquisitions.resistance: Opechancanough's rising of 22 March 1622 killed about 347 colonists in a morning, roughly a quarter of them; the English used it to declare a war of extermination and seize the cleared fields they had wanted all along.

cost.note: Of roughly 7,300 people the Virginia Company sent between 1607 and 1624, only about 1,200 were alive in the colony in 1624. Deaths were mostly from disease, hunger and overwork, not fighting; the figure is a company-records reconstruction and is approximate.

statusPeriods.label: Rule by the Virginia Company of London
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London joint-stock company appointed the governor, owned the land and set martial law; investors, not ministers, decided who was hanged for stealing food.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jamestown, under the Virginia Company in London
statusPeriods.franchise: The General Assembly first met on 30 July 1619, the first elected legislature in English America. Only free adult male landholders voted; the same year the first Africans were sold into the colony.
statusPeriods.note: James I dissolved the company after a royal inquiry into the deaths and the 1622 war.

statusPeriods.label: Royal colony with a House of Burgesses
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown appointed the governor and council; the elected House of Burgesses voted the taxes, so the great tobacco planters ran Virginia by bargaining with London.
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders only. Free Black Virginians were barred from voting in 1723; enslaved people, who were about two in five of the population by 1770, had no legal standing at all.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, governed by Virginians
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor Dunmore fled to a warship in the York River and never governed again; Britain kept claiming Virginia for eight more years while a Virginia convention, and then a state government, actually ran it.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain asserted sovereignty until 1783 but exercised none after Dunmore's flight, apart from coastal raids and the 1781 campaign that ended with Cornwallis surrendering at Yorktown.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: nowhere: the royal government was afloat, then gone
statusPeriods.note: On 7 November 1775 Dunmore offered freedom to enslaved men who would fight for the king. Several hundred joined his Ethiopian Regiment; most died of smallpox at Gwynn's Island.

departures.how: Virginians declared independence in May 1776, fought for seven years, and won when a French fleet sealed the Chesapeake and Washington's army forced Cornwallis to surrender 7,000 men at Yorktown on 19 October 1781.

departures.borders: The 1783 treaty gave the new republic everything east of the Mississippi, including land the Crown had promised in 1763 to Indigenous nations. Not one of those nations was at the table, and none had been defeated.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: Ratified by Congress on 14 January 1784 and by George III on 9 April 1784.

contested.note: When did Virginia stop being British? Choose 4 July 1776 (the declaration), 19 October 1781 (Yorktown) or 3 September 1783 (the treaty). This atlas uses 1783 because that is when Britain agreed, and shows the collapse of British authority from 1775 as a separate control level.

slavery.note: Virginia built the largest enslaved population in mainland British America: about 188,000 people in 1770, roughly two in five Virginians, working tobacco for planters who were simultaneously writing about liberty.

toll.note: Approximate number of Africans landed in the Chesapeake across the whole colonial period, from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. From the 1720s Virginia's enslaved population grew mainly by birth rather than by import, which is why the arrival figure is smaller than the 1770 population.

populationTransfer.note: Two forced migrations and one voluntary: Africans trafficked to the tobacco coast, about 50,000 British convicts transported to the Chesapeake between 1718 and 1775, and indentured servants who made up most white arrivals before 1680.

violence.note: The Anglo-Powhatan wars of 1610-14, 1622-32 and 1644-46 ended with the Powhatan reduced to tributary status on reservations; Virginia's 1705 slave code made lifelong, inheritable slavery a matter of statute.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never been a Commonwealth member. Its exit predates the institution by 150 years.

consequences.economicLegacy: Tobacco tied Virginia to Glasgow and London merchants who held the planters' debts; those debts were one reason the gentry found independence attractive.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, county courts, an Anglican establishment until 1786, and a legislature that has met continuously since 1619.

pedagogy.hook: In 1619 Virginia got two things within weeks of each other: the first elected assembly in English America, and the first Africans sold into the colony.

misconception.belief: The English settled empty wilderness at Jamestown.
misconception.correction: They built inside Tsenacommacah, a chiefdom of roughly 15,000 people under Wahunsenacawh, on cleared riverside fields that were valuable precisely because someone was already farming them. The colony survived its first winters on Powhatan maize, bought, begged and taken at gunpoint.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Virginia is where the English empire learned its Atlantic formula: a chartered company, a cash crop, imported unfree labour, and an elected assembly for the men who owned both the land and the labourers.

namesOverTime.name: Province of Massachusetts Bay
namesOverTime.note: The new charter merged Plymouth Colony, Massachusetts Bay, Maine and, until 1697, Nova Scotia.

namesOverTime.name: The Commonwealth of Massachusetts
namesOverTime.note: The state constitution of 1780, drafted by John Adams and still in force, is the oldest written constitution in continuous use anywhere.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: Maine was governed from Boston until it became a separate state on 15 March 1820.

geoCoverage.label: Plymouth and the Bay
geoCoverage.change: Two separate Puritan colonies, Plymouth from 1620 and Massachusetts Bay from 1630, on the coast between Cape Cod and the Merrimack.

geoCoverage.label: With the District of Maine
geoCoverage.change: The 1691 royal charter folded Plymouth and the Maine settlements into one province governed from Boston.

acquisitions.how: About 102 passengers of the Mayflower, half of them religious separatists, landed at Cape Cod without a valid patent for the place and settled at Patuxet, a Wampanoag village emptied by an epidemic three years earlier.

counterparties.name: The Wampanoag confederation
counterparties.lost: An epidemic of 1616-19, probably carried by earlier European fishermen, had killed perhaps three-quarters of the coastal Wampanoag; the survivors under Ousamequin allied with the newcomers in 1621 and within two generations had lost their land and their independence.
counterparties.note: The English read the empty villages as providence. Plymouth's site was a cleared, planted Wampanoag town whose people were dead.

instrument.name: Mayflower Compact
instrument.note: Not a grant of anything: 41 men signed an agreement to obey their own government because they had landed outside the territory of their patent.

people.name: Ousamequin (Massasoit)
people.role: Wampanoag sachem who made the 1621 treaty that kept Plymouth alive

people.name: Tisquantum (Squanto)
people.role: Patuxet man, kidnapped to Spain and England and returned to find his village dead; interpreted for the colonists

people.name: William Bradford
people.role: governor of Plymouth for most of thirty-six years

acquisitions.resistance: None in 1620: the alliance held for fifty-four years. It broke in 1675 when Ousamequin's son Metacom went to war.

evidence.author: Daniel K. Richter
evidence.work: Facing East from Indian Country: A Native History of Early America
evidence.supports: The epidemic, Wampanoag politics and why the alliance was made.

acquisitions.how: Charles I chartered the Massachusetts Bay Company; its Puritan shareholders then did something no other company did, carrying the charter itself to America so that no governor in London could overrule them.

counterparties.name: The Massachusett, Pawtucket and Nipmuc peoples
counterparties.lost: Land along the Charles and Merrimack rivers, taken under deeds many signers did not understand as permanent alienation, after epidemics in 1616-19 and 1633 had cut their numbers by most of their strength.

instrument.name: Charter of the Massachusetts Bay Company
instrument.note: The charter did not say where the company's government had to sit. John Winthrop's fleet took the document with it in 1630.

people.name: John Winthrop
people.role: led the 1630 fleet and governed for twelve years

statusPeriods.label: Self-governing Puritan commonwealth
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The freemen of the company elected their own governor and magistrates in Boston, coined their own money, hanged Quakers and ignored royal orders for half a century.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Formally a chartered company under the Crown, but between 1630 and 1684 Massachusetts governed itself more completely than any other English colony; the practical degree of British authority was closer to that of a self-governing colony.
statusPeriods.franchise: Until 1664 only male members of an approved Congregational church could vote, perhaps a fifth of adult men. Baptists, Quakers and Anglicans were excluded from the electorate and sometimes from the colony.
statusPeriods.note: The charter was annulled by an English court in 1684 after years of complaints about smuggling and religious persecution.

statusPeriods.label: The Dominion of New England, and its collapse
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: James II abolished the New England assemblies and sent Sir Edmund Andros to rule from Boston with a nominated council; Bostonians arrested him on 18 April 1689 when they heard William of Orange had landed in England.
statusPeriods.franchise: None: Andros governed without an assembly and taxed without one.
statusPeriods.note: After the 1689 revolt the old charter government resumed unofficially until the new charter arrived in 1692.

statusPeriods.label: Royal province with an elected assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: London appointed the governor; the elected General Court voted his salary, which it repeatedly refused to make permanent, so every governor spent his term negotiating with the people he was sent to rule.
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-owning adult men, replacing the old church-membership test. Women, enslaved and most propertyless men could not vote.

statusPeriods.label: Military government under General Gage
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Parliament rewrote the charter, banned town meetings and made the council appointive; General Thomas Gage governed as both governor and army commander, and his writ ran only as far as his sentries.
statusPeriods.franchise: Suspended. The Massachusetts Government Act removed the colony's elected council and its town meetings.
statusPeriods.note: Outside Boston, a Provincial Congress at Concord was already governing. That is the situation the troops marched into on 19 April 1775.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, held by Massachusetts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Washington's guns on Dorchester Heights forced the garrison to sail for Halifax; Britain claimed the province for seven more years and never set foot in it again.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British sovereignty was asserted until 1783 and exercised not at all after the evacuation of Boston.

departures.how: The war began here: on 19 April 1775 British regulars sent to seize powder at Concord were fought back to Boston, and eleven months later the garrison sailed away, taking about 1,100 loyalist refugees with it.

led.name: Samuel Adams
led.role: organiser of the Boston resistance and the committees of correspondence

led.name: John Adams
led.role: lawyer who defended the soldiers of the Boston Massacre and then argued for independence in Congress

led.name: Crispus Attucks
led.role: sailor of African and Wampanoag descent, first man killed in the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770

led.name: Thomas Gage

departures.movement: Sons of Liberty and the Massachusetts Provincial Congress

cost.note: Massachusetts sent more soldiers than any other state and lost heavily at Bunker Hill on 17 June 1775, where about 1,054 British soldiers were killed or wounded taking a hill they could have surrounded. No reliable colony-level death toll exists for the whole war.

departures.borders: Massachusetts kept the District of Maine, whose boundary with British New Brunswick stayed unsettled for another sixty years and was finally drawn by the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 after the bloodless Aroostook confrontation of 1838-39.

violence.note: King Philip's War of 1675-76 killed a larger share of New England's population than any later American war; Metacom's head was displayed on a pole at Plymouth for two decades and hundreds of Wampanoag and Narragansett survivors were sold into Caribbean slavery.

toll.note: Estimates combine roughly 800-1,000 colonists and several thousand Indigenous dead from fighting, starvation and disease. No one counted; the range comes from town records and later reconstructions.

populationTransfer.note: About 20,000 English Puritans emigrated to New England between 1630 and 1642, mostly in families; after King Philip's War hundreds of captured Indigenous people were shipped into slavery in the Caribbean and the Azores.

slavery.note: Massachusetts legalised slavery in 1641, the first English colony to do so by statute, and Boston merchants financed slave voyages long after; a 1783 court ruling in the Quock Walker cases ended slavery in the state.

emancipationDate.note: There was no emancipation statute. Judges held that the 1780 state constitution's declaration that all men are born free was incompatible with slavery.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cod, timber, shipbuilding and the carrying trade: New England's ships supplied the sugar islands and profited from the slave economy without holding many enslaved people at home.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Town meetings, a written constitution of 1780 still in force, and public schooling required by law from 1647.

peak.populationNote: 235,308 in Massachusetts proper plus 31,257 in the District of Maine, from the US Census Bureau's Historical Statistics series. About 4,700 people in the colony were enslaved.

pedagogy.hook: For fifty years Massachusetts elected its own governor, minted its own coins and ignored royal orders. When James II finally took the charter away, Bostonians arrested his governor and put him on a ship.

misconception.belief: The Pilgrims came for religious freedom and founded American democracy.
misconception.correction: They came for freedom for their own church and denied it to everyone else: Baptists were whipped, Quakers were hanged on Boston Common between 1659 and 1661, and only approved church members could vote until 1664. The town meeting was real self-government, and it was self-government for a religiously screened minority of adult men.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Massachusetts shows the empire's weakest point: London could charter a colony but could not staff it, so distance became autonomy, and autonomy became a habit that ended in armed resistance at Concord Bridge.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: The New Hampshire Grants west of the Connecticut River became Vermont, an independent republic from 1777 and a state in 1791.

geoCoverage.label: The Piscataqua settlements
geoCoverage.change: Fishing and timber stations at Odiorne's Point and Dover, planted by the Laconia Company on Pennacook land.

geoCoverage.label: With the New Hampshire Grants
geoCoverage.change: Governor Benning Wentworth began selling townships west of the Connecticut River, land New York also claimed and Abenaki people actually occupied.

geoCoverage.label: East of the Connecticut River
geoCoverage.change: An Order in Council ruled for New York and moved the boundary to the Connecticut River; the settlers who had bought Wentworth's grants refused to accept it.

date.note: Contemporary records disagree on whether David Thomson's party landed in spring 1623; some accounts give 1622 or 1624.

acquisitions.how: Merchants backing John Mason and Ferdinando Gorges landed fishing and timber crews at the mouth of the Piscataqua to cut white pine for masts and dry cod for Catholic Europe.

counterparties.name: The Pennacook and Abenaki peoples
counterparties.lost: The Piscataqua fisheries, the pine forests and eventually the whole river valley. Epidemics in 1616-19 and 1633 had already killed most of the coastal Pennacook; the survivors under Passaconaway kept a wary peace, and his grandson Kancamagus led a war against the settlements in 1689.

instrument.name: Council for New England grant to John Mason
instrument.note: The grant naming the province 'New Hampshire' came six years after the first landing.

people.name: Passaconaway
people.role: Pennacook sachem who chose accommodation with the settlers

people.name: John Mason
people.role: London merchant and proprietor who named the province after Hampshire

contested.note: The founding date is soft. Fishing stations came and went from the early 1620s and only became a permanent colony over the following decade; 1623 is the conventional marker, not a documented event.

statusPeriods.label: Mason's proprietary grant
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The settlements belonged on paper to John Mason and his heirs, who tried to collect rent from men three thousand miles away and mostly failed.

statusPeriods.label: Absorbed by Massachusetts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Piscataqua towns asked Massachusetts to govern them and were run from Boston for thirty-eight years, sending deputies to the General Court.
statusPeriods.franchise: Church membership, then property, as in Massachusetts.

statusPeriods.label: Royal province, chiefly a mast colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown separated New Hampshire from Massachusetts, appointed the governor and reserved every pine over twenty-four inches across for the Royal Navy, marking them with a broad arrow that colonists sawed around.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Crown-appointed governor as in a crown colony, but an elected assembly voted taxes from 1680, so real British authority sat between crown colony and representative colony.
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male property holders. The province and Massachusetts shared a governor from 1699 to 1741.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, governed by its own congress
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor John Wentworth withdrew to a warship and then to Nova Scotia; New Hampshire adopted its own constitution on 5 January 1776, the first colony to do so.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain claimed the province to 1783 and had no officials or troops in it after Wentworth's flight.

departures.how: Four months before Lexington, on 14 December 1774, New Hampshire men raided Fort William and Mary and carried off the king's powder; the royal government never recovered and Britain conceded the province in 1783.

becomes.name: State of New Hampshire, in the United States of America

led.name: John Sullivan
led.role: led the raid on Fort William and Mary and later commanded Continental troops

led.name: John Stark
led.role: commanded the militia that beat a British raiding force at Bennington on 16 August 1777

led.name: John Wentworth
led.role: last royal governor; went on to govern Nova Scotia

cost.note: No battle was fought on New Hampshire soil. The province's losses were among Continental regiments elsewhere, and are not separately counted.

departures.borders: The land New Hampshire lost in 1764 refused to belong to New York either: the Grants declared themselves the independent republic of Vermont in 1777 and joined the United States only in 1791.

violence.note: The Abenaki fought six wars against the northern New England settlements between 1675 and 1763; the Rogers' Rangers raid on the Abenaki village of Odanak in October 1759 destroyed it and killed at least thirty people.

consequences.economicLegacy: White pine masts for the Royal Navy: New Hampshire's forests were a strategic naval resource, and the Broad Arrow policy that protected them was one of the empire's most resented rules.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Town meetings and a state constitution written in 1776, the first adopted anywhere in the thirteen colonies.

pedagogy.hook: Every white pine in New Hampshire more than two feet thick belonged to the Royal Navy, marked with a broad arrow, and colonists were fined for cutting the trees on their own land.

misconception.belief: The thirteen colonies were founded for settlement and freedom.
misconception.correction: New Hampshire was founded to catch fish and cut masts. Its first governing document was a merchant's grant, not a covenant, and its most contested law for a century was a timber regulation written for the navy in London.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows what colonies were for. Strategic raw materials mattered as much as land, and imperial rules about resources bit harder on daily life than taxes on tea did.

geoCoverage.change: Settlers from Massachusetts moved down the Connecticut valley onto Pequot, Mohegan and Podunk land.

acquisitions.how: Congregationalists led by Thomas Hooker walked out of Massachusetts and founded Hartford, Windsor and Wethersfield on the Connecticut River, in country the Pequot controlled and the Dutch also claimed.

counterparties.name: The Pequot nation
counterparties.lost: Their independence and very nearly their existence. On 26 May 1637 English troops and Mohegan and Narragansett allies surrounded the fortified village at Mystic and burned it, killing between 400 and 700 people, most of them women, children and the old. The 1638 Treaty of Hartford declared the Pequot nation dissolved and forbade the use of its name.
counterparties.note: Survivors were enslaved in Connecticut households or shipped to the West Indies; the Pequot were federally recognised again only in the twentieth century.

instrument.name: Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
instrument.note: The towns wrote their own frame of government before they had any charter from England at all.

people.name: Sassacus
people.role: Pequot sachem, killed by Mohawks in 1637 while seeking refuge

people.name: Uncas
people.role: Mohegan sachem who allied with the English against the Pequot and gained by it

people.name: John Mason
people.role: commanded the attack on the Mystic village

acquisitions.resistance: The Pequot War of 1636-38 was the first war between the English and a Native nation in New England, and it set the pattern: total destruction of a village, then a treaty abolishing the enemy's name.

cost.note: Deaths at the Mystic fort on 26 May 1637. The range comes from the English commanders' own accounts, which are the only detailed sources and which boasted of the number.

evidence.author: Alfred A. Cave
evidence.work: The Pequot War
evidence.supports: The causes and conduct of the 1636-38 war and the Mystic attack.

statusPeriods.label: Self-made government, then a royal charter
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The river towns governed themselves from 1639 and in 1662 talked Charles II into a charter that let them keep electing their own governor: no royal official ever ruled Connecticut.
statusPeriods.franchise: Admitted freemen with property; New Haven required church membership until it was absorbed in 1665.
statusPeriods.note: The 1662 charter's generous boundaries also swallowed the separate colony of New Haven, which had hidden two of the judges who condemned Charles I.

statusPeriods.label: Inside the Dominion of New England
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Andros demanded the charter at Hartford in October 1687; tradition says the candles went out and it was hidden in an oak. Whatever happened to the document, the colony's government stopped until the Dominion fell.

statusPeriods.label: Charter government restored
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Connecticut simply resumed its charter after Andros fell and kept electing its own governor for another eighty-seven years; London never appointed anyone to rule it.
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male freemen meeting a property test, roughly half of adult white men.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, still under its own charter
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Connecticut needed no revolution in its government: the same elected assembly and the same governor, Jonathan Trumbull, carried on and simply stopped naming the king.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain claimed the colony until 1783; it never held any of it, though raiding parties burned Danbury in 1777 and New London in 1781.

departures.how: Connecticut kept its 1662 charter as its state constitution until 1818: the only change independence required was to stop mentioning the king in it.

becomes.name: State of Connecticut, in the United States of America

led.name: Jonathan Trumbull
led.role: the only colonial governor in office in 1775 who took the American side, and stayed governor to 1784

led.name: Benedict Arnold
led.role: Connecticut-born general who changed sides and burned New London in September 1781

cost.note: About 150 people were killed in Arnold's raid on New London and the storming of Fort Griswold on 6 September 1781, most of them after the fort surrendered. Colony-wide war deaths are not separately counted.

departures.borders: Connecticut's charter claim to a strip running west to the Pacific outlived the colony: the Western Reserve in Ohio stayed Connecticut land until 1800.

violence.note: The Pequot War of 1636-38 destroyed a nation the English then legislated out of existence; King Philip's War in 1675-76 was fought partly on Connecticut's frontier.

slavery.note: Connecticut held more enslaved people than any other New England colony, about 5,700 in 1770, mostly on farms and in coastal households supplying the West Indies.

emancipationDate.note: A gradual emancipation act of 1784 freed only children born afterwards, and at age 25; the last enslaved people in the state were freed by statute in 1848.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.languageAndLaw: A colonial charter that served as a state constitution until 1818, and town governments that predate any royal grant.

pedagogy.hook: Connecticut was so self-governing that independence changed almost nothing: it kept its royal charter of 1662 as its state constitution for another thirty-five years.

misconception.belief: British colonies were run by governors sent from London.
misconception.correction: Connecticut and Rhode Island elected their own governors under royal charters, and no British official ever administered either. The empire in North America ranged from direct military rule to colonies London could not appoint anyone to.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Connecticut is the clearest proof that 'British colony' was not one thing. Read the charter before you assume who was in charge.

territories.name: Rhode Island
territories.formalName: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

geoCoverage.label: Narragansett Bay
geoCoverage.change: Refugees expelled from Massachusetts settled on land bought from Narragansett sachems around the bay.

acquisitions.how: Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts for arguing that the king could not grant land he did not own, bought ground at the head of Narragansett Bay from the sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi and founded Providence as a refuge.

counterparties.name: The Narragansett nation
counterparties.lost: At first very little: Williams paid, learned the language and published a dictionary of it in 1643. Within forty years the Narragansett had lost almost everything, destroyed in the Great Swamp Fight of 19 December 1675 when colonial troops burned their fortified winter town.
counterparties.note: Between 300 and 1,000 Narragansett people, many of them non-combatants, were killed or burned at the Great Swamp; hundreds of survivors were sold into slavery.

instrument.name: Deed from Canonicus and Miantonomi to Roger Williams
instrument.note: Williams insisted the land had to be bought from its owners, not granted by a king. It was a minority view and the colony around him did not keep to it.

people.name: Canonicus
people.role: Narragansett sachem who granted the Providence land

people.name: Roger Williams
people.role: founder; argued for buying land from the Narragansett rather than taking it, and for separating church from state

people.name: Anne Hutchinson
people.role: banished from Massachusetts for preaching; helped found Portsmouth in 1638

statusPeriods.label: The colony no church could govern
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Four quarrelling towns governed themselves under a 1644 parliamentary patent and then a 1663 royal charter that granted 'full liberty in religious concernments' and let them elect their own governor.
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male freemen with property. Uniquely, no religious test: Baptists, Quakers and Jews all worshipped legally, and Newport's Touro synagogue congregation dates from 1658.

statusPeriods.label: Inside the Dominion of New England
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Andros suspended the charter and ruled Rhode Island from Boston with a nominated council until New England overthrew him.

statusPeriods.label: Charter restored; Newport becomes a slaving port
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The colony resumed electing its governor and its assembly, and Newport merchants built the largest slave-trading fleet in North America under a charter guaranteeing their own liberty of conscience.
statusPeriods.franchise: Freeholders only; by the 1760s a shrinking share of adult men could meet the property test.

statusPeriods.label: First to renounce the king; Newport under British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The assembly renounced allegiance two months before the Declaration of Independence, then watched a British army take Newport on 8 December 1776 and hold it for nearly three years.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain claimed the whole colony and, from December 1776 to October 1779, actually held Newport and Aquidneck Island with about 6,000 troops. Elsewhere it held nothing.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Providence, with Newport under British military rule 1776-79

departures.how: Rhode Island renounced George III on 4 May 1776, two months before Congress did, then lost its richest town to a British army for three years and never fully recovered its trade.

becomes.name: State of Rhode Island, in the United States of America

led.name: Stephen Hopkins
led.role: governor and signer of the Declaration; his own household held enslaved people

led.name: Nathanael Greene
led.role: Quaker-raised Rhode Islander who became Washington's most effective field commander

led.name: Christopher Greene
led.role: commanded the 1st Rhode Island Regiment, which enlisted enslaved men with a promise of freedom

cost.note: About 5,000 people, a third of Newport's population, left during the occupation, and the town's trade never returned to its pre-war level. No reliable count exists of Rhode Islanders killed in the war.

departures.borders: Rhode Island's borders did not move; its economy did. The centre of gravity shifted from occupied Newport to Providence, which it has never left.

slavery.note: Rhode Island merchants, chiefly from Newport and Bristol, mounted roughly a thousand slaving voyages and carried more than 100,000 African people: the colony that guaranteed liberty of conscience ran North America's largest slave trade.

emancipationDate.note: A gradual act freeing children born after 1 March 1784, not those already enslaved. Slavery in the state ended fully only in 1843.

violence.note: The Great Swamp Fight of 19 December 1675 destroyed the Narragansett as a power; hundreds of survivors were shipped out of Rhode Island and sold.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Newport's wealth came from rum distilled for the African coast; the ruins of that triangle are still visible in the town's eighteenth-century mansions.

peak.populationNote: US Census Bureau Historical Statistics estimate; about 3,800 people in the colony were enslaved, the highest proportion in New England.

pedagogy.hook: The colony founded on religious freedom, whose charter promised liberty of conscience to everyone, ran the biggest slave-trading fleet in North America.

misconception.belief: Slavery in British America was a Southern plantation thing.
misconception.correction: Newport and Bristol merchants fitted out roughly a thousand slaving voyages carrying more than 100,000 Africans, and about one Rhode Islander in fifteen was enslaved in 1770. The northern colonies financed and shipped the trade even where they used little plantation labour themselves.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Rhode Island forces the uncomfortable question the empire always raises: liberty for whom, paid for by whom.

namesOverTime.name: New Netherland
namesOverTime.note: A Dutch West India Company colony with a capital at New Amsterdam on Manhattan.

namesOverTime.name: New York
namesOverTime.note: Renamed for James, Duke of York, the king's brother, who was given it before it was taken.

namesOverTime.name: New Orange
namesOverTime.note: A Dutch fleet retook the colony for fifteen months during the Third Anglo-Dutch War.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: The New Hampshire Grants that New York claimed became Vermont, a separate state in 1791.

geoCoverage.label: The Hudson valley and the Iroquois frontier
geoCoverage.change: An English fleet took the Dutch colony; the province's western two-thirds remained Haudenosaunee country in which the English had trading rights, not sovereignty.

geoCoverage.label: With the disputed Grants
geoCoverage.change: An Order in Council awarded New York the land between the Connecticut River and Lake Champlain that New Hampshire's governor had already sold to settlers.

geoCoverage.label: Without Vermont
geoCoverage.change: The Grants settlers declared themselves the independent republic of Vermont and refused both New York and the king.

acquisitions.how: Four English warships anchored off Manhattan in peacetime and demanded the surrender of New Netherland; Peter Stuyvesant wanted to fight, the burghers refused, and the colony changed hands without a shot.

counterparties.name: The Dutch Republic and the Dutch West India Company
counterparties.lost: New Netherland: about 9,000 colonists, the Hudson fur trade and the best deep-water harbour on the coast, all confirmed to England by the Treaty of Westminster in 1674 in exchange for Suriname.

counterparties.name: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy)
counterparties.lost: Nothing in 1664, and that is the point: the Five Nations dealt with the English as they had with the Dutch, as partners in a Covenant Chain alliance. Their land was taken by treaty and fraud over the next century and a half, not in the conquest.

instrument.name: Treaty of Breda
instrument.note: Breda let each side keep what it held: England kept New Netherland, the Dutch kept Suriname and Pulau Run. The Treaty of Westminster confirmed it in 1674 after the Dutch briefly retook the colony.

people.name: Peter Stuyvesant
people.role: Dutch director-general who surrendered New Amsterdam against his own wishes

people.name: Richard Nicolls
people.role: commanded the English squadron and became the first governor

people.name: James, Duke of York
people.role: the king's brother, granted the colony before it was captured; later James II

acquisitions.resistance: The Dutch inhabitants did not resist and kept their property, language and Reformed churches under the Articles of Capitulation. A Dutch fleet retook the colony in 1673 and gave it back by treaty in 1674.

evidence.author: Russell Shorto
evidence.work: The Island at the Center of the World
evidence.supports: New Netherland, the 1664 surrender and the Dutch legacy in New York.

statusPeriods.label: The Duke of York's private province
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The colony belonged personally to James, Duke of York, who ruled it through a governor under his own code of laws and refused to call an assembly for twenty years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: New York City, under the Duke of York in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1683, when an assembly finally met and passed a Charter of Liberties that James vetoed once he became king.
statusPeriods.note: The Dutch recaptured the province from August 1673 to November 1674 and renamed it New Orange.

statusPeriods.label: Royal province, the Dominion, and Leisler's rebellion
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: James became king and his colony became the Crown's; in 1688 it was folded into the Dominion of New England, and when that collapsed the merchant Jacob Leisler seized the government for two years.
statusPeriods.note: Leisler was hanged and beheaded on 16 May 1691 after a trial his opponents controlled; Parliament reversed the attainder four years later.

statusPeriods.label: Royal governor and an assembly of landlords
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor from London shared power with an elected assembly dominated by the Hudson valley manor families, who held tens of thousands of acres and the tenants on them.
statusPeriods.franchise: Freeholders worth £40 and freemen of the city. Tenant farmers on the great manors, who were a large part of the rural population, could not vote against their landlords.
statusPeriods.note: The 1735 acquittal of the printer John Peter Zenger for seditious libel became a founding case in the law of press freedom.

statusPeriods.label: British military headquarters in America
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Howe's army took Manhattan and held New York City, Long Island and Staten Island under martial law for seven years as the base for the whole British war effort in North America.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: New York City, under the commander-in-chief
statusPeriods.franchise: None: the city was governed by the army and a police magistracy, while a rebel state government sat at Kingston and Poughkeepsie.
statusPeriods.note: The city's population roughly doubled with loyalist refugees and self-emancipated Black people who had reached British lines; a quarter of it burned in the fire of 21 September 1776.

departures.how: The last British troops rowed out of New York harbour on 25 November 1783, eleven weeks after the peace treaty and seven years after taking the city; New Yorkers still called it Evacuation Day a century later.

becomes.name: State of New York, in the United States of America

led.name: George Clinton
led.role: first governor of the independent state, in office for eighteen years

led.name: Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea)
led.role: Mohawk leader who fought for the Crown and led his people to Canada when Britain gave away their land

led.name: Guy Carleton
led.role: British commander who insisted on honouring promises of freedom to formerly enslaved people and recorded them in the Book of Negroes

departures.movement: New York Provincial Congress and the Continental Army

instrument.note: The treaty was signed in September; the New York garrison did not leave until 25 November.

populationTransfer.note: New York was the funnel of the loyalist exodus: about 30,000 people, including some 3,000 Black Loyalists whose names were written into the Book of Negroes, sailed from its harbour in 1783, mostly for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

slavery.note: About 19,000 people were enslaved in New York in 1770, a fifth of them in the city: the largest enslaved population north of Maryland, and the reason the 1741 conspiracy panic ended with thirty executions.

emancipationDate.note: An 1799 act freed only children born afterwards, and only in adulthood; full emancipation in the state came on 4 July 1827.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1783 border ran through Haudenosaunee territory and split the Six Nations between two countries; the Jay Treaty of 1794 gave them a right of free passage across it that is still asserted today.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Hudson-Mohawk corridor was the only water-level route through the Appalachians, which is why New York became the continent's chief port.

evidence.supports: The 1783 evacuation of New York and where the refugees went.

pedagogy.hook: Britain held New York City for seven years and left it last, on 25 November 1783 — eleven weeks after signing away the country it stood in.

misconception.belief: New York was founded by the English.
misconception.correction: It was Dutch for forty years. England took New Netherland by threat in 1664 without firing, kept the Dutch inhabitants, their language and their churches, and renamed the place after the king's brother. New York was a conquest of Europeans, not a settlement of empty land.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New York is where the empire's promises collided: Britain freed enslaved people who reached its lines and shipped them to Nova Scotia, and in the same treaty handed its Haudenosaunee allies' country to the United States.

geoCoverage.label: Between the Hudson and the Delaware
geoCoverage.change: Taken from the Dutch with New Netherland and immediately granted away to two of the Duke of York's friends.

acquisitions.how: The land between the Hudson and the Delaware fell with New Netherland, and the Duke of York gave it away within months to John Berkeley and George Carteret as a private estate before he had even seen it.

counterparties.name: The Lenape (Delaware) nation
counterparties.lost: Their whole homeland, bought parcel by parcel in deeds that the Lenape understood as shared use and the English enforced as exclusive ownership; by 1758 the survivors were confined to the Brotherton reservation at Edgepillock, and most had moved west by 1802.
counterparties.note: The 1758 Treaty of Easton and the Brotherton settlement are among the earliest formal reservations in North America.

counterparties.name: The Dutch Republic
counterparties.lost: The Bergen and Delaware settlements, part of the New Netherland surrender.

instrument.name: Grant from the Duke of York to Berkeley and Carteret
instrument.note: Signed before the fleet had even taken the colony, and named for Carteret's defence of Jersey in the civil war.

people.name: Teedyuscung
people.role: Lenape leader who negotiated at Easton in 1758 for land his people were losing

people.name: George Carteret
people.role: proprietor; the province is named after his island

statusPeriods.label: Two proprietary colonies, East and West Jersey
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The province split in 1676 into East Jersey, run by Scottish proprietors, and West Jersey, run by Quakers with an unusually liberal frame of government; both collected quitrents from settlers who mostly refused to pay them.
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-holding men. West Jersey's Concessions and Agreements of 1677 promised trial by jury, no imprisonment for debt and religious liberty.

statusPeriods.label: Royal colony, at first sharing New York's governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The proprietors surrendered the government to the Crown; until 1738 New Jersey had to share the governor of New York, and afterwards had its own, always with an elected assembly voting the money.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Perth Amboy and Burlington, the capital alternating
statusPeriods.franchise: Freeholders worth £50. The 1776 state constitution's wording accidentally let some unmarried property-owning women and free Black men vote, until the legislature closed the loophole in 1807.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain; the crossroads of the war
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The provincial congress arrested the royal governor and Britain never restored civil government, but armies crossed New Jersey so often that Continental and British troops raided it alike for five years.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: No British civil administration after June 1776. British armies occupied large parts of the province repeatedly, but as a theatre of operations rather than a governed colony.
statusPeriods.note: More engagements were fought in New Jersey than in any other state: Trenton, Princeton, Monmouth and hundreds of small raids.

departures.how: On 19 June 1776 New Jersey militia arrested their own royal governor, William Franklin, the loyalist son of Benjamin Franklin, and sent him to Connecticut as a prisoner; he never returned and died in London.

becomes.name: State of New Jersey, in the United States of America

led.name: William Livingston
led.role: first governor of the state, in office fourteen years

led.name: William Franklin

cost.note: New Jersey saw more separate military actions than any other colony and its farms were stripped by both armies. No reliable count of civilian deaths exists.

departures.borders: New Jersey's borders were unchanged. Its internal division into East and West Jersey survived in property law, and the surveyed line between them can still be traced.

slavery.note: New Jersey had about 8,200 enslaved people in 1770, the most of any northern colony after New York, concentrated on the Dutch-settled farms of Bergen and Somerset counties.

emancipationDate.note: New Jersey's 1804 act freed only children born later, and in 1846 recategorised the remaining enslaved as 'apprentices for life'. A handful were still held when the Thirteenth Amendment was ratified.

populationTransfer.note: Lenape people were pushed out over a century and a half; those at Brotherton sold their reservation in 1802 and moved to New Stockbridge in New York, then west again.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Quaker West Jersey's Concessions of 1677 anticipated jury trial and religious liberty guarantees later written into American constitutions.

misconception.belief: The revolution split Britain from America.
misconception.correction: It split families and neighbourhoods. William Franklin stayed loyal and died in exile while his father negotiated the peace; perhaps a fifth of colonists were loyalists, and about 60,000 of them left, taking 15,000 enslaved people with them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: New Jersey shows the war as a civil war fought among neighbours, not a clean contest between two countries, which is why the loyalist exodus reshaped Canada.

geoCoverage.label: From the Delaware to the Ohio country
geoCoverage.change: A charter grant to one man, of which only the eastern third was under any English authority for the first seventy years.

acquisitions.how: Charles II cancelled a £16,000 debt he owed to the late Admiral Penn by giving his Quaker son a slice of America the size of England, and William Penn then bought the same land again from the Lenape because he did not think the king's grant was enough.

counterparties.name: The Lenape (Delaware) nation
counterparties.lost: At first, land they were paid for in treaties Penn kept. Then everything: the Walking Purchase of 1737, run by Penn's sons with a forged deed and hired runners, took about 4,900 square kilometres, and the Lenape were forced west into the Ohio country.

departures.how: North Carolina militia destroyed a loyalist Highland force at Moore's Creek Bridge on 27 February 1776, authorised independence six weeks later, and in 1781 bled Cornwallis's army so badly at Guilford Courthouse that he marched to Virginia and to surrender.

statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A royal governor arrived, but the Commons House of Assembly, elected by rice and indigo planters, controlled money and patronage in the richest colony per head in British America.

statusPeriods.note: The Stono Rebellion of 9 September 1739 was answered by the 1740 Negro Act, which banned teaching enslaved people to write and taxed new imports for a decade.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, governed by South Carolinians
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor Lord William Campbell fled to a warship in September 1775; a provincial congress governed and beat off an attack on Charles Town in June 1776.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: No British authority in the province between Campbell's flight and the siege of Charles Town.

statusPeriods.label: Reconquered: British rule restored for thirty-one months
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Clinton's siege captured Charles Town and 5,000 men, the worst American defeat of the war; Britain re-established royal government, and lost the countryside to partisans within a year.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Charles Town, under the British commander and a restored royal council
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Britain demanded oaths of allegiance, which drove many neutrals into the rebellion.
statusPeriods.note: This is the strongest evidence against the idea that 1776 settled anything: Britain governed South Carolina again from 1780 to 1782.

statusPeriods.label: Evacuated; claimed to the treaty
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The British army sailed from Charles Town on 14 December 1782 with more than 5,000 loyalists and several thousand formerly enslaved people, and Britain gave up the claim nine months later.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Claimed but not held after the evacuation of Charles Town.

departures.how: South Carolina was lost, reconquered and lost again: Britain took Charles Town in May 1780 and ruled for thirty-one months before partisan war and defeat at Cowpens and Eutaw Springs forced the evacuation of December 1782.

becomes.name: State of South Carolina, in the United States of America

led.name: Henry Laurens
led.role: president of the Continental Congress and former slave trader, captured at sea and held in the Tower of London

led.role: British cavalry commander whose conduct at the Waxhaws in May 1780 became a rebel recruiting argument

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Rice and indigo made South Carolina the richest colony per free head in British America, and Charles Town the fourth-largest city in it.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The 1740 Negro Act, itself descended from the Barbados code of 1661, shaped slave law across the American South for a century.

misconception.belief: Enslaved Africans arrived with no skills and learned everything from their owners.
misconception.correction: South Carolina's rice fortune was built on West African knowledge. Planters advertised for captives from rice-growing regions of the Senegambia and Windward Coast, and the banked fields, tidal sluices and winnowing baskets of the lowcountry follow African practice. The expertise came off the ships.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: South Carolina is the Caribbean model transplanted to the mainland: it was settled from Barbados, copied Barbados's slave code, and produced the only mainland colony where enslaved people were the majority.

geoCoverage.label: The Savannah River and the coast
geoCoverage.change: A buffer colony planted between South Carolina's plantations and Spanish Florida, on Yamacraw and Creek land.

acquisitions.how: James Oglethorpe landed 114 settlers on Yamacraw Bluff under a trust charter that banned slavery, rum and lawyers, intending a colony of small farmers who would also stop a Spanish march on Charles Town.

counterparties.name: The Yamacraw and the Creek Confederacy
counterparties.lost: The coastal strip, ceded in a 1733 treaty negotiated by the Yamacraw mico Tomochichi, who wanted an ally against the Spanish; the Creek lost the rest by successive cessions and, in 1836-38, by removal to Indian Territory.
counterparties.note: Mary Musgrove, a Creek and English woman, interpreted every one of those negotiations and later sued the colony for what she was owed.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Its claim to the land between the Savannah and the St Johns, contested until Oglethorpe beat a Spanish invasion at Bloody Marsh on St Simons Island on 7 July 1742.

instrument.name: Charter of the Trustees for Establishing the Colony of Georgia in America
instrument.note: A twenty-one-year trust, not a proprietorship: the trustees could take no profit and no land, which is why the experiment collapsed when the money ran out.

people.role: Yamacraw mico who granted the Savannah site and travelled to England in 1734

people.role: trustee, founder and soldier; drove the ban on slavery and led the defence against Spain

evidence.supports: The trustees' ban on slavery, the campaign against it and its repeal in 1751.

statusPeriods.label: Trustee Georgia: the colony that banned slavery
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Twenty-one trustees in London governed without an assembly, allotted 50-acre farms that could not be sold, and forbade rum and, from 1735, enslaved labour; settlers petitioned against the ban for fifteen years and won in 1751.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: A charitable trust rather than a proprietorship, but the practical relationship, an English board governing a colony it owned the government of, matches a proprietary colony.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Savannah, under the Trustees in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None: Georgia had no elected assembly for its first eighteen years.

statusPeriods.label: Royal colony, and a rice-and-slavery boom
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The trustees surrendered the charter a year early; a royal governor and an elected assembly arrived, and so did the plantation economy the trustees had tried to prevent.
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders with 50 acres. The enslaved population went from zero in 1750 to about 15,000 by 1775.

statusPeriods.label: Claimed by Britain, governed by a provincial congress
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor James Wright was arrested in January 1776 and escaped to a warship in February; Georgia's own congress governed until a British army landed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: No British administration between Wright's escape and his return in July 1779, although Savannah was recaptured on 29 December 1778.

statusPeriods.label: Royal government restored under Governor Wright
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: James Wright came back to Savannah and ran a functioning royal government, with courts and an assembly, for three years: the only colony where the empire was fully restored after the Declaration of Independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: White male freeholders who would swear allegiance to the king.
statusPeriods.note: A French and American attempt to retake Savannah in October 1779 failed with about a thousand casualties.

statusPeriods.label: Evacuated; claimed to the treaty
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The garrison, about 3,000 loyalists and some 5,000 enslaved people sailed from Savannah for East Florida, Jamaica and Britain; the claim survived on paper for another year.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Claimed but not held after the July 1782 evacuation.

departures.how: Georgia is the exception that tests the rule: Britain retook Savannah in December 1778, restored its royal governor in July 1779 and governed the colony normally until it evacuated in July 1782, a year before the peace.

departures.borders: Georgia's charter claim ran to the Mississippi, and the 1783 treaty gave it away over the heads of the Creek and Choctaw nations who lived there; the Yazoo land frauds of the 1790s grew directly out of that paper claim.

slavery.note: Georgia is the only British colony that banned slavery and then legalised it: prohibited from 1735, permitted from 1 January 1751, and holding about 15,000 enslaved people by 1775.

abolitionDate.note: The trustees' prohibition, repealed by them on 8 August 1750 with effect from 1 January 1751.

emancipationDate.note: Ended by the Thirteenth Amendment to the US Constitution.

populationTransfer.note: The trustees settled Salzburger Protestant refugees, Highland Scots and one of the earliest Jewish communities in North America; the Creek were removed to Indian Territory in the 1830s, long after the empire had gone.

commonwealth.note: The United States has never joined the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: Within twenty-five years of legalising slavery Georgia had become a rice and indigo colony indistinguishable from South Carolina.

peak.populationNote: US Census Bureau Historical Statistics estimate; about 15,000 of Georgia's roughly 33,000 people were enslaved by 1775. It was the smallest and newest of the thirteen colonies.

pedagogy.hook: Georgia banned slavery in 1735 and its own settlers spent sixteen years campaigning for the right to own people. They won in 1751.

misconception.belief: Britain imposed slavery on unwilling colonists and later freed them from it.
misconception.correction: In Georgia the ban came from London and the demand for slavery came from the settlers, who argued they could not compete with South Carolina without it. When the trustees gave way, the enslaved population went from none in 1750 to about 15,000 in twenty-five years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Georgia was designed as an experiment in a colony without slavery and lost, which shows how strong the plantation economy's pull had become by the 1750s.

namesOverTime.name: La Florida
namesOverTime.note: St Augustine, founded in 1565, is the oldest continuously occupied European town in the continental United States.

namesOverTime.name: Florida
namesOverTime.note: Returned to Spain in 1783 and ceded to the United States in 1821; East and West Florida were joined into one territory in 1822.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: Spain got Florida back in 1783 and sold it to the United States under the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819, effective in 1821.

geoCoverage.label: The peninsula, from the St Marys to the Keys
geoCoverage.change: Spain ceded Florida to get Havana back after Britain captured it in 1762; British authority reached little beyond St Augustine and the St Johns River plantations.

acquisitions.how: Spain handed Florida to Britain to buy back Havana, which a British expedition had taken in August 1762 at a cost of thousands of lives, most of them to yellow fever.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Florida, held since 1565. Almost the entire Spanish population of about 3,000, and the Catholic Yamasee and Guale communities with them, evacuated to Cuba rather than live under Protestant rule.

counterparties.name: The Seminole and Creek peoples
counterparties.lost: Nothing immediately, and they gained: the peninsula's Indigenous population had been destroyed by Carolina slave raids after 1700, and Creek migrants moving south into the emptied land became the Seminole. Britain treated with them at Picolata in 1765 for the coastal strip only.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: The same treaty gave Britain Canada and everything east of the Mississippi, and gave France's Louisiana to Spain in compensation.

people.name: James Grant
people.role: first British governor; recruited planters and imported indentured Mediterranean labourers

people.name: Cowkeeper (Ahaya)

statusPeriods.label: The fourteenth colony, loyal to the end
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and council at St Augustine ruled with a Crown salary paid from London, which is exactly why East Florida never had a tax quarrel and never rebelled: its government did not depend on an assembly.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. A general assembly was authorised in 1767 but never met; the province was governed by a nominated council throughout.
statusPeriods.note: East Florida became the refuge for southern loyalists: its free population roughly quadrupled in 1782 as Georgians and Carolinians fled there with the enslaved people they claimed.

departures.how: Britain handed Florida back to Spain in the peace settlement, in exchange for the Bahamas and to end a Spanish siege of Gibraltar, and told the loyalists who had fled there for safety that they had eighteen months to leave.

led.name: Patrick Tonyn

pedagogy.hook: There were fifteen British colonies on the American mainland in 1775, not thirteen. East and West Florida never rebelled — and Britain gave them both to Spain anyway.

misconception.belief: All of Britain's American colonies rebelled in 1775.
misconception.correction: Five did not: East Florida, West Florida, Quebec, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland stayed loyal, and so did the Caribbean islands. The colonies that rebelled were the ones with strong elected assemblies and no need of British troops. Where the governor was paid from London and the garrison was needed, loyalty held.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: East Florida shows what the thirteen colonies had in common — self-government and security — and shows that the empire treated even loyal colonies as bargaining counters at the peace table.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: The Gulf coast from the Mississippi to the Apalachicola is now Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and the Florida panhandle.

geoCoverage.label: Pensacola, Mobile and the Natchez district
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the Gulf coast between the Mississippi and the Apalachicola from France and Spain at once, and moved the northern boundary up to 32 degrees 28 minutes in 1764 to take in the Natchez bluffs.

acquisitions.how: France gave up Mobile and Spain gave up Pensacola in the same treaty, so Britain took a 900-kilometre stretch of Gulf coast with two small garrison towns and almost no settlers.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Mobile and the Gulf coast east of the Mississippi, held since 1702. The rest of Louisiana went secretly to Spain rather than to Britain.

counterparties.name: Spain
counterparties.lost: Pensacola, in the same bargain that bought back Havana.

counterparties.name: The Choctaw, Chickasaw and Creek nations
counterparties.lost: Very little in 1763 and a great deal by 1783: at Mobile in 1765 and Pensacola in 1765 and 1771 they ceded coastal districts, but the interior remained theirs, and British West Florida existed only on their sufferance.

people.name: George Johnstone

people.name: John Stuart

statusPeriods.label: The fifteenth colony: garrisons, planters and Indigenous power
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor at Pensacola with a Crown salary and a small garrison governed a strip of coast; twenty kilometres inland, the Choctaw, Chickasaw and Creek governed themselves and Britain paid them presents to keep the peace.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Formally a crown colony with a governor, council and, from 1766, an elected assembly at Pensacola; in practice British authority extended only as far as the garrisons and the river plantations.
statusPeriods.franchise: A small assembly of Protestant freeholders met from 1766. Most of the province's inhabitants were Choctaw, Chickasaw or Creek and were not subjects at all.

statusPeriods.label: Conquered by Spain
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Bernardo de Galvez took Baton Rouge and Natchez in 1779, Mobile in 1780 and Pensacola after a two-month siege in May 1781; Britain never got the province back.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Under Spanish military occupation from May 1781. Britain retained a paper claim only until the peace treaty confirmed the loss.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Havana and New Orleans, under Spain

departures.how: West Florida is the one British colony in the Americas that Spain simply took: Galvez besieged Pensacola with 7,000 men and the garrison of about 1,100 surrendered on 9 May 1781, two years before the treaty made it official.

consequences.economicLegacy: West Florida's real business was the deerskin trade with the Choctaw and Chickasaw, run out of Mobile by firms that outlasted three flags.

pedagogy.hook: Spain conquered a British colony during the American Revolution. West Florida fell to Bernardo de Galvez two years before the peace treaty, and Britain never got it back.

misconception.belief: The American Revolution was a war between Britain and its colonists.
misconception.correction: It became a world war. France joined in 1778, Spain in 1779 and the Dutch Republic in 1780; fighting ran from the Gulf of Mexico to Gibraltar to southern India. Britain lost West Florida to Spain and Menorca to a Franco-Spanish force, and nearly lost Jamaica.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: West Florida shows the limits of colonial power: twenty kilometres from the coast, the Choctaw and Chickasaw were sovereign, and Britain paid them to stay friendly rather than trying to rule them.
