acquisitions.resistance: Pontiac's War of 1763-66: a coalition of nations took eight of the twelve British forts west of the Appalachians in a summer, and Britain answered with the Proclamation because it could not answer with an army.

contested.note: Historians disagree about the Proclamation's purpose. Some read it as genuine protection of Indigenous land after Pontiac's War; others as a device to control the pace of settlement, keep colonists near the coast where they could be taxed and governed, and reserve the profits of land purchase to the Crown. Both motives appear in the ministers' own correspondence.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The Scratch of a Pen: 1763 and the Transformation of North America
evidence.supports: The Proclamation, Pontiac's War and what 1763 meant to Indigenous nations.

statusPeriods.label: Indian Country under Crown protection
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Two Superintendents of Indian Affairs, not governors, handled relations with the nations; British authority ran only inside a handful of forts, and the Crown's own soldiers could not stop settlers crossing the line.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British sovereignty was asserted and Indigenous land rights were recognised; on the ground the nations governed themselves and Britain negotiated with them as powers, so the label describes a legal relationship rather than an administration.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Johnson Hall in New York for the northern district and Charleston for the southern
statusPeriods.franchise: The reserve had no colonial government and no electorate. Its people were subjects of their own nations, not of the Crown.
statusPeriods.note: The Fort Stanwix treaty of 1768 and the Hard Labour and Lochaber treaties moved the line west, opening Kentucky to settlers over Shawnee objections that the Haudenosaunee had sold land that was not theirs.

departures.how: Britain gave the whole reserve to the United States in the peace treaty without informing, consulting or compensating a single one of the nations who lived in it, and who had not been defeated.

becomes.name: United States territory west of the Appalachians

led.name: Thayendanegea (Joseph Brant)
led.role: Mohawk leader who organised the Western Confederacy to resist American expansion after Britain abandoned it

led.name: Alexander McGillivray
led.role: Creek leader who turned to Spain for arms once Britain had gone

led.name: Richard Oswald
led.role: British negotiator at Paris, a former slave trader, who conceded the western boundary

cost.note: No one died at the signing. The consequences were the Northwest Indian War of 1785-95, in which the Western Confederacy destroyed an American army at the Wabash on 4 November 1791, killing about 630 soldiers, before losing at Fallen Timbers in 1794; then the removals of the 1830s.

departures.borders: The 1783 line ran from the St Croix to the Mississippi through country Britain did not control and had promised to protect. Britain kept its western forts on American soil until 1796 as a hedge, and armed its former allies from them.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: Article 2 drew the boundary. No article mentioned the Indigenous nations who lived inside it.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The American Revolution in Indian Country: Crisis and Diversity in Native American Communities
evidence.supports: The abandonment of Britain's Indigenous allies in 1783 and its consequences.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Proclamation line failed in the United States and survived in Canada: it is the legal root of Aboriginal title there, cited in the Constitution Act 1982 and in Supreme Court judgments to this day.

violence.note: Pontiac's War killed perhaps 400 British soldiers and 2,000 settlers, and an unknown but large number of Indigenous people; at Fort Pitt in June 1763 officers gave besieging Lenape emissaries blankets from a smallpox hospital, and Amherst approved the idea in writing.

populationTransfer.note: Settlers crossed the line in tens of thousands regardless of the law; Kentucky alone had about 73,000 non-Indigenous inhabitants by 1790, seven years after the reserve was signed away.

commonwealth.note: The land is in the United States, which has never been a Commonwealth member.

peak.populationNote: No reliable population figure exists. Estimates for the Indigenous population of the trans-Appalachian region in the 1760s range widely; contemporary British returns counted warriors, not people, and were guesses.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The Scratch of a Pen: 1763 and the Transformation of North America
evidence.supports: The 1763 settlement, the Proclamation and its meaning for Indigenous nations.

evidence.author: Gregory Evans Dowd
evidence.work: War under Heaven: Pontiac, the Indian Nations, and the British Empire
evidence.supports: Pontiac's War, Amherst's policy and the smallpox blankets at Fort Pitt.

evidence.author: Richard White
evidence.work: The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650-1815
evidence.supports: How British authority in the interior depended on negotiation rather than force.

contested.note: Whether the Indian Reserve should count as British territory at all is a real question. Britain claimed sovereignty and recognised Indigenous land rights inside it; the nations concerned governed themselves and did not consider themselves subjects. This atlas draws it as British-claimed and shades it as a protectorate, and says so.

pedagogy.hook: In 1763 George III promised the nations west of the Appalachians that their land was theirs and settlers must stay out. In 1783 he signed the same land over to the United States without telling them.

misconception.belief: Britain simply took Indigenous land in North America by force.
misconception.correction: It was more tangled than that. The Crown recognised Indigenous land rights in law from 1763, required that only the Crown could buy land, and used treaties for two centuries. It also broke the line whenever settlers pushed hard enough, and abandoned its allies wholesale in 1783. Legal recognition and dispossession happened at the same time, in the same documents.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Proclamation is the reason American colonists were furious in 1763 and the reason Indigenous title exists in Canadian law today. One document, two opposite legacies.

keyDates.what: Pontiac's forces begin the siege of Detroit
The Royal Proclamation closes the west to settlers
Treaty of Fort Stanwix moves the line west, opening Kentucky
The Quebec Act attaches the Ohio country to Quebec
Britain cedes the reserve to the United States

from.note: Named for the Spanish navigator Juan de Bermudez, who sighted but did not settle it; the exact year is uncertain.

namesOverTime.name: The Somers Isles
namesOverTime.note: For Admiral George Somers, whose shipwreck put the English there. The name survives in the Corporation of Hamilton's older documents.

namesOverTime.name: Bermuda
namesOverTime.note: The Crown annulled the Somers Isles Company's charter in 1684 and took the colony over. Both names stayed in the statute book — the formal title is still 'Bermuda, or the Somers Islands' — but Bermuda is the name on every chart and passport since.

geoCoverage.label: The whole archipelago
geoCoverage.change: About 150 people wrecked on an uninhabited island chain 1,000 kilometres from the nearest land and stayed.

acquisitions.how: The Sea Venture, carrying supplies and a governor to starving Jamestown, was driven onto Bermuda's reefs in a hurricane; the 150 survivors spent ten months building two new ships from cedar, and England claimed the islands they had left behind.

counterparties.name: No resident population
counterparties.lost: Nothing: Bermuda had no human inhabitants when the Sea Venture struck. Spanish and Portuguese ships had known the islands for a century and avoided them because of the reefs, and no archaeological evidence of earlier settlement has been found.
counterparties.note: Bermuda is the rare case where 'uninhabited' is simply true. The cahow petrel and the Bermuda cedar paid for it instead: the birds were eaten almost to extinction within two decades.

instrument.name: Third Virginia Charter
instrument.note: Extended the Virginia Company's grant to take in Bermuda; the Somers Isles Company took over in 1615.

people.name: George Somers
people.role: admiral of the Sea Venture; returned to Bermuda in 1610 and died there

people.name: William Strachey
people.role: wrote an account of the wreck that is widely thought to have reached Shakespeare and shaped The Tempest

evidence.author: Michael J. Jarvis
evidence.work: In the Eye of All Trade: Bermuda, Bermudians, and the Maritime Atlantic World, 1680-1783
evidence.supports: Bermuda's settlement and its maritime economy.

statusPeriods.label: The Somers Isles Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London company owned the islands, divided them into what it called 'tribes' — the nine share-divisions that are Bermuda's parishes today — and into shares, appointed the governor and forbade islanders to build ships, which is exactly what they did anyway.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St George's, under the Somers Isles Company in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Landholding white men. The House of Assembly first met on 1 August 1620 and has met ever since, making it the oldest continuously sitting legislature outside the British Isles.
statusPeriods.note: The company's charter was revoked by writ of scire facias in 1684 after decades of complaints from islanders who wanted to trade freely.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony with an elected assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor appointed in London worked with an assembly elected by Bermudian property holders, a small, white, intermarried group of merchant families who ran the islands for nearly three centuries.
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise that excluded almost all Black Bermudians, who were the majority of the population from about 1700. Universal adult suffrage came only in 1968, and the vote was tied to property until 1963.

statusPeriods.label: Self-governing British Overseas Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Bermudians elect a Parliament and a Premier who run everything except defence, external affairs, internal security and the police, which the UK-appointed Governor keeps.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage since the 1968 constitution; the voting age fell to 18 in 1989.
statusPeriods.note: Bermudians voted against independence by 73 per cent to 26 per cent in a referendum on 16 August 1995, on a turnout of 58 per cent.

departures.how: Bermuda has been continuously British since 1609 and voted to stay so in 1995: it is the oldest surviving British overseas territory and the empire's longest unbroken possession.
departures.movement: The franchise campaign: the Bermuda Workers' Association, the 1959 Theatre Boycott and the Progressive Group

led.name: Mary Prince
led.role: born enslaved at Brackish Pond in Devonshire Parish; her History of Mary Prince (1831) was the first account of a Black woman's life published in Britain and was read into the parliamentary abolition campaign

led.name: Sarah Bassett
led.role: enslaved Bermudian woman burned at the stake at Crow Lane on 6 June 1730 for attempting to poison the family that held her; a statue of her stands outside the Cabinet Building in Hamilton

led.name: Edgar Fitzgerald Gordon
led.role: doctor who led the Bermuda Workers' Association and carried its petition for universal adult suffrage to London in 1946

stillBritish.note: Bermuda is a self-governing British Overseas Territory whose people rejected independence in a 1995 referendum by roughly three to one.

slavery.note: Bermuda's enslaved people were sailors, pilots, shipwrights and salt rakers rather than field hands: by 1774 about 40 per cent of Bermudian merchant seamen were enslaved Black men who sailed the Atlantic and came back because their families were hostages.

emancipationDate.note: Bermuda, like Antigua, freed its roughly 4,000 enslaved people outright in 1834 instead of imposing the four-year apprenticeship used elsewhere.

toll.note: Number freed in Bermuda on 1 August 1834, from the compensation commissioners' returns. Bermuda imported few Africans directly; its enslaved population grew mostly by birth and by transfers from other colonies.

warrant.author: The Slave Compensation Commission, in its returns for Bermuda
warrant.work: Returns of the Slave Compensation Commission
warrant.supports: Number freed in Bermuda on 1 August 1834, from the compensation commissioners' returns. Bermuda imported few Africans directly; its enslaved population grew mostly by birth and by transfers from other colonies.
warrant.check: T 71 at The National Archives, Kew, indexed award by award in the Legacies of British Slavery database at ucl.ac.uk/lbs.
warrant.note: The most exact count of enslaved people in this atlas is the one made to pay their owners.

populationTransfer.note: Bermuda was a place people were sent: Scottish and Irish prisoners under Cromwell, enslaved Africans, Indigenous captives from King Philip's War, and about 9,000 British convicts held in prison hulks at Ireland Island between 1824 and 1863.

retainedTerritory.note: Bermuda is still British, one of fourteen overseas territories, and its dockyard was a Royal Navy base from 1809 until 1995.

commonwealth.note: As a British territory rather than a state, Bermuda is not a separate Commonwealth member, though it competes separately at the Commonwealth Games.

consequences.economicLegacy: Salt from Turks Islands, then privateering, then shipbuilding in Bermuda cedar, then tourism, then insurance and reinsurance: an island of 54 square kilometres with one of the highest incomes per head in the world.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, a Parliament sitting since 1620, and a governor who still opens it in a plumed hat.

peak.populationNote: 2016 census. In 1774 the islands held about 11,000 people, over half of them enslaved.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Bermuda’s largest recorded population: 64,055 people, counted in 2016.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Michael J. Jarvis
evidence.work: In the Eye of All Trade: Bermuda, Bermudians, and the Maritime Atlantic World, 1680-1783
evidence.supports: The maritime economy, enslaved sailors and Bermuda's Atlantic role.

evidence.author: Virginia Bernhard
evidence.work: Slaves and Slaveholders in Bermuda, 1616-1782
evidence.supports: The distinctive character of Bermudian slavery.

pedagogy.hook: Bermuda has been British without a break since a hurricane wrecked a ship on its reefs in 1609 — longer than Scotland has been in a union with England.

misconception.belief: The empire ended in the twentieth century.
misconception.correction: Fourteen British Overseas Territories remain, and Bermuda is the oldest. In 1995 Bermudians voted 73 per cent to 26 per cent against independence. Some of the empire ended because Britain was pushed out; some of it stayed because the people in it chose to.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Bermuda is the empire's living exhibit: a parliament sitting since 1620, a slave system built on ships rather than fields, a naval dockyard, and a population that voted to remain British in living memory.

keyDates.what: The Sea Venture wrecks; the survivors stay
The House of Assembly meets for the first time
About 4,000 enslaved Bermudians freed outright, with no apprenticeship
New constitution and universal adult suffrage
Bermudians vote against independence, 73 to 26 per cent

namesOverTime.name: Ktaqmkuk

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact period. Mi'kmaq presence on the island is long-standing; the Beothuk were its other people.

namesOverTime.note: 'Land across the water'.

namesOverTime.name: Terra Nova / Newfoundland
namesOverTime.note: John Cabot, sailing from Bristol for Henry VII, made landfall somewhere on the island or nearby in June 1497. The exact place is unknown.

namesOverTime.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
namesOverTime.note: The province was renamed by constitutional amendment in 2001 to put Labrador, two and a half times its size, into the name.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Newfoundland and Labrador is Canada's tenth and last province.

geoCoverage.label: The island, and Labrador after 1809
geoCoverage.change: A claim made over an existing international fishery. France kept treaty rights to fish and dry on the French Shore until 1904, and the Labrador boundary with Quebec was not settled until 1927.

acquisitions.how: Humphrey Gilbert sailed into St John's harbour, where thirty-six fishing ships of four nations were already at anchor, read out letters patent claiming the place for Elizabeth I, and drowned on the voyage home.

counterparties.name: The Beothuk
counterparties.lost: Everything. Pushed off the coast and away from the sea resources they depended on, cut off from iron and hunted by settlers and by Mi'kmaq armed by the French, the Beothuk were extinct as a people by 1829, when Shanawdithit died in St John's.
counterparties.note: Whether to call this a genocide is debated by historians; that a distinct people ceased to exist under British colonisation is not.

counterparties.name: The Mi'kmaq and the Innu
counterparties.lost: Access to coastal camps and, in Labrador, to the fur trade on their own terms; both peoples remain in Newfoundland and Labrador today.

counterparties.name: France, Spain, Portugal and the Basque country
counterparties.lost: Free use of a fishery all four had worked since about 1500. The Basque whaling station at Red Bay in Labrador predates Gilbert's claim by fifty years.

instrument.name: Letters patent to Sir Humphrey Gilbert
instrument.note: The patent authorised him to claim lands 'not actually possessed of any Christian prince', which is how the fishermen already there were reasoned away.

people.name: Humphrey Gilbert
people.role: made the claim at St John's and was lost at sea weeks later

people.name: Shanawdithit
people.role: the last known Beothuk; her drawings and vocabulary are almost all that survives of her people's own record

contested.note: Newfoundland's founding date is genuinely disputed. Candidates are 1497 (Cabot's landfall), 1583 (Gilbert's claim, which established nothing permanent), 1610 (John Guy's colony at Cupids, the first attempt to overwinter) and 1713 (Utrecht, when Britain's title became exclusive). This atlas uses 1583 for the claim and shows the others as key dates.

acquisitions.how: John Guy landed thirty-nine colonists at Cuper's Cove, now Cupids, for the London and Bristol Company, the first attempt to keep English people on the island through a winter rather than only through a fishing season.

counterparties.name: The Beothuk
counterparties.lost: The inner reaches of Conception Bay. Guy met and traded peacefully with Beothuk people in 1612; it was almost the last friendly contact recorded.

instrument.name: Charter of the London and Bristol Company for the Colonization of Newfoundland

people.name: John Guy
people.role: Bristol merchant and first governor of the Cupids colony

acquisitions.how: France gave up Placentia and its claim to the island at Utrecht, keeping only the right to fish and dry catch along a stretch of coast that Newfoundlanders spent the next 191 years calling the French Shore and resenting.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Plaisance, its fortified base since 1662, and sovereignty over the island. French fishing rights on the north and west coasts survived until the Entente Cordiale of 1904 abolished them.

instrument.name: Treaty of Utrecht
instrument.note: The same treaty gave Britain Acadia, Hudson Bay and the Asiento contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America.

statusPeriods.label: Rule of the fishing admirals
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For nearly 150 years the island had no governor at all: the first ship's captain into each harbour each spring became its admiral for the season and settled disputes, and London actively discouraged permanent settlement to protect the migratory fishery.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain claimed sovereignty but provided no civil government whatever; the fishing admirals were merchants exercising customary authority, not Crown officers.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: nowhere; the West Country merchant ports of Dartmouth, Poole and Bristol set policy
statusPeriods.franchise: None. There was no government to elect.

statusPeriods.label: Naval governors, summer only
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A naval officer was commissioned as governor each year and sailed home with the fleet in the autumn, leaving the island without a government for six months of every year until a resident governor was appointed in 1817.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Newfoundland had no assembly, and building a permanent house was technically illegal into the eighteenth century.

statusPeriods.label: An assembly at last
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After a campaign led by the physician William Carson and the merchant Patrick Morris, Newfoundland got an elected House of Assembly, though the governor and his council could still block it.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male householders. Elections in the 1830s and 1860s were fought partly along Irish Catholic and English Protestant lines and were sometimes violent.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ministers responsible to the elected assembly ran the colony's internal affairs; in 1869 Newfoundlanders voted decisively against joining the new Dominion of Canada.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male householders and, from 1925, women over 25.

statusPeriods.label: Dominion of Newfoundland
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Newfoundland became a self-governing dominion alongside Canada, Australia and New Zealand, with its own prime minister, its own regiment in the First World War and its own crushing war debt.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal male suffrage; women over 25 gained the vote in 1925.
statusPeriods.note: On 1 July 1916 at Beaumont-Hamel the Newfoundland Regiment went over the top with about 800 men; the next morning 68 answered the roll call. The island of 240,000 people never recovered financially or demographically.

statusPeriods.label: Commission of Government: self-rule given up
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Bankrupt and unable to service a war and railway debt of about $100 million, Newfoundland's own legislature voted itself out of existence and asked Britain to govern it through a commission of six appointed men and the governor.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: St John's, under the Dominions Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None. A self-governing dominion of a quarter of a million people had no elections for fifteen years.
statusPeriods.note: This is unique in the empire's history: nowhere else did a dominion voluntarily surrender responsible government.

departures.how: After two referendums in 1948, the second of which chose Canada over a return to responsible government by 78,323 votes to 71,334, Newfoundland joined Canada at midnight on 31 March 1949 and stopped being a British territory.

becomes.name: Province of Newfoundland, in Canada

led.name: Joseph Smallwood
led.role: broadcaster and pig farmer who led the confederation campaign and became the province's first premier for twenty-three years

led.name: Peter Cashin
led.role: led the responsible-government campaign and called confederation a British-Canadian stitch-up

led.name: Clement Attlee
led.role: British prime minister whose government wanted Newfoundland's debt and defence costs off its books

cost.note: Nobody died. The cost was measured in bitterness: the vote was 52.3 per cent to 47.7 per cent, Catholic districts voted heavily against, and Newfoundlanders were still arguing about whether the ballot was fair fifty years later.

departures.borders: The border did move, in 1927: the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London gave Newfoundland a Labrador four times larger than Quebec had expected, drawing the line at the height of land. Quebec has never formally accepted it and Quebec government maps still show it as undefined.

instrument.name: British North America Act 1949 (Newfoundland Act)
instrument.note: Royal assent 23 March 1949; union took effect at midnight on 31 March.

contested.note: Whether the 1948 referendums were fairly run is still argued in Newfoundland. Critics point to the exclusion of responsible government from the first ballot's likely winner, British and Canadian officials' open preference for confederation, and the narrowness of the second result; historians who have worked the archives generally find pressure and partiality but no rigged count.

evidence.author: Peter Neary
evidence.work: Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1929-1949
evidence.supports: The Commission of Government, the referendums and the terms of union.

violence.note: The Beothuk were driven from the coast, cut off from food and hunted; Shanawdithit, the last known member of the people, died of tuberculosis in St John's in 1829.

populationTransfer.note: Migrant fishermen from Devon, Dorset and southern Ireland became a settled population against London's own policy; between 1954 and 1975 the province resettled about 30,000 people from some 300 outport communities into larger centres.

commonwealth.note: Newfoundland was a dominion in its own right until 1934 and is now part of Canada, which is a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1927 Privy Council line between Labrador and Quebec is still shown as undefined on Quebec government maps.
consequences.economicLegacy: Four centuries of cod ended on 2 July 1992, when Canada closed the northern cod fishery and about 30,000 people lost their work in a single announcement.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Newfoundland English preserves West Country and Irish speech patterns that have died out where they came from.

peak.populationNote: 1945 census of Newfoundland and Labrador, the last before confederation.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Newfoundland’s largest recorded population: 321,819 people, counted in 1945.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Sean T. Cadigan
evidence.work: Newfoundland and Labrador: A History
evidence.supports: The fishery, settlement, the Beothuk and the road to confederation.

evidence.author: Jerry Bannister
evidence.work: The Rule of the Admirals: Law, Custom, and Naval Government in Newfoundland, 1699-1832
evidence.supports: Government by fishing admirals and naval governors.

evidence.author: Peter Neary
evidence.work: Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1929-1949
evidence.supports: Bankruptcy, the Commission of Government and confederation.

contested.note: Newfoundland's founding date, the fairness of the 1948 referendums, and whether the destruction of the Beothuk should be called genocide are all live arguments. All three are shown here rather than resolved.

pedagogy.hook: In 1934 Newfoundland gave up democracy. Bankrupt, it voted its own parliament out of existence and asked Britain to send six commissioners to rule it — the only dominion ever to hand self-government back.

misconception.belief: Colonies always wanted more self-government and eventually got it.
misconception.correction: Newfoundland went the other way. It became a dominion in 1907, was ruined by war debt and the Depression, and in 1934 its own legislature voted to abolish itself. Fifteen years of unelected commission rule followed, and the island then chose Canada over getting its parliament back, by 52 per cent to 48.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Newfoundland breaks the tidy story of colonies marching towards independence, and it shows how debt, not armies, decided the fate of small states inside the empire.

Utrecht: France gives up the island, keeps fishing rights
Shanawdithit, the last known Beothuk, dies in St John's
Beaumont-Hamel: the Newfoundland Regiment is destroyed in a morning

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact period. Mi'kma'ki is the Mi'kmaq name for their territory, divided into seven districts, and it is still used.

namesOverTime.name: Acadie
namesOverTime.note: A French colony from 1604, whose farmers built dyked marshland farms around the Bay of Fundy and called themselves Acadians.

namesOverTime.name: Nova Scotia
namesOverTime.note: 'New Scotland', from a Scottish charter granted eighty-nine years before Britain actually held the place.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: One of the four founding provinces of the Dominion of Canada.

geoCoverage.label: Sir William Alexander's New Scotland
geoCoverage.change: James VI and I granted a Scottish courtier the whole of Acadia while France was living in it; a small Scottish colony at Port Royal lasted three years.

geoCoverage.label: Cromwell's Acadia
geoCoverage.change: Robert Sedgwick took the French forts for the Commonwealth in peacetime; Charles II handed them back at Breda thirteen years later.

geoCoverage.label: The peninsula, and a disputed mainland
geoCoverage.change: Port Royal fell in 1710 and Utrecht ceded Acadia 'with its ancient limits' in 1713; Britain said that meant the mainland too, France said it meant the peninsula only, and the argument was settled by war.

geoCoverage.label: With Cape Breton and St John's Island
geoCoverage.change: Louisbourg fell on 26 July 1758 and Ile Royale and Ile Saint-Jean were occupied at once; the Royal Proclamation formally annexed them to Nova Scotia on 7 October 1763.

geoCoverage.label: Without St John's Island
geoCoverage.change: St John's Island was made a separate colony so that its absentee landlords in London could deal with a government of their own.

geoCoverage.label: The peninsula and Cape Breton
geoCoverage.change: Fourteen thousand loyalist refugees forced a reorganisation: New Brunswick and Cape Breton became separate colonies, and Cape Breton was reannexed to Nova Scotia in 1820.

acquisitions.how: James VI and I granted Sir William Alexander a charter over the whole of Acadia, and to pay for it invented the baronets of Nova Scotia, who bought a hereditary title and a paper estate in a country France was already farming.

counterparties.name: The Mi'kmaq nation
counterparties.lost: Nothing that they recognised. The Mi'kmaq had been allied and intermarried with the French since 1610, had a Catholic concordat, and never ceded their territory; their treaties with Britain from 1725 to 1779 are peace and friendship treaties, not land surrenders, and Canadian courts have upheld the rights in them.

counterparties.name: France and the Acadians
counterparties.lost: On paper, everything; in practice, nothing for another eighty-nine years. The Scottish colony at Port Royal was returned to France in 1632.

instrument.name: Charter of Nova Scotia to Sir William Alexander

people.name: William Alexander, Earl of Stirling
people.role: Scottish poet and courtier who was granted Acadia and lost it by treaty

acquisitions.how: A New England force of about 3,500 men under Francis Nicholson besieged Port Royal for a week; the garrison of 300 surrendered, the town was renamed Annapolis Royal, and Utrecht made the conquest permanent in 1713.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Acadia, ceded at Utrecht in 1713 along with Newfoundland and Hudson Bay. France kept Ile Royale and Ile Saint-Jean and built Louisbourg to compensate.

counterparties.name: The Acadians
counterparties.lost: Their French government, and then, in 1755, their homes. About 2,500 farming people became British subjects overnight and spent forty-five years refusing to swear an unqualified oath that would have obliged them to fight their Mi'kmaq neighbours and French kin.

counterparties.name: The Mi'kmaq nation
counterparties.lost: Their principal European ally. The Mi'kmaq fought Britain in six wars between 1722 and 1761 and were never conquered; the wars ended in treaties, not surrenders.

instrument.name: Treaty of Utrecht
instrument.note: Ceded 'all Nova Scotia or Acadia with its ancient boundaries'. Neither side agreed what those boundaries were, and the ambiguity produced two more wars.

people.name: Francis Nicholson
people.role: commanded the 1710 expedition and became governor

people.name: Daniel d'Auger de Subercase
people.role: French governor who surrendered Port Royal with 300 men against 3,500

acquisitions.resistance: The Mi'kmaq and Wabanaki fought on for fifty years. Britain's answer included the Halifax scalping proclamation of 1749, which offered a bounty for Mi'kmaq scalps, including those of women and children.

evidence.author: Geoffrey Plank
evidence.work: An Unsettled Conquest: The British Campaign Against the Peoples of Acadia
evidence.supports: The conquest of 1710, Mi'kmaq resistance and British policy towards the Acadians.

acquisitions.how: Amherst and Boscawen took Louisbourg after a seven-week siege with 14,000 men and 150 ships, opening the St Lawrence to the fleet that would take Quebec the next year, and Britain then blew the fortress up.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Ile Royale and Ile Saint-Jean, the last French footholds in the Maritimes, confirmed to Britain at Paris in 1763.

counterparties.name: The Acadians of Ile Saint-Jean and Ile Royale
counterparties.lost: Their homes and, for many, their lives. About 3,100 Acadians were deported from Ile Saint-Jean in the autumn of 1758; roughly 1,600 of them drowned when the transports Duke William and Violet went down in the Atlantic in December.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: France kept only the tiny islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, which are French to this day.

cost.note: Deaths among Acadians deported from Ile Saint-Jean in 1758, chiefly by shipwreck and disease at sea. The figure comes from ships' returns and is close to half of those embarked.

warrant.note: Close to half of those embarked did not arrive. The returns count both ends of the voyage, which is how that is known.

statusPeriods.label: Alexander's Scottish grant
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Scottish courtier held the charter and sold baronetcies to finance a colony of about seventy people at Port Royal, which Charles I traded away for his queen's unpaid dowry.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Royal, under the proprietor in Scotland

statusPeriods.label: Commonwealth occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Cromwell's expedition held the Acadian forts under military command for thirteen years while the Acadian farmers were left alone to farm.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Acadia was French between 1632 and 1654, and again between 1667 and 1710. Those years are not British and are deliberately left blank.

statusPeriods.label: A garrison colony with a French-speaking majority
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For forty years a governor and a few hundred soldiers at Annapolis Royal ruled a country of about 10,000 Acadian farmers and a Mi'kmaq nation that had never surrendered; officials called the Acadians the French Neutrals and did not trust them.
statusPeriods.franchise: None, and the exclusion was deliberate: Catholics could not vote or hold office under British law, and the population was almost entirely Catholic.
statusPeriods.note: Halifax was founded in 1749 with 2,500 settlers as a military counterweight to Louisbourg. The Mi'kmaq treated it as a treaty violation and war resumed.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Acadia was returned to France at Breda in 1667 and was French again until Port Royal fell in 1710. Those forty-three years are not British and are left blank.

statusPeriods.label: The first elected assembly in Canada
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nova Scotia's House of Assembly first met at Halifax on 2 October 1758, three years after the government it now advised had deported the majority of the province's people; the governor still ran the executive.
statusPeriods.franchise: Protestant male freeholders. Catholics were barred from voting until 1789 and from sitting until 1830; the first Black Nova Scotians to vote did so on the same property basis, and few could meet it.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government, first in the empire
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: On 2 February 1848 the governor called a ministry that commanded a majority in the elected assembly and resigned the executive to it: the first responsible government anywhere in the British Empire outside the British Isles, and it was achieved without a shot.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders; the property test was widened in 1854 and briefly abolished, then restored.
statusPeriods.note: Joseph Howe campaigned for it for a decade after winning an 1835 libel trial for attacking the Halifax magistrates in his newspaper.

departures.how: Nova Scotia stopped being a separate British colony at midnight on 30 June 1867 and became a province of the new Dominion of Canada. British sovereignty did not end that night; the colony did.

becomes.name: Province of Nova Scotia, in the Dominion of Canada

led.name: Charles Tupper
led.role: premier who took Nova Scotia into Confederation without an election on the question

led.name: Joseph Howe
led.role: won responsible government, then led the Anti-Confederation campaign that took 18 of 19 federal seats in September 1867

departures.movement: Anti-Confederation League, which won and lost anyway

cost.note: No one died. The cost was consent: Nova Scotians were never asked, and at the first federal election in September 1867 they returned eighteen anti-Confederates out of nineteen seats and a repeal majority in their own legislature. Britain refused to undo the union.

departures.borders: No borders moved. What moved was authority: from a colonial legislature at Halifax that London dealt with directly, to a federal parliament at Ottawa that Halifax could be outvoted in.

instrument.name: British North America Act 1867
instrument.note: Royal assent 29 March 1867; the union took effect on 1 July.

contested.note: Calling 1867 a departure is a modelling choice, and this atlas makes it openly. Nova Scotia did not leave the British Empire in 1867; it stopped existing as a separate British colony and became part of a self-governing dominion that was still British. The end of British sovereignty over Nova Scotia is told in the Canada record, and it happened in stages between 1867 and 1982.

populationTransfer.note: Nova Scotia was made and remade by forced and sponsored migration: about 10,000 Acadians deported from 1755, some 8,000 New England Planters settled on their farms, 14,000 loyalists in 1783 including 3,000 Black Loyalists, and 2,000 Jamaican Maroons deported here in 1796.

toll.note: Acadians deported between 1755 and 1764 from Nova Scotia, Ile Saint-Jean and Ile Royale. Roughly a third died of disease, shipwreck and exposure. The range comes from parish and shipping records, which are incomplete.

warrant.supports: Acadians deported between 1755 and 1764 from Nova Scotia, Ile Saint-Jean and Ile Royale. Roughly a third died of disease, shipwreck and exposure. The range comes from parish and shipping records, which are incomplete.

violence.note: The deportation of the Acadians in 1755, ordered by Governor Charles Lawrence without instructions from London, burned about 6,000 people out of their farms; the 1749 Halifax proclamation offered a cash bounty for Mi'kmaq scalps.

slavery.note: Loyalist owners brought about 1,200 enslaved people to Nova Scotia in 1783, alongside 3,000 free Black Loyalists whose promised land was smaller, worse and slower to arrive; 1,196 of them left for Sierra Leone in January 1792.

emancipationDate.note: Slavery in Nova Scotia had already been eroded by judges who demanded proof of ownership that owners could rarely produce; the Abolition Act ended it formally.

commonwealth.note: Nova Scotia is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.economicLegacy: Halifax was the Royal Navy's North American base from 1758 to 1905 and the convoy assembly port in both world wars; on 6 December 1917 a collision in the harbour killed about 1,950 people in the largest accidental explosion before the atomic bomb.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Acadian French survives in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Louisiana, where deportees became Cajuns; the Mi'kmaq peace and friendship treaties of 1725-1779 are enforceable law in Canada today.

populationWarrant.supports: Nova Scotia’s largest recorded population: 330,857 people, counted in 1861.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.

evidence.supports: The deportation of 1755-64, its planning and its human cost.

evidence.supports: British policy towards the Acadians and the Mi'kmaq wars.

evidence.author: Simon Schama
evidence.work: Rough Crossings: Britain, the Slaves and the American Revolution
evidence.supports: The Black Loyalists in Nova Scotia and the 1792 migration to Sierra Leone.

pedagogy.hook: In 1755 Britain deported about 10,000 of its own subjects from Nova Scotia because they would not swear an unconditional oath. Roughly a third died at sea or in the camps.

misconception.belief: Ethnic cleansing is something that happened in other empires, or in the twentieth century.
misconception.correction: Governor Charles Lawrence and the Nova Scotia council decided in July 1755 to remove the entire Acadian population, burn their farms and scatter them among colonies that did not want them. About 10,000 people were deported over nine years and roughly a third died. Britain's own historians have called it a deportation for two centuries; the Canadian Crown apologised in 2003.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nova Scotia holds two firsts and one atrocity: the first elected assembly in Canada, the first responsible government in the empire, and the deportation of the Acadians. All three came from the same government within a hundred years.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: A founding province of Canada, and its only officially bilingual one.

geoCoverage.label: The Saint John and Miramichi valleys
geoCoverage.change: Carved out of Nova Scotia to give 14,000 loyalist refugees a government of their own, on Wolastoqiyik and Mi'kmaq land that was never ceded.

acquisitions.how: The Colonial Office split the northern half of Nova Scotia into a new province because about 14,000 loyalist refugees had landed at the mouth of the Saint John River in 1783 and demanded land, offices and a legislature of their own.

counterparties.name: The Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet) and Mi'kmaq nations
counterparties.lost: The river valleys that fed them. The loyalist surveys cut up the Saint John River lands their families had farmed and fished for centuries; their peace and friendship treaties of 1725-1779 had ceded no land, and no land-cession treaty was ever signed in New Brunswick.
counterparties.note: That absence still matters: New Brunswick, like most of the Maritimes, sits on unceded territory, and Canadian courts have repeatedly enforced the eighteenth-century treaty rights, most famously in the Marshall decision of 1999.

counterparties.name: The Acadians
counterparties.lost: The best land a second time. Acadian families who had escaped the deportation and returned to the Saint John and Petitcodiac valleys were moved on again to make room for loyalists, and settled the north and east shores where their descendants still form a third of the province.

instrument.name: Commission and instructions to Thomas Carleton as Governor of New Brunswick

people.name: Thomas Carleton
people.role: first governor; brother of Guy Carleton and in office for thirty-three years

people.name: Pierre Tomah
people.role: Wolastoqiyik chief who negotiated with the incoming British authorities over the Saint John lands

evidence.author: Ann Gorman Condon
evidence.work: The Envy of the American States: The Loyalist Dream for New Brunswick
evidence.supports: The loyalist founding of the province and the plans of its elite.

statusPeriods.label: The loyalist province
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and an appointed council drawn from loyalist officers ran the province and the timber licences; the elected assembly fought them for control of the Crown land revenue and won it in 1837.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders. Catholics could not sit until 1810 and were excluded by oath before that, which mattered in a province a third Acadian and heavily Irish after the 1840s.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Following Nova Scotia by a few months, New Brunswick's governor accepted a ministry answerable to the assembly, and colonial officials stopped running the timber economy from Government House.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders and, from 1855, most adult male ratepayers.

departures.how: New Brunswickers voted Confederation down in March 1865 and voted it up in June 1866 after Fenian raiders massed on the border and the Colonial Office made its preference plain; the province joined Canada on 1 July 1867.

becomes.name: Province of New Brunswick, in the Dominion of Canada

led.name: Samuel Leonard Tilley
led.role: premier who lost an election over Confederation in 1865 and won one for it in 1866

led.name: Albert Smith
led.role: led the anti-Confederation government of 1865-66

led.name: Arthur Gordon
led.role: lieutenant-governor who used his office to help defeat the anti-Confederates

cost.note: Nobody died over Confederation in New Brunswick. The Fenian scare that helped carry it produced no fighting on the province's soil.

departures.borders: New Brunswick had already lost its northern claim: the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 9 August 1842 split the disputed Aroostook country with Maine after a bloodless border confrontation in 1838-39, giving Britain the road link to Quebec it needed and Maine most of the timber land.

contested.note: As with Nova Scotia, treating 1867 as a departure is a modelling choice: New Brunswick left the Colonial Office's direct oversight, not the British Empire. The Canada record carries the end of British sovereignty, which came in stages to 1982.

populationTransfer.note: About 14,000 loyalists arrived in 1783 and roughly 30,000 Irish famine migrants between 1845 and 1852; at Partridge Island quarantine station in 1847 alone, some 600 of them died.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Maine boundary was the last land border Britain and the United States disputed, and the 1842 line still runs where Webster and Ashburton drew it with the help of a map neither side showed the other.

commonwealth.note: New Brunswick is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.economicLegacy: Square timber for the Royal Navy and, later, ships: in the 1860s New Brunswick and Nova Scotia together had one of the world's largest merchant fleets, and steel hulls destroyed it in a generation.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Canada's only officially bilingual province, because the Acadians the empire deported came back.

populationWarrant.supports: New Brunswick’s largest recorded population: 252,047 people, counted in 1861.

evidence.supports: The loyalist founding and the province's early politics.

evidence.author: Margaret Conrad
evidence.work: A Concise History of Canada
evidence.supports: Maritime colonial development, responsible government and Confederation.

pedagogy.hook: New Brunswick exists because 14,000 Americans who backed the losing side in 1783 refused to live under Nova Scotia's government and were given a province of their own.

misconception.belief: The loyalists were British people going home.
misconception.correction: Most were Americans, born in the colonies, and about a tenth of those who came to the Maritimes were Black. Britain gave them land in a province that had to be invented for them, on Wolastoqiyik and Mi'kmaq territory nobody had bought. The refugees of one empire's collapse became the settlers of another's frontier.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The loyalist migration is the hinge between the two British empires in North America: losing thirteen colonies is what built the fourteenth.

from.note: A marker for the pre-contact period; the Mi'kmaq name means something like 'resting on the waves'.

namesOverTime.name: Prince Edward Island
namesOverTime.note: Renamed for the Duke of Kent, then commanding at Halifax and later Queen Victoria's father, partly to stop confusion with Saint John and St John's.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Canada's smallest province, which hosted the 1864 conference that began Confederation and then refused to join it for nine years.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: Separated from Nova Scotia as a colony of its own, at the request of the London landlords who had won its land in a lottery.

acquisitions.how: Britain surveyed the island into 67 lots of about 20,000 acres each and drew them by lottery in London on 23 July 1767 among army officers and creditors of the Crown, then gave the proprietors their own colony so they would not have to argue with Halifax.

counterparties.name: The Mi'kmaq of Epekwitk
counterparties.lost: Their island. The 1767 lottery divided all of it without reserving an acre for the Mi'kmaq, who had lived there for millennia and had signed peace and friendship treaties that ceded no land; a reserve at Lennox Island was bought for them by a British missionary society only in 1870.

counterparties.name: The Acadians of Ile Saint-Jean
counterparties.lost: Nearly everything. About 4,600 Acadians lived on the island in 1758 and around 3,100 were deported that autumn; some 1,600 drowned when their transports sank. A few hundred hid in the woods and their descendants are the island's Acadian community.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Ile Saint-Jean, taken with Louisbourg in 1758 and ceded at Paris in 1763.

instrument.name: Commission constituting St John's Island a separate government

people.name: Walter Patterson
people.role: first governor, who granted himself land and was eventually dismissed for it

people.name: Jacques Girard
people.role: Acadian parish priest of Saint-Pierre-du-Nord who was deported with his people in 1758

evidence.author: J. M. Bumsted
evidence.work: Land, Settlement, and Politics on Eighteenth-Century Prince Edward Island
evidence.supports: The 1767 lottery, the proprietorial system and its consequences.

statusPeriods.label: The landlords' island
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and council appointed in London governed for absentee proprietors who owned virtually the whole colony; farmers were tenants who could be evicted, and every assembly for eighty years tried and failed to break the estates.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders and, unusually, leaseholders, so tenants could vote. That is why the assembly was permanently at war with the proprietors and permanently overruled by London.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government, and the Tenant League
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Islanders got a ministry answerable to their own assembly and used it to attack the land system; when tenants organised the Tenant League and refused rent in 1864-65, the lieutenant-governor called in British troops from Halifax.
statusPeriods.franchise: Near-universal adult male suffrage from 1853, early by the standards of the empire.
statusPeriods.note: The island hosted the Charlottetown Conference in September 1864, which began Confederation, and then voted against joining it.

departures.how: The island refused Confederation in 1864, 1866 and 1870, then bankrupted itself building a railway and joined on 1 July 1873 because Canada agreed to take over the debt and buy out the absentee landlords.

becomes.name: Province of Prince Edward Island, in the Dominion of Canada

led.name: James Colledge Pope
led.role: premier who negotiated the terms of union including the buyout of the estates

led.name: William Cooper
led.role: leader of the Escheat movement in the 1830s, which demanded the estates be confiscated and given to those who farmed them

departures.movement: Escheat movement and the Tenant League

cost.note: Nobody was killed. British troops were sent from Halifax in 1865 to enforce rent collection against the Tenant League, and the sheriff's men were regularly driven off by tin horns and crowds; the land question was finally settled by Canadian money in the Land Purchase Act of 1875.

departures.borders: No borders changed. What changed was ownership: within two years of joining Canada the province had compulsorily bought out the proprietors and ended a century of absentee landlordism.

warrant.supports: Acadian deaths in the 1758 deportation from Ile Saint-Jean, mostly by shipwreck. The transports Duke William and Violet sank in December 1758 with the loss of about 700 people between them; the figure is from ships' returns and is incomplete.
warrant.check: Transport, embarkation and evacuation returns are in the ADM, CO and T series at The National Archives, Kew.

consequences.economicLegacy: A century of tenancy shaped island politics: the province bought out the last of the proprietors' estates only in the 1870s, and land ownership by non-residents is still legally capped.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Acadian French survives in the western communities, and the Mi'kmaq at Lennox Island hold the only reserve on the island.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1871 census of Prince Edward Island

evidence.work: Land, Settlement, and Politics on Eighteenth-Century Prince Edward Island
evidence.supports: The lottery of 1767 and the proprietorial land system.

evidence.author: Rusty Bittermann
evidence.work: Rural Protest on Prince Edward Island: From British Colonization to the Escheat Movement
evidence.supports: Tenant resistance, the Escheat movement and the Tenant League.

pedagogy.hook: In 1767 the British government divided an entire island into 67 lots and handed them out by lottery in a London room. The people who lived there were not in the room.

misconception.belief: Colonies were settled by people who came to own their own land.
misconception.correction: On Prince Edward Island almost nobody could. Every acre was granted to absentee proprietors in one afternoon in 1767, and settlers arrived as tenants. It took an Escheat movement, a Tenant League, British troops, and finally Confederation in 1873 to break the system.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The island shows the empire as a property machine: colonisation here was a land speculation run from London, and the politics of the next century were about undoing it.

territories.name: Quebec
territories.formalName: Province of Quebec, later Lower Canada and Canada East

namesOverTime.name: Canada, in New France
namesOverTime.note: Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. The name Canada is Iroquoian, from kanata, a village.

namesOverTime.name: Lower Canada
namesOverTime.note: Lower because it lies downstream on the St Lawrence, not because of any judgement about it.

namesOverTime.name: Canada East
namesOverTime.note: The Act of Union merged the two Canadas into one legislature in which the French-speaking majority was deliberately given no more seats than the English-speaking minority.

namesOverTime.name: Quebec / Quebec
namesOverTime.note: A province of Canada since Confederation. Its civil law, its language law and its two referendums on sovereignty all descend from the Quebec Act of 1774.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: The province of Quebec, whose civil law, language and school system all descend from the settlement Britain made with its conquered Catholic subjects in 1774.

geoCoverage.label: Conquered Canada under military rule
geoCoverage.change: Quebec surrendered five days after the battle on the Plains of Abraham; Montreal followed on 8 September 1760 and the whole of French Canada came under British military government.

geoCoverage.label: The Proclamation province
geoCoverage.change: The Royal Proclamation shrank Quebec to a strip along the St Lawrence and promised English law and an assembly, neither of which suited a colony of 70,000 French-speaking Catholics.

geoCoverage.label: With the Ohio country
geoCoverage.change: The Quebec Act attached everything between the Ohio, the Mississippi and the Great Lakes to Quebec, which the thirteen colonies read as a deliberate wall against their westward expansion.

geoCoverage.label: Back to the lakes
geoCoverage.change: The peace treaty gave the Ohio country to the United States, though Britain kept its forts there until 1796 and its fur traders far longer.

geoCoverage.label: Lower Canada, then Canada East
geoCoverage.change: The Constitutional Act split the province in two so that loyalist settlers upstream could have English law and Catholic seigneurial Quebec could keep its own.

acquisitions.how: After a summer of bombardment that burned much of the town and the surrounding parishes, Wolfe's army climbed the cliff at the Anse au Foulon overnight and beat Montcalm's on the Plains of Abraham in about twenty minutes; both commanders died and Quebec surrendered five days later.

counterparties.name: France and the Canadiens
counterparties.lost: New France: about 70,000 French-speaking Catholic colonists, the fur trade of the interior and the St Lawrence itself. France chose to keep Guadeloupe and Martinique at the peace and let Canada go.

counterparties.name: The Haudenosaunee, Wendat, Anishinaabe and Abenaki nations
counterparties.lost: The balance of power that had kept them useful to both empires. With France gone there was only one European power to play against, and the presents and gunsmiths that had come with French alliance stopped. That is a direct cause of Pontiac's War in 1763.

instrument.name: Articles of Capitulation of Quebec
instrument.note: Montreal capitulated on 8 September 1760, and those articles guaranteed the free exercise of the Catholic religion, a promise that shaped everything afterwards.

people.name: James Wolfe
people.role: commanded the British army; ordered the burning of the Canadian parishes below Quebec and was killed on 13 September 1759

people.name: Louis-Joseph de Montcalm
people.role: commanded the French army; mortally wounded in the same battle

people.name: Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil
people.role: Canadian-born governor general who capitulated at Montreal and negotiated the terms for his people

acquisitions.resistance: The Canadian militia fought on around Montreal for a year after Quebec fell, and Britain needed a second campaign of 18,000 men from three directions in 1760 to end it.

cost.note: Killed and wounded on the Plains of Abraham, roughly 660 British and 640 French by the two armies' own returns. Civilian deaths from the bombardment and the burning of the parishes were not counted.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The campaign of 1759-60, the capitulations and the consequences of the conquest.

acquisitions.how: France formally ceded Canada and everything east of the Mississippi, choosing to keep the sugar islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique instead, and gave its Canadian subjects eighteen months to leave if they would not become British.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Canada, Ile Royale, and its claim to the interior. Fewer than 2,000 of about 70,000 Canadiens took the offer to leave; the rest, mainly farmers, stayed and became Catholic subjects of a Protestant king.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris
instrument.note: Article 4 allowed the free exercise of the Catholic religion 'as far as the laws of Great Britain permit' — a qualification that mattered, because British law then barred Catholics from office.

statusPeriods.label: Military government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Three army officers governed the districts of Quebec, Montreal and Trois-Rivieres, kept the French civil law they found, and used the existing militia captains as their local officials, because there was no one else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Quebec, Montreal and Trois-Rivieres, under the commander-in-chief
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: The Proclamation province, then the Quebec Act
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and nominated council governed; the promised assembly never met because it would have had to exclude every Catholic, which would have handed a colony of 70,000 French speakers to a few hundred English merchants.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Governor Murray and then Carleton refused to call an assembly rather than create one that excluded Catholics.
statusPeriods.note: The Quebec Act of 22 June 1774, in force from 1 May 1775, restored French civil law, allowed Catholics to hold office by replacing the Test oath, and confirmed the church's right to collect tithes.

statusPeriods.label: Under the Quebec Act
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor and appointed council, with French civil law, English criminal law, and Catholics eligible for office: a settlement designed to keep the Canadiens quiet, and it worked when the Americans invaded in 1775.
statusPeriods.franchise: None, but Catholics could sit on the council and hold office, which no Catholic in Britain or Ireland could do until 1829.
statusPeriods.note: An American army took Montreal in November 1775 and failed to take Quebec on 31 December; the Canadien population mostly stayed neutral and the invasion collapsed in the spring.

statusPeriods.label: Lower Canada: an assembly without power
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected assembly with a French-speaking majority voted the taxes but could not appoint the government; a governor and an appointed council of English merchants known as the Chateau Clique ran the executive and blocked what the assembly passed.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male and, until 1849, some female property holders: women who met the property test voted in Lower Canada until the franchise was explicitly narrowed to men.
statusPeriods.note: The Ninety-Two Resolutions of 1834 set out the assembly's grievances; London's flat rejection of them in 1837 led straight to rebellion.

statusPeriods.label: Constitution suspended after the rebellions
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After the risings of 1837-38 Britain suspended the constitution and ruled Lower Canada through an appointed Special Council; twelve Patriotes were hanged and 58 transported to Australia.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Direct rule by an appointed council under martial law, with the elected assembly abolished: occupation of a British colony by its own government.
statusPeriods.franchise: None: the assembly was abolished.

statusPeriods.label: Canada East, inside the united Province of Canada
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lord Durham's recommendation was carried out: the two Canadas were merged into one legislature with equal seats each, so that Canada East's larger French-speaking population would be permanently outvoted, and its share of a debt it had not run up.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston, then Montreal, then alternating between Quebec and Toronto
statusPeriods.franchise: Male property holders; French was banned as an official language of the legislature until 1848.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor General Elgin called the Baldwin-Lafontaine ministry because it had the assembly's majority, and in 1849 signed a bill compensating rebels of 1837 even though a Montreal mob burned the parliament building over it.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male property holders. Women were explicitly disfranchised in 1849.

departures.how: Canada East became the province of Quebec on 1 July 1867, getting back the separate legislature and the control of civil law, education and language that the Union of 1841 had taken away.

becomes.name: Province of Quebec, in the Dominion of Canada

led.name: George-Etienne Cartier
led.role: led the French-Canadian bloc into Confederation on the argument that a federal province was safer than a united legislature

led.name: Antoine-Aime Dorion
led.role: led the Rouge opposition, warning that Confederation would leave French Canadians a permanent minority

cost.note: No one died. The cost had been paid thirty years earlier: about 325 people were killed in the rebellions of 1837-38, twelve Patriotes were hanged and 58 transported to Australia.

departures.borders: Quebec's own boundary kept moving after 1867: it was extended north to Ungava in 1912, and the Privy Council awarded interior Labrador to Newfoundland in 1927 in a decision Quebec has never accepted.

contested.note: Whether Confederation was a compact between two founding peoples or a straightforward act of the imperial Parliament is one of the oldest arguments in Canadian politics, and the 1980 and 1995 Quebec referendums were fought over it. Treating 1867 as this territory's ending is a modelling choice: British sovereignty over Quebec ended with Canada's, in stages to 1982.

violence.note: Wolfe's troops burned about 1,400 farms below Quebec in 1759 to break the colony's food supply; in 1837-38 about 325 people were killed in the Lower Canadian rebellions, twelve Patriotes were hanged and 58 were transported to Australia.

populationTransfer.note: Fewer than 2,000 of 70,000 Canadiens left after 1763, so the conquest produced a British colony with a French Catholic majority that has never gone away; about 900,000 Quebecers emigrated to the New England mills between 1840 and 1930.

commonwealth.note: Quebec is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm; Quebecers voted to stay in Canada by 60-40 in 1980 and by 50.6 to 49.4 in 1995.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Quebec still uses French civil law for private matters and English common law for crime, exactly as the Quebec Act of 1774 arranged it.
consequences.borderLegacy: The 1791 line between Upper and Lower Canada is still the Ontario-Quebec boundary.

peak.populationNote: 1861 census of Canada East, the last before Confederation. In 1763 the colony had about 70,000 French-speaking inhabitants.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Quebec’s largest recorded population: 1,111,566 people, counted in 1861.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The conquest of 1759-60 and the settlement that followed.

evidence.author: Hilda Neatby
evidence.work: Quebec: The Revolutionary Age, 1760-1791
evidence.supports: Military government, the Quebec Act and the American invasion.

evidence.author: Allan Greer
evidence.work: The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada
evidence.supports: The 1837-38 rebellions and their suppression.

pedagogy.hook: In 1774 Britain gave Catholics in Quebec the right to hold office. Catholics in Britain and Ireland had to wait another fifty-five years for the same right.

misconception.belief: Britain tried to stamp out French language and Catholicism in Quebec after conquering it.
misconception.correction: It tried the opposite, for hard-headed reasons. With 70,000 French Catholics and a garrison of a few thousand, and thirteen restless colonies to the south, the Quebec Act of 1774 restored French civil law, let Catholics hold office and let the church collect tithes. It worked: Quebec did not join the American revolution. The thirteen colonies listed the Quebec Act among their grievances.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Quebec is the clearest case of the empire buying loyalty with concessions instead of enforcing it with troops, and the concessions are still visible in Canadian law and language today.

keyDates.what: The battle on the Plains of Abraham; Quebec surrenders five days later
France cedes Canada and keeps Guadeloupe instead
The Quebec Act restores French civil law and admits Catholics to office

territories.name: Upper Canada
territories.formalName: Province of Upper Canada, later Canada West

namesOverTime.name: Upper Canada
namesOverTime.note: Upper because it lies upstream on the St Lawrence.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: The province of Ontario.

geoCoverage.label: The lakes and the Ottawa
geoCoverage.change: Split from Quebec so that loyalist settlers could have English law, freehold land and an assembly; the north of the province remained Anishinaabe and Cree country under Hudson's Bay Company trade.

acquisitions.how: Parliament divided Quebec in two so that the roughly 10,000 loyalist refugees settled above the Ottawa could have English freehold tenure, English civil law and an elected assembly, none of which the Quebec Act allowed.

counterparties.name: The Anishinaabe (Mississauga), Haudenosaunee and Wendat nations
counterparties.lost: The north shore of Lake Ontario and the Grand River lands, bought in a rapid series of purchases from 1781 onwards, several of which were later found to be defective. The Toronto Purchase of 1787 was so badly documented that Canada re-settled it for $145 million in 2010.
counterparties.note: Britain's Haudenosaunee allies, who had lost their New York homeland in the 1783 treaty, were given the Haldimand Tract along the Grand River in 1784; roughly five per cent of it is still in Six Nations hands.

counterparties.name: The Province of Quebec
counterparties.lost: Its western half, and with it any prospect of a French-speaking majority in a single province of Canada.

instrument.name: Constitutional Act 1791
instrument.note: Royal assent June 1791; in force by proclamation from 26 December 1791.

people.name: John Graves Simcoe
people.role: first lieutenant-governor; founded York, now Toronto, and pushed through the 1793 anti-slavery act

people.name: Thayendanegea (Joseph Brant)
people.role: Mohawk leader who secured the Haldimand Tract for the Six Nations after Britain gave away their New York land

people.name: Chloe Cooley
people.role: an enslaved woman whose violent sale across the Niagara River in March 1793, and her screaming resistance to it, prompted Simcoe's Act Against Slavery

evidence.author: Alan Taylor
evidence.work: The Divided Ground: Indians, Settlers, and the Northern Borderland of the American Revolution
evidence.supports: Loyalist and Six Nations settlement, land purchases and the new border.

statusPeriods.label: Upper Canada under the Family Compact
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor and an appointed council drawn from a small circle of loyalist families, the Family Compact, held the executive, the courts, the bank and the Anglican clergy reserves; the elected assembly could vote money and little else.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Newark, then York, renamed Toronto in 1834
statusPeriods.franchise: Male freeholders worth forty shillings a year, a wide franchise by British standards, which is why the reform majority in the assembly was so frustrating to the men who ignored it.
statusPeriods.note: The Act Against Slavery of 9 July 1793 banned the importation of enslaved people and freed the children of enslaved women at 25: the first legislation of its kind in the empire, and a reason Upper Canada became the destination of the Underground Railroad.

statusPeriods.label: Between constitutions
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Act of Union came into force on 10 February 1841 and abolished the separate province, but the first united parliament did not sit until 14 June: for four months Upper Canada was governed by the governor general alone.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: A short interregnum with no legislature of any kind, under the governor general's authority alone.

statusPeriods.label: Canada West, inside the united Province of Canada
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: One legislature for both Canadas with equal representation, which gave the smaller English-speaking population of Canada West the same weight as the larger French-speaking population of Canada East, until migration reversed the numbers and the same men demanded representation by population.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kingston, Montreal, then alternating between Toronto and Quebec
statusPeriods.franchise: Male property holders.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Robert Baldwin and Louis-Hippolyte Lafontaine formed a ministry that the governor general had to accept because it commanded the assembly, and thereafter the colony's own politicians ran its internal affairs.
statusPeriods.franchise: Male property holders; the property test was lowered in 1853.

departures.how: Canada West became the province of Ontario on 1 July 1867, and its politicians got the representation by population and the western expansion they had been demanding for fifteen years.

becomes.name: Province of Ontario, in the Dominion of Canada

led.name: John A. Macdonald
led.role: chief architect of Confederation and Canada's first prime minister

led.name: George Brown
led.role: newspaper editor who forced the deadlock open by demanding representation by population and then joining his enemies to get it

cost.note: No one died in 1867. The rebellion of 1837 had cost perhaps a few dozen lives in Upper Canada, with two men, Samuel Lount and Peter Matthews, hanged at Toronto in April 1838 and about ninety transported.

departures.borders: Ontario's northern and western boundary was left vague in 1867 and was argued with Manitoba and Ottawa until the Privy Council settled it in Ontario's favour in 1884, more than doubling the province.

contested.note: As with the other founding provinces, 1867 ended Upper Canada as a colony rather than ending British sovereignty over it. The end of that sovereignty is recorded in the Canada entry and came in stages between 1867 and 1982.

slavery.note: Upper Canada's Act Against Slavery of 1793 was the first legislation anywhere in the empire to restrict slavery, and by the 1850s roughly 30,000 people had escaped slavery in the United States and reached Canada, many of them settling in Chatham, Buxton and Amherstburg.

emancipationDate.note: The 1793 act freed nobody immediately: it banned imports and freed the children of enslaved women only at 25. Full abolition came with the empire-wide act in 1834.

populationTransfer.note: About 10,000 loyalists came in the 1780s and roughly 800,000 British and Irish migrants between 1815 and 1860; the Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee were moved onto reserves under the Bagot Commission and the Indian Act system that followed.

violence.note: Mackenzie's rising of December 1837 was small and quickly beaten; the reprisals that followed, including the hanging of Lount and Matthews and the transportation of about ninety men to Van Diemen's Land, were what people remembered.

commonwealth.note: Ontario is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Canada-United States boundary through the Great Lakes, drawn in 1783 and surveyed after 1818, is the longest undefended land border in the world and has not moved since.

peak.populationNote: 1861 census of Canada West, the last before Confederation. In 1791 the province had roughly 14,000 non-Indigenous inhabitants.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Upper Canada’s largest recorded population: 1,396,091 people, counted in 1861.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Alan Taylor
evidence.work: The Civil War of 1812: American Citizens, British Subjects, Irish Rebels, and Indian Allies
evidence.supports: Upper Canada's loyalist and American settlers and the war that tested them.

evidence.author: Alan Taylor
evidence.work: The Divided Ground: Indians, Settlers, and the Northern Borderland of the American Revolution
evidence.supports: Land purchases, the Haldimand Tract and the new border.

evidence.author: Margaret Conrad
evidence.work: A Concise History of Canada
evidence.supports: The Family Compact, the 1837 rebellion and responsible government.

pedagogy.hook: Upper Canada banned bringing enslaved people into the province in 1793, forty years before the empire abolished slavery, because a woman named Chloe Cooley fought so loudly as she was dragged across the Niagara River.

misconception.belief: Canada was always the free country and the United States the slave one.
misconception.correction: Slavery was legal in both. Upper Canada's 1793 act was a compromise that freed nobody living: it banned imports and freed children of enslaved women at 25. Slavery in British North America ended with the empire-wide act in 1834. What made Canada a destination was that it ended there first, and that Britain refused to return people who escaped.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Upper Canada is where the loyalist migration turned into a province, where the border with the United States was tested in 1812, and where responsible government was won in 1848 by politicians rather than by soldiers.

keyDates.what: Upper Canada created by the Constitutional Act
The Act Against Slavery, first in the empire
