territories.name: Rupert's Land
territories.formalName: Rupert's Land, the territory of the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay

namesOverTime.name: Rupert's Land
namesOverTime.note: Named for Prince Rupert of the Rhine, the king's cousin and the company's first governor, who never went there.

namesOverTime.name: Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Nunavut and the Northwest Territories
namesOverTime.language: English, French, Cree, Inuktitut and others
namesOverTime.note: The land the charter granted in 1670 is now most of five provinces and territories of Canada, and the treaties over it are still being litigated.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: The charter territory became Manitoba and the North-West Territories, and from them Saskatchewan, Alberta, Nunavut and the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec.

geoCoverage.label: Everything that drains into Hudson Bay
geoCoverage.change: A charter defined the grant by hydrology: all the land whose rivers run into Hudson Bay, about 3.9 million square kilometres, which nobody had mapped.

acquisitions.how: Charles II granted eighteen investors led by his cousin Prince Rupert a monopoly of trade, the ownership of the soil and the right to govern in every land drained by rivers flowing into Hudson Bay, an area he had never seen and whose peoples had never heard of him.

counterparties.name: The Cree, Anishinaabe, Assiniboine, Dene, Inuit and later Metis nations
counterparties.lost: In law, everything; in fact, nothing for a century and a half. The charter gave away about 3.9 million square kilometres inhabited by perhaps 100,000 people who were never consulted, but the company depended on Cree and Anishinaabe hunters and traders and could not have survived a week without them.
counterparties.note: Cree women who married company men created the Home Guard Cree and, on the plains, the Metis: peoples brought into being by the fur trade itself.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Its rival claim to Hudson Bay, fought over for forty years. Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville captured most of the company's posts in the 1680s and 1690s; France gave up the Bay at Utrecht in 1713.

instrument.name: Royal Charter of the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay
instrument.note: The company still exists. Its charter made it the oldest continuously operating commercial corporation in the English-speaking world.

people.name: Pierre-Esprit Radisson
people.role: French Canadian trader who, rebuffed in Quebec, persuaded London that the fur country could be reached by sea

people.name: Medard Chouart des Groseilliers
people.role: his brother-in-law and partner; sailed on the Nonsuch to James Bay in 1668

people.name: Prince Rupert of the Rhine
people.role: the king's cousin and the company's first governor

people.name: Thanadelthur
people.role: Dene woman, escaped from Cree captivity, who in 1715-16 negotiated the peace that let the company build at Churchill; the traders called her the Slave Woman

acquisitions.resistance: Not from the peoples of the Bay, who wanted the trade and set its terms: the company's own records show Cree traders driving hard bargains over the standard of trade and walking away when the price was wrong.

evidence.author: Ann M. Carlos
evidence.work: Commerce by a Frozen Sea: Native Americans and the European Fur Trade
evidence.supports: Indigenous bargaining power in the Hudson Bay trade, from the company's own account books.

acquisitions.how: France returned the Hudson Bay posts it had taken by force and abandoned its claim to the Bay, ending forty years in which the company's forts changed hands almost as often as its governors.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: Its claim to Hudson Bay and its posts on James Bay, though French traders from Montreal kept competing overland for another fifty years and the North West Company took up the competition after 1779.

instrument.name: Treaty of Utrecht
instrument.note: Article 10 restored the Bay to Britain and named commissioners to fix the southern boundary. They never agreed on one.

statusPeriods.label: Sleeping by the frozen sea
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: For 150 years the company governed almost nothing: a few hundred men in half a dozen forts on the coast waited for Cree and Anishinaabe middlemen to bring furs down the rivers, and the terms of trade were negotiated every spring.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fenchurch Street, London, through factors at York Factory and Fort Albany
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The company's governing body was its shareholders, meeting in London.
statusPeriods.note: The Montreal-based North West Company broke the monopoly after 1779 by going inland; the two fought a trade war that included the killing of twenty-one settlers and officials at Seven Oaks in 1816.

statusPeriods.label: Company government over half a continent
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After absorbing the North West Company, the Hudson's Bay Company held a licence of exclusive trade over the whole British west and governed it: Governor George Simpson ran a territory larger than western Europe from a canoe, with company courts, company magistrates and no elections.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Garry and Norway House, under the London committee
statusPeriods.franchise: None anywhere in the territory. The Council of Assiniboia, the only governing body, was appointed by the company.

departures.how: Britain bought the company's charter rights for £300,000 and handed a territory the size of India to Canada; the people living in it were told nothing until surveyors arrived, and the Metis of Red River stopped the transfer for eight months until they got terms.

becomes.name: Manitoba and the North-West Territories, in Canada

led.name: Louis Riel
led.role: led the Metis provisional government that blocked the transfer and negotiated the terms that became the Manitoba Act

led.name: George-Etienne Cartier
led.role: negotiated the transfer in London for Canada

led.name: William McDougall
led.role: the lieutenant-governor Canada sent ahead of the transfer, turned back at the border by Metis horsemen in October 1869

cost.note: The transfer itself killed no one. Its consequences did: the Wolseley expedition's arrival in August 1870 drove Riel into exile and began months of violence against Metis people at Red River, and the treaty and reserve system that followed coincided with the destruction of the bison herds and famine across the plains.

departures.borders: The Deed of Surrender moved a border in London that had never been surveyed on the ground. The company kept a twentieth of the fertile belt, about 2.8 million hectares, and its posts, which is why Hudson's Bay land grants shaped prairie town sites for the next century.

instrument.name: Rupert's Land Act 1868 and the Deed of Surrender
instrument.note: The Act passed on 31 July 1868; the company signed the Deed of Surrender on 19 November 1869; the transfer took effect on 15 July 1870 after the Red River Resistance delayed it.

evidence.author: J. M. Bumsted
evidence.work: The Red River Rebellion
evidence.supports: The transfer negotiations, the resistance and the Manitoba Act.

populationTransfer.note: The fur trade created new peoples rather than displacing old ones for its first century and a half; the transfer of 1870 reversed that, bringing surveyors, homestead law and, within twenty years, more settlers than the territory had ever held.

violence.note: Between 1870 and 1890 the plains bison were destroyed, Treaties 1 to 7 were signed under the pressure of hunger, and government rations were used to force Cree and Blackfoot bands onto reserves; James Daschuk's research links federal food policy directly to mass deaths from starvation and tuberculosis.

commonwealth.note: The territory is now part of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.economicLegacy: Two centuries of beaver pelts funded a London company that still trades; the standard of trade, priced in Made Beaver, was one of the first sustained commercial contacts between Europeans and Indigenous North Americans.
consequences.borderLegacy: The charter's watershed boundary is why Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta's northern lines fall where they do, and why the prairie provinces did not own their own natural resources until 1930.

peak.populationNote: No census was ever taken. The company's own estimates for the 1850s put the Indigenous population of its territories at roughly 100,000 and the settled population of Red River at about 10,000. Both figures are guesses by traders, not counts.

evidence.author: Ann M. Carlos
evidence.work: Commerce by a Frozen Sea: Native Americans and the European Fur Trade
evidence.supports: Indigenous bargaining power and the economics of the Bay trade.

evidence.author: Arthur J. Ray
evidence.work: Indians in the Fur Trade
evidence.supports: Cree and Assiniboine middlemen and the structure of the trade.

evidence.author: James Daschuk
evidence.work: Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life
evidence.supports: The collapse of the bison economy and the use of food policy after 1870.

pedagogy.hook: In 1670 Charles II gave a London company every acre of land whose rivers flow into Hudson Bay — 3.9 million square kilometres, about a twelfth of North America — in a document that took one afternoon to seal.

misconception.belief: Europeans dominated Indigenous people in the fur trade because of superior technology.
misconception.correction: For 150 years it was the other way round. The Hudson's Bay Company sat in a handful of coastal forts, could not travel inland, and depended entirely on Cree and Anishinaabe traders who set prices, played the English against the French, and walked away when the terms were poor. The company's own account books show it. Power shifted only when the bison and beaver went and the railway came.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Rupert's Land is the largest single grant in the empire's history and the clearest case of a company being handed sovereignty; when Canada bought it in 1870 the people living there were not asked, and that omission produced two armed resistances and the hanging of Louis Riel.

keyDates.what: Charles II charters the Hudson's Bay Company
Utrecht: France gives up Hudson Bay
Merger with the North West Company; company rule over the whole west
The company signs Rupert's Land away for £300,000

territories.name: Red River Colony
territories.formalName: The Colony of Assiniboia (Red River Settlement)

namesOverTime.name: Assiniboia
namesOverTime.note: From the Assiniboine nation, whose name the district took.

namesOverTime.name: Manitoba
namesOverTime.note: The province Louis Riel's provisional government negotiated into existence, on terms Canada then largely failed to keep.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: The province of Manitoba, created in 1870 by an act the Metis themselves largely wrote.

geoCoverage.label: The forks of the Red and Assiniboine
geoCoverage.change: A Scottish earl was granted 300,000 square kilometres by the company he had bought into, in the middle of the Metis bison hunt and the North West Company's supply route.

acquisitions.how: Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, bought enough Hudson's Bay Company stock to control it and then granted himself 300,000 square kilometres for ten shillings a year, to settle Highlanders and Irish cleared off their own land at home.

counterparties.name: The Metis Nation
counterparties.lost: Their bison hunt and their freight route. The colony's Pemmican Proclamation of 1814 banned the export of the dried meat the Metis sold to the fur brigades, which is what turned a land dispute into a shooting war.

counterparties.name: The Anishinaabe (Saulteaux) and Cree
counterparties.lost: The forks of the Red and Assiniboine, covered by the Selkirk Treaty of 18 July 1817, in which chiefs including Peguis granted a strip two miles deep along the rivers for an annual payment of tobacco. Peguis and his successors argued for the rest of the century that they had granted use, not ownership.

counterparties.name: The North West Company
counterparties.lost: Control of the route between Montreal and the Athabasca country, which the settlement sat across.

instrument.name: Grant of Assiniboia to Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk
instrument.note: The purchase price was ten shillings a year and a commitment to supply the company with servants.

people.name: Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk
people.role: bought the grant to resettle Highlanders cleared from Scottish estates, including his own family's tenants

people.name: Peguis
people.role: Anishinaabe chief who fed the starving settlers in 1812 and signed the 1817 treaty, then spent decades protesting how it was interpreted

people.name: Cuthbert Grant
people.role: Metis leader at Seven Oaks in 1816, later Warden of the Plains for the company

acquisitions.resistance: On 19 June 1816 a Metis party under Cuthbert Grant met Governor Robert Semple's men at Seven Oaks; Semple and twenty of his people were killed, and one Metis. Selkirk answered by hiring disbanded Swiss mercenaries and seizing the North West Company's Fort William.

cost.note: Deaths at Seven Oaks on 19 June 1816: Governor Semple and twenty of his men, and one Metis. The two sides' accounts of who fired first have never been reconciled.

evidence.author: W. L. Morton
evidence.work: Manitoba: A History
evidence.supports: The Selkirk settlement, the fur trade war and the growth of the Red River community.

statusPeriods.label: Selkirk's settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Scottish peer owned the district and appointed its governor; his colonists were burned out twice, in 1815 and 1816, by the rival company and the Metis whose economy they had cut across.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Douglas, under the Selkirk family
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Company district with an appointed council
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Hudson's Bay Company bought Assiniboia back from Selkirk's heirs and governed through a Council of Assiniboia it appointed; in 1849 a jury convicted the Metis trader Guillaume Sayer of illegal trading and the court dared not punish him, which ended the monopoly in practice.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Upper Fort Garry, under the company's Northern Department
statusPeriods.franchise: None. By 1870 the settlement had about 12,000 people, some 10,000 of them Metis and Anglo-Metis, and not one of them could vote for anything.

departures.how: The Metis seized Fort Garry in November 1869, formed a provisional government, drew up a List of Rights and negotiated it into the Manitoba Act; Canada agreed to their terms, then sent an army, and Louis Riel fled the country he had just brought into Confederation.

becomes.name: Province of Manitoba, in Canada

led.name: Louis Riel
led.role: president of the provisional government; negotiated the Manitoba Act, was elected to Parliament three times without being able to take his seat, and was hanged at Regina on 16 November 1885

led.name: Ambroise-Dydime Lepine
led.role: adjutant general of the provisional government; sentenced to death for Thomas Scott's execution and reprieved

led.name: Thomas Scott
led.role: Orangeman from Ontario executed by the provisional government on 4 March 1870, whose death made Riel unpardonable in Protestant Ontario

led.name: Garnet Wolseley
led.role: commanded the 1,200-man expedition sent to Red River, which arrived on 24 August 1870 after Riel had gone

cost.note: Thomas Scott was executed by the provisional government in March 1870; at least two Metis men, Elzear Goulet and Francois Guillemette, were killed by soldiers or settlers after the Wolseley expedition arrived, and others were beaten. Nobody counted, and Manitoba's own historians describe the months after August 1870 as a reign of terror against Metis families.

departures.borders: The Manitoba Act created a province of only about 36,000 square kilometres, the postage stamp province, and promised 1.4 million acres to Metis children. The land was distributed through scrip that speculators bought up, and by 1885 most Metis families at Red River had left for the Saskatchewan valley.

instrument.name: Manitoba Act 1870
instrument.note: Passed by the Canadian Parliament on 12 May 1870 and in force with the Rupert's Land transfer on 15 July. It guaranteed French and English, Catholic and Protestant schools, and the Metis land grant; Manitoba abolished the school and language guarantees in 1890.

contested.note: Whether 1869-70 was a rebellion or a legitimate assertion of self-government by a people about to be transferred without consent is still argued, and the answer has changed in Canadian law: in 2013 the Supreme Court of Canada held that the Crown had failed to fulfil the Manitoba Act's land promise to Metis children.

populationTransfer.note: The Metis of Red River, about 10,000 people in 1870, were mostly gone within fifteen years: scrip speculation, surveyors and Ontario settlers pushed them west to Batoche and Prince Albert, where the second resistance broke out in 1885.

violence.note: Seven Oaks in 1816 killed twenty-two people; the aftermath of the Wolseley expedition in 1870 saw Metis men killed and families driven out with no prosecutions; Riel was hanged in 1885.

commonwealth.note: Manitoba is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Michif, a language combining Cree verbs and French nouns, was born at Red River; the Manitoba Act's guarantee of French was struck down in 1890 and restored by the Supreme Court in 1979.

peak.populationNote: The 1870 census of Red River counted 11,963 people, of whom about 5,700 were French-speaking Metis, 4,000 English-speaking Metis and roughly 1,600 of European origin. The grant's area is Selkirk's paper claim, not the settled district.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1870 census of Red River Colony
populationWarrant.supports: Red River Colony’s largest recorded population: 11,963 people, counted in 1870.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: W. L. Morton
evidence.work: Manitoba: A History
evidence.supports: Selkirk's colony, the Council of Assiniboia and the growth of Red River.

evidence.author: J. M. Bumsted
evidence.work: The Red River Rebellion
evidence.supports: The resistance of 1869-70 and the Manitoba Act.

evidence.author: Gerald Friesen
evidence.work: The Canadian Prairies: A History
evidence.supports: Metis society, the scrip system and the settlement of the west.

pedagogy.hook: In 1869 a 25-year-old Metis surveyor's son stopped Canada from taking a territory the size of India, and made it negotiate. Sixteen years later Canada hanged him.

misconception.belief: Canada expanded west into empty land.
misconception.correction: The land was inhabited, farmed and governed. At Red River in 1870 there were about 12,000 people, most of them Metis, with river-lot farms, a bison-hunt constitution, courts, a cathedral and their own language. They were not consulted about being sold, so they seized the fort, elected a government and negotiated the terms of their own province.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Red River is where Canada's westward expansion met a people who could stop it, and the settlement they extracted, and Canada's failure to keep it, is the origin of a land claim the Supreme Court upheld in 2013.

keyDates.what: Selkirk is granted Assiniboia
Seven Oaks: twenty-two people killed in the fur trade war
Riel's men take Upper Fort Garry and stop the transfer
The provisional government executes Thomas Scott
The Manitoba Act creates a province on Metis terms
Louis Riel is hanged at Regina

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Part of British Columbia, whose capital, Victoria, is on the island.

geoCoverage.label: The island and its coastal nations
geoCoverage.change: Granted outright to the Hudson's Bay Company on condition it settled the island, to keep the Americans out after the Oregon boundary was fixed at the 49th parallel in 1846.

acquisitions.how: Britain granted the whole island to the Hudson's Bay Company for seven shillings a year on condition it planted a colony, because the Oregon settlement of 1846 had just shown that unoccupied coast could be claimed by the United States.

counterparties.name: The Lekwungen, Songhees, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth and other island nations
counterparties.lost: Between 1850 and 1854 James Douglas signed fourteen agreements, the Douglas Treaties, covering about 3 per cent of the island; for the rest, no treaty was ever made. Smallpox in 1862 killed perhaps a third of the Indigenous population of the coast.
counterparties.note: The Douglas Treaties are the only pre-Confederation land treaties in British Columbia, which is why most of the province is unceded territory and why modern treaty negotiation there is still unfinished.

instrument.name: Royal Grant of Vancouver Island to the Hudson's Bay Company
instrument.note: The rent was seven shillings a year. The grant was revoked in 1859 when the company failed to bring settlers.

people.name: James Douglas
people.role: company chief factor and then governor; signed the fourteen treaties and governed both colonies

people.name: Amelia Connolly Douglas
people.role: Cree and Irish, Douglas's wife, whose kin networks were part of how the colony's diplomacy actually worked

people.name: Maquinna
people.role: the Nuu-chah-nulth title held at Nootka Sound, which had negotiated with Spain and Britain since the 1790s

evidence.author: Robin Fisher
evidence.work: Contact and Conflict: Indian-European Relations in British Columbia, 1774-1890
evidence.supports: The Douglas Treaties, the fur trade and the effect of settlement on coastal nations.

statusPeriods.label: A colony run by a fur company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Hudson's Bay Company owned the island and chose who could buy land, at a pound an acre with five labourers attached, which is why after ten years the colony had a few hundred settlers and the grant was cancelled.
statusPeriods.franchise: Freeholders of twenty acres. When the first assembly was elected in 1856 the whole electorate was about forty men, the smallest in the empire.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown resumed the island and governed it through James Douglas, who was governor of Vancouver Island and of the mainland colony at the same time and had to give up his company shares to do it.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: A governor appointed in London held the executive, but an elected assembly survived from the company period, so authority sat between crown colony and representative colony.
statusPeriods.franchise: A small property franchise; Victoria's Black community, refugees from California, voted and served in the militia, which was unusual for the period.

departures.how: Both colonies were broke after the gold rush ended, so Britain merged them; the island lost its assembly, and the mainland lost the argument about the capital when Victoria kept it in 1868.

becomes.name: United Colony of British Columbia

led.name: Arthur Kennedy
led.role: last governor of Vancouver Island, whose colony was abolished under him

led.name: Amor De Cosmos
led.role: Victoria newspaper editor who campaigned for union and then for Confederation, and became premier of British Columbia

cost.note: Nobody died. The island's debt, about £100,000 from roads and a failed harbour scheme, was one of the reasons union was forced on it.

departures.borders: The island's boundary with the United States was still unfixed: the San Juan Islands were occupied by British and American troops together from 1859 and awarded to the United States by the German emperor's arbitration in 1872, after a dispute that began when an American shot a company pig.

instrument.name: British Columbia Act 1866
instrument.note: Proclaimed at Victoria on 19 November 1866.

violence.note: The smallpox epidemic of 1862, which spread after Victoria's authorities expelled Indigenous camps from the town and sent infected people home by canoe, killed perhaps 20,000 people on the coast, a third of the Indigenous population of the region.

toll.note: Estimates of deaths in the 1862 coastal smallpox epidemic vary widely because there was no census before or after; historians generally give a range around a third of the coastal Indigenous population.

populationTransfer.note: About 800 Black Californians moved to Victoria in 1858 at Douglas's invitation, escaping worsening racial laws in California; thousands of Chinese miners arrived in the same rush and were later taxed under a head tax.

commonwealth.note: Vancouver Island is part of British Columbia, in Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1846 line at the 49th parallel bends south around Vancouver Island so that the whole island stayed British; the San Juan Islands went to the United States in 1872.

peak.populationNote: A rough estimate of the non-Indigenous population at union, most of it in Victoria. The Indigenous population of the island before the 1862 smallpox epidemic is not reliably known.

evidence.author: Robin Fisher
evidence.work: Contact and Conflict: Indian-European Relations in British Columbia, 1774-1890
evidence.supports: The Douglas Treaties and the transition from fur trade to settlement.

evidence.author: Jean Barman
evidence.work: The West Beyond the West: A History of British Columbia
evidence.supports: The colony of Vancouver Island, its assembly and the union of 1866.

pedagogy.hook: When Vancouver Island elected its first assembly in 1856, the entire electorate was about forty men — the smallest legislature-electing public in the British Empire.

misconception.belief: British colonies in Canada were all settled by treaty with Indigenous nations.
misconception.correction: In British Columbia almost none were. James Douglas made fourteen small treaties on Vancouver Island between 1850 and 1854, covering about 3 per cent of it, and then stopped because London would not pay. Most of British Columbia is unceded territory to this day, which is why treaty negotiations there are still going on.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Vancouver Island shows the empire using a trading company as a cheap way to hold a coast, and shows the legal gap that follows when a colony takes land without buying it.

keyDates.what: The island is granted to the Hudson's Bay Company
The first of the fourteen Douglas Treaties is signed
The Crown takes the island back from the company
Smallpox reaches Victoria and spreads along the whole coast
Union with the mainland colony of British Columbia

namesOverTime.name: New Caledonia
namesOverTime.note: The fur traders' name for the interior. Queen Victoria chose British Columbia instead, to avoid confusion with the French colony in the Pacific.

namesOverTime.name: British Columbia
namesOverTime.note: A province of Canada since 1871. Most of it was never covered by a treaty, which is why title cases such as Delgamuukw and Tsilhqot'in were brought here.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Canada's sixth province, which joined on the promise of a transcontinental railway.

geoCoverage.label: The mainland colony
geoCoverage.change: Created in eight weeks because 30,000 gold miners, most of them American, had poured up the Fraser River and Britain had no government there at all.

geoCoverage.label: United colony
geoCoverage.change: The two bankrupt Pacific colonies were merged; Victoria became the capital of the whole in 1868.

acquisitions.how: Gold was found on the Fraser in 1857 and about 30,000 miners arrived from California in a single season, so Parliament created a colony in eight weeks to make sure the country did not simply become American by occupation.

counterparties.name: The Nlaka'pamux, Secwepemc, St'at'imc, Tsilhqot'in, Dakelh and coastal nations
counterparties.lost: Their land, without a treaty. British Columbia signed no land treaties after 1854 and denied that Aboriginal title existed until the courts said otherwise in 1973 and 1997; the Fraser Canyon War of August 1858 saw armed American miner companies burn Nlaka'pamux villages before Governor Douglas imposed a peace.
counterparties.note: In 1864 the Tsilhqot'in fought a road-building party in their territory; five Tsilhqot'in leaders were tricked into peace talks, tried and hanged. British Columbia exonerated them in 2014 and Canada in 2018.

instrument.name: An Act to provide for the Government of British Columbia
instrument.note: Proclaimed at Fort Langley on 19 November 1858. The Hudson's Bay Company's exclusive trade licence over the mainland was revoked at the same time.

people.name: James Douglas
people.role: governor of both colonies; imposed licences on the miners and kept the peace in the Fraser Canyon

people.name: Matthew Baillie Begbie
people.role: the colony's first judge, sent out with the act in his luggage to make the law arrive before the miners did

people.name: Klatsassin
people.role: Tsilhqot'in war chief in 1864, hanged at Quesnel; exonerated by Canada in 2018

people.name: Spintlum (Cexpe'nthlEm)
people.role: Nlaka'pamux chief who negotiated the peace that ended the Fraser Canyon War in 1858

acquisitions.resistance: The Fraser Canyon War of 1858 and the Tsilhqot'in War of 1864 were both fought against incursions the colony had not authorised and could not control; both ended with Indigenous leaders bearing the punishment.

evidence.author: Cole Harris
evidence.work: The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change
evidence.supports: The gold rush, the reserve system and dispossession without treaty.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony on the gold frontier
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor with a judge and a detachment of Royal Engineers governed by proclamation: no assembly at all until 1864, and a legislative council with a minority of elected members after that.
statusPeriods.franchise: A property franchise for British subjects. Chinese and Indigenous residents were excluded by law from 1872, and Indigenous people in British Columbia could not vote provincially until 1949 or federally until 1960.
statusPeriods.note: The Cariboo Wagon Road, built by the Royal Engineers between 1862 and 1865, cost the colony so much that bankruptcy forced the union with Vancouver Island.

departures.how: Bankrupt, outnumbered by Americans and offered a railway to the Pacific within ten years plus the assumption of its debts, the colony chose Canada over annexation to the United States and joined on 20 July 1871.

becomes.name: Province of British Columbia, in Canada

led.name: Amor De Cosmos
led.role: editor and politician who led the Confederation League and became premier in 1872

led.name: John Sebastian Helmcken
led.role: sceptic who negotiated the terms in Ottawa and got the railway promise written in

led.name: Anthony Musgrave
led.role: governor sent specifically to steer the colony into Confederation

cost.note: Nobody died. The bill came due elsewhere: the Canadian Pacific Railway that bought British Columbia's assent was built between 1881 and 1885 largely by about 15,000 Chinese labourers, of whom several hundred to more than a thousand died, and Canada then imposed a head tax on Chinese immigrants in 1885.

departures.borders: The colony joined with its northern boundary against Alaska undefined. The Klondike rush made that intolerable, and a tribunal in 1903 drew the line where the United States wanted it, leaving British Columbia and Yukon without a Pacific port north of Prince Rupert.

instrument.name: British Columbia Terms of Union
instrument.note: Union took effect on 20 July 1871. Term 13 also transferred responsibility for Indigenous people to Canada while leaving the province in charge of the land.

populationTransfer.note: About 30,000 miners arrived in 1858 and most left again; the railway brought some 15,000 Chinese workers, and from 1885 Canada charged them a head tax that rose to $500 by 1903 and was replaced by outright exclusion in 1923.

violence.note: The Tsilhqot'in War of 1864 ended with five chiefs hanged after being invited to talks; Canada formally exonerated them in 2018. Indigenous children in British Columbia were taken to residential schools from the 1860s to 1984.

commonwealth.note: British Columbia is a province of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: British Columbia is the only large part of Canada settled almost entirely without land treaties, which is why the Nisga'a treaty of 2000 and the modern treaty process exist.
consequences.economicLegacy: Gold, then salmon, then timber, then coal: an export economy facing the Pacific rather than the Atlantic, which is why the railway mattered so much.

peak.populationNote: The 1871 estimate at Confederation counted about 10,500 non-Indigenous residents and roughly 25,700 Indigenous people, and the Indigenous figure was a guess. The province's Indigenous population had fallen by perhaps two thirds since 1835 through smallpox and other epidemics.

evidence.author: Jean Barman
evidence.work: The West Beyond the West: A History of British Columbia
evidence.supports: The gold rush colony, union and Confederation.

evidence.author: Cole Harris
evidence.work: The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change
evidence.supports: Dispossession without treaty and the reserve system.

pedagogy.hook: Britain invented British Columbia in eight weeks in 1858 because 30,000 American gold miners had already arrived and there was nobody there to stop them staying.

misconception.belief: Colonies were founded deliberately, after planning.
misconception.correction: British Columbia was an emergency. Gold on the Fraser drew a mostly American rush in 1858; the Colonial Office rushed an act through Parliament, sent a judge and a company of Royal Engineers, and hoped a government would arrive before an American majority did. Much of the empire was improvised like this, in response to other people's movements.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: British Columbia is the province built without treaties, and that gap is the reason land questions there are still open in the courts today.

keyDates.what: Parliament creates the colony during the Fraser gold rush
The Tsilhqot'in War begins; five chiefs are hanged that October
Union with Vancouver Island
British Columbia joins Canada for a railway
The Alaska boundary tribunal rules against Canada

territories.name: Oregon Country
territories.formalName: The Oregon Country, jointly occupied by Great Britain and the United States

namesOverTime.name: The Columbia District
namesOverTime.note: The Hudson's Bay Company's name for its Pacific slope operation, run from Fort Vancouver on the Columbia.

namesOverTime.name: Oregon, Washington and Idaho
namesOverTime.note: South of the 49th parallel the joint occupation became American; north of it, British Columbia.

modernSuccessors.name: United States of America
modernSuccessors.note: Oregon, Washington, Idaho and parts of Montana and Wyoming.

geoCoverage.label: Jointly occupied, unclaimed by either
geoCoverage.change: Britain and the United States agreed to leave the country between the Rockies and the Pacific open to both, and to argue about it later.

acquisitions.how: Britain and the United States could not agree who owned the Pacific slope, so they signed a convention leaving it open to the citizens of both for ten years, renewed indefinitely in 1827, and Britain then occupied it commercially through the Hudson's Bay Company.

counterparties.name: The Chinook, Nez Perce, Cayuse, Salish and other nations of the Columbia basin
counterparties.lost: Their country, divided on paper between two states that had never asked them. A malaria epidemic between 1830 and 1834 killed perhaps three quarters of the Chinookan-speaking people of the lower Columbia, opening the valley to American settlers in the 1840s.
counterparties.note: The Hudson's Bay Company traded with these nations rather than governing them; the American settlers who followed came to farm, which is a different kind of arrival.

counterparties.name: The United States
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet; each side gave up its exclusive claim for the duration.

counterparties.name: Spain and Russia
counterparties.lost: Their own claims to the coast, given up by Spain in 1819 and by Russia in 1824-25 in treaties that fixed 54 degrees 40 minutes as Russia's southern limit.

instrument.name: Anglo-American Convention of 1818
instrument.note: The same convention fixed the boundary from Lake of the Woods to the Rockies at the 49th parallel, which is why that line stops at the mountains until 1846.

people.name: John McLoughlin
people.role: Hudson's Bay Company chief factor at Fort Vancouver, who ran the region for twenty years and fed the American settlers who displaced him

people.name: George Simpson
people.role: company governor who ordered the Snake River country trapped bare to make it worthless to Americans

people.name: Tuekakas (Old Joseph)
people.role: Nez Perce leader in the Wallowa country during the years of joint occupation

acquisitions.resistance: There was no war of conquest here. The company's strategy was deliberate ecological policy: it stripped the Snake River country of beaver in the 1820s to create a fur desert that would discourage American trappers.

evidence.author: Richard Somerset Mackie
evidence.work: Trading Beyond the Mountains: The British Fur Trade on the Pacific, 1793-1843
evidence.supports: The Columbia District, Fort Vancouver and the company's fur desert policy.

statusPeriods.label: Joint occupation: two flags, no government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Neither state governed. British subjects were answerable to courts in Upper Canada under an act of 1821, Americans to nobody, and in practice the Hudson's Bay Company's chief factor at Fort Vancouver was the only authority anyone obeyed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Formally a condominium, but neither power administered the territory; British influence ran through a trading company, so the real degree of control was closer to an informal sphere until American settlers arrived in the 1840s.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Vancouver on the Columbia, and London
statusPeriods.franchise: None until American settlers organised their own provisional government in the Willamette valley in 1843 and voted it into being, 52 to 50.

departures.how: About 5,000 American settlers had walked the Oregon Trail into the Willamette valley by 1845 while the British population stayed a few hundred company men; with a war against Mexico beginning, Washington dropped its claim to 54 degrees 40 minutes and Britain took the 49th parallel.

becomes.name: Oregon Territory, in the United States

led.name: James K. Polk
led.role: US president elected on the slogan Fifty-four Forty or Fight, who settled for the 49th parallel

led.name: Richard Pakenham
led.role: British minister in Washington who negotiated the 1846 treaty

led.name: Robert Peel
led.role: British prime minister who preferred a Pacific boundary to a second American war

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the transfer: this is the empire's clearest example of a large territory given up by negotiation rather than defeat. The Cayuse War of 1847-55 that followed, between American settlers and the Cayuse, was another matter and killed hundreds.

departures.borders: The line runs along the 49th parallel to the sea, then dips south around Vancouver Island so that Britain kept the whole island. It left the San Juan Islands ambiguous, which produced a joint military occupation from 1859 to 1872 in which the only casualty was a pig.

instrument.name: Oregon Treaty
instrument.note: Ratified 19 June 1846. Britain kept navigation rights on the Columbia and the Hudson's Bay Company kept its posts, which the United States bought out in 1869 for $450,000.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 49th parallel from the Rockies to the Pacific is the world's longest straight international boundary, and it exists because two governments preferred a line on a map to a war neither could afford.

populationTransfer.note: The Oregon Trail carried roughly 5,000 American settlers to the Willamette by 1845 and perhaps 400,000 people west by 1869; the malaria epidemic of the early 1830s had emptied much of the lower Columbia before they arrived.

commonwealth.note: The Pacific Northwest is part of the United States, which has never been in the Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: British interest here was never settlement; it was beaver, salmon and the Pacific trade run from a single company fort.

peak.populationNote: A rough estimate of the non-Indigenous population in 1845, of whom roughly 5,000 were American settlers and a few hundred were company employees and their families. The Indigenous population, already devastated by epidemics, is not reliably known.

evidence.author: Frederick Merk
evidence.work: The Oregon Question: Essays in Anglo-American Diplomacy and Politics
evidence.supports: The diplomacy of joint occupation and the 1846 settlement.

evidence.author: Richard Somerset Mackie
evidence.work: Trading Beyond the Mountains: The British Fur Trade on the Pacific, 1793-1843
evidence.supports: The Columbia District and the company's operations.

pedagogy.hook: Britain and the United States shared the Pacific Northwest for twenty-eight years without either of them governing it. The only authority anyone obeyed was a fur company doctor at Fort Vancouver.

misconception.belief: Empires always expanded when they could.
misconception.correction: Britain gave up a territory the size of France in 1846 without a shot. It had the naval power to fight and chose not to: there were 5,000 American farmers in the Willamette and a few hundred British fur traders, a war with the United States would have cost more than the beaver were worth, and Peel's government wanted the corn laws repealed more than it wanted Oregon.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Oregon is the counter-example to the idea that empires only grow. It shows a British government doing a cost-benefit calculation on territory and walking away, which is exactly the calculation that ended the empire a century later.

keyDates.what: Joint occupation agreed; the 49th parallel stops at the Rockies
Fort Vancouver founded; the company runs the region for twenty years
American settlers vote themselves a provisional government, 52 to 50
The Oregon Treaty sets the border at the 49th parallel

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Saskatchewan and Alberta became provinces in 1905; Nunavut was divided off in 1999.

geoCoverage.label: The prairies and the Arctic
geoCoverage.change: Everything Canada bought from the Hudson's Bay Company except the small province of Manitoba, governed at first by a lieutenant-governor who lived in Manitoba and visited.

geoCoverage.label: The northern remainder
geoCoverage.change: Saskatchewan and Alberta were carved out as provinces, without control of their own natural resources, which Ottawa kept until 1930.

acquisitions.how: Canada took over Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory from the Hudson's Bay Company on 15 July 1870 and administered everything outside Manitoba as one territory, ruled from Ottawa through an appointed lieutenant-governor and council.

counterparties.name: The Cree, Blackfoot, Saulteaux, Assiniboine, Dene, Inuit and Metis nations
counterparties.lost: Their independence, in the space of fifteen years. Treaties 1 to 7, signed between 1871 and 1877, exchanged about 1.4 million square kilometres for reserves, annuities and farm equipment; they were signed as the bison disappeared and hunger became the negotiating position.

counterparties.name: The Hudson's Bay Company
counterparties.lost: Its charter rights, sold for £300,000 plus a twentieth of the fertile belt and its trading posts.

instrument.name: Rupert's Land and North-Western Territory Order
instrument.note: The imperial order admitting the territories to Canada, effective 15 July 1870. It is part of Canada's constitution to this day.

people.name: Mistahimaskwa (Big Bear)
people.role: Cree chief who refused to sign Treaty 6 for six years while trying to negotiate a single large territory for all Cree bands

people.name: Pitikwahanapiwiyin (Poundmaker)
people.role: Cree chief and negotiator at Treaty 6, later convicted of treason-felony on evidence Canada set aside in 2019

people.name: Isapo-muxika (Crowfoot)
people.role: Siksika chief who signed Treaty 7 in 1877 and kept the Blackfoot out of the 1885 fighting

people.name: Alexander Morris
people.role: lieutenant-governor who negotiated Treaties 3 to 6 for Canada

acquisitions.resistance: The North-West Resistance of March to May 1885: Metis at Batoche under Louis Riel and Gabriel Dumont, joined by some Cree bands, fought Canadian troops brought west on the unfinished railway. Riel was hanged and eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together at Battleford on 27 November 1885, the largest mass execution in Canadian history.

evidence.author: Blair Stonechild
evidence.work: Loyal till Death: Indians and the North-West Rebellion
evidence.supports: Cree politics in 1885 and the trials and executions that followed.

statusPeriods.label: Ruled from Ottawa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor and an appointed council legislated by ordinance for a territory larger than India; the North-West Mounted Police, formed in 1873 after the Cypress Hills massacre, were the government most people ever saw.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Not a British crown colony but a Canadian territory under direct federal rule, with no responsible government and an appointed executive: the same relationship, one step further out.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Garry, then Battleford from 1876 and Regina from 1883
statusPeriods.franchise: Elected members were added to the council from 1888, but Indigenous people living on reserves could not vote federally without giving up their status, a rule that lasted until 1960.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1880 and 1885 government rations were withheld from Cree bands to force them onto reserves; historians estimate several thousand deaths from starvation and disease in those years.

to.note: British authority over Canada, and so over its territories, ended in stages: self-government from 1867, full legislative independence with the Statute of Westminster on 11 December 1931, and the last British power over the constitution removed on 17 April 1982.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government, then partition into provinces
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The territories won a responsible executive under Frederick Haultain in 1897; he wanted one big province called Buffalo, and Ottawa made two instead, keeping their natural resources for itself until 1930.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Regina, then Ottawa for the northern remainder after 1905
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male property holders, then most adults; women in the prairie provinces won the vote in 1916, before women anywhere else in Canada.

date.note: The territories never left British sovereignty separately; they left with Canada, and historians date that to 1867, to the Statute of Westminster in 1931, or to patriation in 1982.

departures.how: The North-West Territories never negotiated with Britain at all. They were Canadian from 1870 and left British sovereignty on exactly the same timetable as the rest of Canada, without a vote, a treaty or a shot.

becomes.name: Northwest Territories and Nunavut, in Canada

led.name: Frederick Haultain
led.role: premier of the territories who won responsible government in 1897 and lost the argument for a single large province in 1905

led.name: Tagak Curley
led.role: Inuit leader, a founder of the Inuit Tapirisat in 1971, whose campaign led to the creation of Nunavut in 1999

cost.note: The constitutional change cost nothing. What it did not undo was the 1885 executions, the residential schools that operated in the territories into the 1990s, and the High Arctic relocations of 1953 and 1955, when Inuit families were moved from northern Quebec to Ellesmere and Cornwallis Islands partly to assert Canadian sovereignty; Canada apologised and paid compensation in 1996 and 2010.

departures.borders: The territory shrank four times: Manitoba's boundaries were extended in 1881 and 1912, Saskatchewan and Alberta were carved out in 1905, Ontario and Quebec were extended north in 1912, and Nunavut was divided off on 1 April 1999 after an Inuit land claim settlement and an 85 per cent yes vote.

instrument.name: Statute of Westminster 1931
instrument.note: Ended the British Parliament's power to legislate for Canada except over the constitution itself, which was removed by the Canada Act 1982.

contested.note: Dating this is genuinely contested. The Statute of Westminster is the usual answer for legislative independence; Canadian scholars also argue for 1867, for the Balfour Declaration of 1926, and for patriation in 1982. This record uses 1931 with the full range shown.

violence.note: Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together at Battleford on 27 November 1885, the largest mass execution in Canadian history; Poundmaker's conviction was set aside by Canada in 2019 and Big Bear died a year after his release.

populationTransfer.note: Treaties 1 to 11 moved Indigenous nations onto reserves between 1871 and 1921; residential schools took children from them from the 1880s until the 1990s, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented at least 3,200 deaths in those schools nationally, a figure it called a floor.

commonwealth.note: The territories are part of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: Nunavut, created on 1 April 1999, is the only Canadian jurisdiction with an Inuit majority, and it exists because of a land claim rather than a colonial boundary.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census of the North-West Territories, before Saskatchewan and Alberta were separated. Indigenous people were counted separately and incompletely in this period.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1901 census of The North-West Territories
populationWarrant.supports: The North-West Territories’s largest recorded population: 98,967 people, counted in 1901.

pedagogy.hook: Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together at Battleford in November 1885 while Indigenous children from the nearby school were made to watch. It is still the largest mass execution in Canadian history.

misconception.belief: Canada settled the west peacefully, unlike the American frontier.
misconception.correction: It was quieter, not gentler. There was no cavalry war, but between 1880 and 1885 the government withheld rations from Cree bands to force them onto reserves as the bison vanished; historians estimate thousands died of starvation and tuberculosis. Riel was hanged, eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together, and children were taken to residential schools for a century afterwards.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Canadian west shows how a settler state could take a continent with treaties, police and rations rather than armies, and why the paperwork of that process is now being tested in court.

territories.formalName: Yukon Territory, formerly part of the North-Western Territory

namesOverTime.name: The North-Western Territory
namesOverTime.note: Everything British west and north of Rupert's Land that did not drain into Hudson Bay: the Mackenzie basin, the Yukon and the northern interior of British Columbia.

namesOverTime.name: Yukon
namesOverTime.note: Made a separate territory of Canada during the Klondike rush; 'the Yukon Territory' in law until 2003, 'Yukon' since.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Yukon, a Canadian territory since 13 June 1898.

geoCoverage.label: The North-Western Territory
geoCoverage.change: Parliament gave the Hudson's Bay Company an exclusive trade licence over the British territory beyond the Rupert's Land watershed; the company built posts and traded, and governed nobody.

geoCoverage.label: Yukon within Canada
geoCoverage.change: Transferred to Canada with Rupert's Land, administered as part of the North-West Territories, and made a separate territory on 13 June 1898 when 30,000 gold seekers arrived.

acquisitions.how: After the Hudson's Bay Company absorbed its Montreal rival, Parliament gave it a twenty-one-year exclusive licence to trade in all British territory in North America outside Rupert's Land and the settled colonies, which is how the Yukon basin became British on paper.

counterparties.name: The Gwich'in, Han, Northern Tutchone, Southern Tutchone, Kaska and Tlingit nations
counterparties.lost: Nothing in 1821 and a great deal after 1896. Coastal Tlingit had controlled the mountain passes and the trade through them for generations, and the gold rush broke that control; the fourteen Yukon First Nations signed no treaty until the Umbrella Final Agreement of 1993.
counterparties.note: Yukon's modern land claim agreements, signed from 1993 onwards, are among the most complete self-government settlements in Canada.

counterparties.name: Russia
counterparties.lost: Its claim to the interior. The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1825 fixed the boundary at the 141st meridian and along the coastal mountains, wording that was clear about the meridian and vague about the coast, which is exactly what the 1903 Alaska tribunal argued over.

instrument.name: An Act for regulating the Fur Trade, and establishing a Criminal and Civil Jurisdiction within certain Parts of North America
instrument.note: The licence itself was issued on 5 December 1821 and renewed in 1838; it lapsed in 1859.

people.name: Robert Campbell
people.role: Hudson's Bay Company trader who built Fort Selkirk in 1848; Chilkat Tlingit destroyed it in 1852 for cutting across their trade

people.name: Skookum Jim (Keish)
people.role: Tagish man who was one of the party that found gold on Rabbit Creek in August 1896 and started the Klondike rush

people.name: Kate Carmack (Shaaw Tlaa)
people.role: Tagish woman present at the Klondike discovery, whose share of it was taken by her husband

contested.note: Dating British authority in the Yukon is awkward. The 1821 licence is a trading monopoly, not a government; the 1825 convention fixed a boundary with Russia; no British official governed there until Canada sent Mounted Police in 1894. This record uses 1821 and says plainly that it marks a claim, not an administration.

statusPeriods.label: Fur posts on Indigenous terms
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Half a dozen company posts traded with Gwich'in and Tutchone people who set the terms; when Fort Selkirk cut across the Chilkat Tlingit trade route in 1852, the Tlingit pulled it down and the company did not rebuild.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

to.note: British sovereignty over Yukon ended with Canada's, which historians date to 1867, 1931 or 1982.

statusPeriods.label: Canadian territory, run from Ottawa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ottawa appointed a commissioner and sent the North-West Mounted Police; during the Klondike rush the police controlled the passes, turned back anyone without a year's supplies, and gave the Yukon a reputation for order that the Alaskan side never had.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Not a British crown colony but a Canadian territory under direct federal administration with an appointed commissioner: the same degree of top-down rule at one further remove.
statusPeriods.franchise: An elected territorial council from 1908, on a residence and property basis. First Nations people could not vote federally without losing their status until 1960.

date.note: Yukon left British sovereignty with Canada. Historians date Canadian independence to 1867, to the Statute of Westminster of 11 December 1931, or to patriation on 17 April 1982.

departures.how: Yukon was Canadian from 1870 and never negotiated with Britain on its own account; it left British sovereignty with the rest of Canada, and its own self-government from Ottawa came much later, between 1979 and 2003.

becomes.name: Yukon, in Canada

led.name: Elijah Smith
led.role: Champagne and Aishihik leader who presented Together Today for our Children Tomorrow to the Canadian prime minister in 1973 and began Yukon's land claims process

led.name: Erik Nielsen
led.role: long-serving Yukon MP who pressed for responsible territorial government

cost.note: The constitutional change cost nothing. The Klondike rush had cost a great deal: the Han people of Tr'ondek Hwech'in were moved off their fishing camp at the mouth of the Klondike to make room for Dawson City, and epidemics followed the miners in.

departures.borders: Yukon's western boundary is the 141st meridian, agreed with Russia in 1825 and inherited by the United States in 1867. Its southern boundary with Alaska was settled by the 1903 tribunal, which gave the United States the coastal strip and left Yukon landlocked.

contested.note: As with the rest of Canada, the date of independence is disputed between 1867, 1931 and 1982. The full range is shown rather than a single answer.

populationTransfer.note: About 100,000 people set out for the Klondike in 1897-98 and roughly 30,000 to 40,000 arrived; Dawson City had some 30,000 people in 1898 and fewer than 1,000 by 1911.

violence.note: There was no war in the Yukon. The damage was epidemic disease, the loss of fishing sites and, from 1911, the residential school at Carcross that operated until 1969.

commonwealth.note: Yukon is a territory of Canada, a Commonwealth realm.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1825 Anglo-Russian line is now the Yukon-Alaska border, one of the few imperial boundaries in North America drawn by two powers neither of which now exists in that form.

peak.populationNote: 1901 census, taken at the tail of the Klondike rush. The territory's population fell below 5,000 by 1921 and did not pass 27,000 again until the 1990s.

evidence.work: Land of the Midnight Sun: A History of the Yukon
evidence.supports: The fur trade, the Klondike rush and territorial administration.

evidence.author: Morris Zaslow

evidence.supports: Northern administration, the Mounted Police and the gold rush economy.

pedagogy.hook: The Klondike gold was found by a Tagish man, Skookum Jim, and his sister Kate. The claim was registered in her white husband's name, and history books called it Carmack's strike for a century.

misconception.belief: The North was empty land that gold rushes opened up.
misconception.correction: The Yukon was Gwich'in, Han, Tutchone, Kaska and Tlingit country with trade routes the Chilkat Tlingit controlled so tightly that they tore down a Hudson's Bay Company fort in 1852 for undercutting them. The rush of 1898 broke that order in two years, and the fourteen Yukon First Nations got no treaty at all until 1993.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Yukon shows the last stage of the imperial map being drawn, in the 1890s, by a police force and a mining registry rather than an army, and it shows a boundary settlement Canadians still resent.

namesOverTime.name: Dominion of Canada
namesOverTime.note: The delegates wanted Kingdom of Canada; the Colonial Office feared it would annoy the Americans, and Samuel Leonard Tilley suggested Dominion from Psalm 72.

namesOverTime.name: Canada
namesOverTime.note: The word Dominion was never repealed; it simply fell out of use after the 1950s.

modernSuccessors.name: Canada
modernSuccessors.note: Ten provinces and three territories, assembled between 1867 and 1949 and completed as a constitutional state in 1982.

geoCoverage.label: Four provinces
geoCoverage.change: Three British colonies, one of them already double, united into one federal dominion on 1 July 1867.

geoCoverage.label: With Rupert's Land and the North-West
geoCoverage.change: Canada bought the Hudson's Bay Company's charter rights for £300,000 and grew by a factor of about eight overnight; Manitoba was created the same week on Metis terms.

geoCoverage.label: To the Pacific
geoCoverage.change: British Columbia joined on the promise of a railway to the coast within ten years.

geoCoverage.label: With Prince Edward Island
geoCoverage.change: Prince Edward Island joined once Canada agreed to pay its railway debt and buy out its absentee landlords; Britain transferred the Arctic islands in 1880.

to.note: British authority over Canada ended in stages, not on one day: self-government from 1867, the Balfour formula in 1926, legislative independence with the Statute of Westminster on 11 December 1931, and the last British power over the constitution removed on 17 April 1982.

geoCoverage.label: Complete, with Newfoundland
geoCoverage.change: Newfoundland voted to join by 52.3 per cent to 47.7 and became the tenth province at midnight on 31 March 1949, eighty-two years after the first four.

acquisitions.how: Three British colonies merged into a federal dominion by an act of the British Parliament, after conferences at Charlottetown and Quebec in 1864 and London in 1866, and with no popular vote anywhere on whether to do it.

counterparties.name: The colonial legislatures of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
counterparties.lost: Their separate existence and their direct relationship with the Colonial Office. Nova Scotians were never consulted and elected an anti-Confederation majority months later; Britain refused to let them out.

counterparties.name: The First Nations, Inuit and Metis peoples of British North America
counterparties.lost: The Crown's direct treaty relationship. Section 91(24) of the new constitution gave the federal parliament authority over 'Indians, and Lands reserved for the Indians', and the Indian Act of 1876 built a system of wardship out of it that took ninety years to begin dismantling.

instrument.name: British North America Act 1867
instrument.note: Now called the Constitution Act 1867. It was passed at Westminster in about four days of debate, less than the same session gave to a dog licensing bill.

people.name: John A. Macdonald
people.role: first prime minister; architect of Confederation, of the railway and of the residential school system

people.name: George-Etienne Cartier
people.role: brought French Canada in on the promise of a province of its own

people.name: George Brown
people.role: reform editor whose demand for representation by population broke the deadlock

people.name: Charles Tupper
people.role: Nova Scotian premier who joined without asking his voters

acquisitions.resistance: Nova Scotia voted eighteen anti-Confederate MPs out of nineteen in September 1867 and petitioned for repeal; Britain said no. The Metis of Red River stopped the next expansion by force in 1869.

evidence.author: P. B. Waite
evidence.work: The Life and Times of Confederation, 1864-1867
evidence.supports: The conferences, the politics and the passage of the act.

acquisitions.how: Canada paid the Hudson's Bay Company £300,000 and let it keep a twentieth of the fertile belt, and took over a territory of about 3.9 million square kilometres whose inhabitants learned about the sale from newspapers and surveyors.

counterparties.name: The Hudson's Bay Company
counterparties.lost: Its charter rights of 1670, sold for £300,000, about 2.8 million hectares of prairie land and its posts.

counterparties.name: The Metis Nation and the Cree, Saulteaux, Blackfoot, Assiniboine and Dene nations
counterparties.lost: Any say in the transaction. The Metis of Red River seized Fort Garry and negotiated the Manitoba Act; the plains nations negotiated Treaties 1 to 7 over the following seven years as the bison collapsed.

instrument.name: Rupert's Land Act 1868 and the Deed of Surrender of 19 November 1869
instrument.note: The imperial Order in Council admitting the territories took effect on 15 July 1870, delayed eight months by the Red River Resistance.

acquisitions.how: Canada bought the Pacific with a railway: it promised to begin a transcontinental line within two years and finish it within ten, and assumed British Columbia's debt of about $1 million.

counterparties.name: The Colony of British Columbia
counterparties.lost: Its separate colonial status, by a vote of its legislative council rather than of its people; the province gained a railway and a debt-free start.

counterparties.name: The First Nations of British Columbia
counterparties.lost: The chance of treaties. Term 13 handed responsibility for Indigenous people to Ottawa while the province kept the land, and the province then denied that Aboriginal title existed at all until the courts overruled it in 1973 and 1997.

acquisitions.how: The island that had hosted the first Confederation conference and then refused to join for nine years came in once Canada agreed to take on its railway debt and fund the buyout of its absentee landlords.

counterparties.name: The Colony of Prince Edward Island
counterparties.lost: Its separate colonial status; it gained the money to end a century of tenancy.

instrument.name: Prince Edward Island Terms of Union

acquisitions.how: Newfoundland, a bankrupt former dominion under British commission rule since 1934, voted 52.3 per cent to 47.7 for union and became Canada's tenth province at midnight on 31 March 1949.

counterparties.name: The people of Newfoundland and Labrador
counterparties.lost: Their separate statehood, by a narrow vote many of them contested; they gained Canadian family allowances, pensions and unemployment insurance, which the confederation campaign had put at the centre of its case.

instrument.name: British North America Act 1949
instrument.note: The union took effect immediately before the expiration of 31 March 1949, so Newfoundland's first full day as a province was 1 April.

statusPeriods.label: Self-governing at home, British abroad
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Canada ran its own domestic affairs completely and had no foreign policy of its own: when Britain declared war in 1914, Canada was at war, and 61,000 Canadians died in a conflict its parliament never voted to enter.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Ottawa, with a governor general appointed in London and a Colonial Office veto never used after 1873
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-holding men, widening to most adult men by 1900 and to women federally in 1918. Status Indians could not vote federally without giving up their status until 1960; Chinese and South Asian Canadians were disfranchised in British Columbia until 1947-49; Japanese Canadians until 1948.
statusPeriods.note: The 1922 Chanak crisis, when Mackenzie King refused to commit troops on London's say-so, and Canada's separate signature at Versailles in 1919 are the practical steps that made the 1926 formula possible.

to.note: There is no agreed date for Canadian independence. The Balfour Declaration of 1926 declared the dominions equal in status to Britain; the Statute of Westminster of 11 December 1931 gave that legal force; and the Canada Act 1982 removed Westminster's last power, over the constitution itself, on 17 April 1982.

statusPeriods.label: Equal in status, still amending in London
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After 1931 Britain could not legislate for Canada, but Canadians could not amend their own constitution without asking Westminster, because the provinces and Ottawa could not agree a formula for fifty-one years.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage, reached in stages: women federally in 1918, Chinese and South Asian Canadians in 1947, Japanese Canadians in 1948, Inuit in 1950, and status First Nations people without conditions only in 1960.

date.note: Canada has no independence day. Candidates are 1 July 1867 (self-government), 19 November 1926 (the Balfour formula), 11 December 1931 (the Statute of Westminster, legislative independence) and 17 April 1982 (patriation, the end of Westminster's power over the constitution). This record uses 1931 as the point of legislative independence and shows the whole range.

departures.how: Nobody fought and nobody voted: Canada became independent by a series of conferences, statutes and refusals, spread over 115 years, and the last British power over its constitution was given up by an act of Parliament in 1982 at Canada's own request.

becomes.name: Canada

led.name: Robert Borden
led.role: prime minister who won Canada a separate signature at Versailles in 1919 and a seat in the League of Nations

led.name: William Lyon Mackenzie King
led.role: refused to send troops on London's word in 1922 and pushed the dominions to the Balfour formula in 1926

led.name: Pierre Trudeau
led.role: prime minister who patriated the constitution in 1982 with a Charter of Rights, over Quebec's objection

led.name: Rene Levesque
led.role: Quebec premier who lost the 1980 sovereignty referendum and refused to sign the 1982 constitution

departures.movement: Dominion autonomy, argued at imperial conferences rather than in the streets

cost.note: Nobody died fighting Britain. Canada's price for its place in the world was paid on Britain's behalf: about 61,000 Canadian war dead in 1914-18 and about 45,000 in 1939-45, from a country of 8 million and then 11 million. These are Commonwealth War Graves Commission and Canadian official figures.

warrant.check: cwgc.org — search by force and conflict; the Commission is named as the source in this record’s own note.

departures.borders: Canada's borders were drawn by Britain in treaties with other powers, and Canada disliked several of them: the Alaska panhandle in 1903, the Labrador line in 1927, and the maritime boundary at Machias Seal Island, which is still disputed with the United States today.

instrument.name: Statute of Westminster 1931, completed by the Canada Act 1982
instrument.note: The Canada Act 1982 received royal assent on 29 March 1982 and Elizabeth II proclaimed the Constitution Act 1982 in Ottawa on 17 April 1982.

contested.note: Canadians genuinely disagree about their independence date, and the disagreement is the lesson: constitutional independence can be a fifty-year process with no flag-raising moment. School textbooks variously use 1867, 1931 and 1982.

positions.claim: Canada became a self-governing state in 1867 and everything after that was tidying up.
Legislative independence arrived with the Statute of Westminster on 11 December 1931.
Canada was not fully sovereign until patriation on 17 April 1982, because until then only Westminster could amend its constitution.
positions.heldBy: constitutional lawyers and much recent scholarship

populationTransfer.note: Canada was built by immigration and by removal at the same time: roughly 3 million immigrants arrived between 1896 and 1914, while about 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Metis children were taken to residential schools between the 1880s and 1996.

toll.note: Deaths of children in residential schools recorded by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 2015. The Commission identified at least 3,200 named and unnamed deaths and said the true number is higher because records were destroyed and many deaths were never reported; ground-penetrating radar surveys since 2021 have located many unmarked graves.

warrant.author: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada
warrant.work: Canada’s Residential Schools: Missing Children and Unmarked Burials (Final Report, volume 4)
warrant.supports: At least 3,200 named and unnamed deaths of children in the residential schools, with the true number stated by the Commission to be higher.
warrant.check: McGill-Queen’s University Press, 2015; the register is held by the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, nctr.ca.

violence.note: Canada fought no war of independence and two resistances at home: Red River in 1869-70 and the North-West in 1885, after which Louis Riel and eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged.

commonwealth.note: Canada is a founding member of the modern Commonwealth and remains a realm with the British monarch as head of state, represented by a governor general Canada itself chooses.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain retains no territory in North America apart from Bermuda, which is not part of Canada and never was.

consequences.borderLegacy: Every one of Canada's international boundaries was drawn by Britain in negotiation with another power, and Canada was in the room for only the last of them.
consequences.economicLegacy: The Canadian Pacific Railway, finished in 1885, was the price of British Columbia and the instrument of prairie settlement; it was built with a land grant of 10 million hectares and by about 15,000 Chinese labourers Canada then taxed to keep out.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Two official languages, two legal traditions, a Westminster parliament, and a Charter of Rights added in 1982 that made the courts a bigger force in Canadian life than they are in Britain.

peak.populationNote: Estimated population in 1949 when Newfoundland joined, from Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures. Canada is the second-largest country in the world by area and was the largest single territory in the British Empire.

evidence.author: P. B. Waite
evidence.work: The Life and Times of Confederation, 1864-1867
evidence.supports: The making of Confederation.

evidence.author: Phillip Buckner
evidence.work: Canada and the British Empire
evidence.supports: Canada's changing constitutional relationship with Britain from 1763 to 1982.

evidence.author: Margaret Conrad
evidence.work: A Concise History of Canada
evidence.supports: The overall national narrative, expansion and the residential school system.

contested.note: Canada has no agreed independence date; 1867, 1926, 1931 and 1982 are all defended in print. Whether Confederation was a compact between founding peoples or an act of the imperial Parliament is a second live argument, and it was at the centre of the 1980 and 1995 Quebec referendums.

pedagogy.hook: Canada has no independence day. It got self-government in 1867, control of its own foreign policy in 1931, and the right to change its own constitution only in 1982 — and nobody fought a war over any of it.

misconception.belief: Countries become independent on a particular day, usually after a struggle.
misconception.correction: Canada did it in slow motion and by agreement: British North America Act 1867, Versailles signature 1919, Balfour Declaration 1926, Statute of Westminster 1931, Canada Act 1982. Ask a Canadian when their country became independent and you will get three different answers, all defensible. The empire's settler colonies mostly left like this; the colonies of rule mostly did not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Canada is the model the empire wanted: a self-governing settler dominion that stayed loyal, fought Britain's wars and separated without violence. Which is exactly why comparing it with India, Kenya or Ireland shows what the difference really was, and race was the operative criterion.

events.title: The Hudson's Bay Company Charter
events.summary: Charles II granted eighteen investors led by Prince Rupert a monopoly of trade and the ownership of every land drained by rivers flowing into Hudson Bay: about 3.9 million square kilometres, sight unseen.
events.significance: It is the largest single land grant in the empire's history and the template for rule by chartered company that Britain used again in India, Africa and Borneo. The company still exists, and the territory it sold to Canada in 1870 is a third of that country.

places.name: York Factory
places.note: The company's principal depot on Hudson Bay for two centuries.

places.name: Hudson's Bay House, London
places.note: The company was governed from the City of London, not from America.

people.name: Prince Rupert of the Rhine
people.role: the king's cousin and the company's first governor

people.name: Pierre-Esprit Radisson
people.role: French Canadian trader who brought the idea to London after Quebec refused it

pedagogy.hook: One document, one afternoon, one twelfth of North America handed to eighteen investors who had never seen it.

misconception.belief: Governments built empires.
misconception.correction: Companies did much of it. The Hudson's Bay Company, the East India Company, the Royal African Company and the British South Africa Company all held territory, raised forces and governed people under charter, and the government could disclaim responsibility when things went wrong.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Rule by chartered company is the mechanism students most often miss, and Hudson Bay is its longest-running example: two hundred years of company government before any state arrived.
