evidence.work: Commerce by a Frozen Sea: Native Americans and the European Fur Trade
evidence.supports: The company's operations and its dependence on Indigenous traders.

events.title: King Philip's War
events.summary: Metacom, the Wampanoag sachem the English called King Philip, led a coalition against the New England colonies after fifty years of land loss and colonial courts. Twelve towns were destroyed and about a tenth of the region's fighting men were killed.
events.significance: Proportionally the deadliest war in New England's history. It ended Indigenous military power in southern New England, sent hundreds of survivors into Caribbean slavery, and taught the colonies that they could fight a war without England's help.

places.name: Mount Hope, Bristol, Rhode Island
places.note: Metacom's home ground, where he was killed on 12 August 1676.

places.name: The Great Swamp, South Kingstown
places.note: Where colonial troops burned the Narragansett winter town on 19 December 1675.

people.name: Metacom (King Philip)
people.role: Wampanoag sachem who led the coalition; killed and dismembered, his head displayed at Plymouth for about twenty years

people.name: Weetamoo
people.role: Pocasset saunkskwa who led several hundred fighters and drowned fleeing in August 1676

people.name: Mary Rowlandson
people.role: captive whose 1682 narrative became the first American bestseller and shaped how the war was remembered

people.name: Josiah Winslow
people.role: governor of Plymouth who commanded the Great Swamp attack

toll.note: Roughly 800 to 1,000 colonists and several thousand Indigenous people, from fighting, starvation and disease. Nobody counted the Indigenous dead; the range comes from town records, later reconstructions and estimates of the pre-war population, which are themselves uncertain.

pedagogy.hook: Metacom's father had kept the Plymouth colony alive in 1621. Fifty-four years later Metacom went to war, and when he was killed the English cut off his head and displayed it for twenty years.

misconception.belief: Indigenous people in New England simply faded away after the Pilgrims arrived.
misconception.correction: They fought a war that destroyed twelve English towns and killed about one in ten New England men of fighting age. They lost, and the peace was brutal: hundreds of Wampanoag and Narragansett people, including Metacom's nine-year-old son, were sold into slavery in the Caribbean.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows colonisation as a war rather than a spread, and shows the enslavement of Indigenous North Americans, which most accounts leave out entirely.

evidence.author: Jill Lepore
evidence.work: The Name of War: King Philip's War and the Origins of American Identity
evidence.supports: The war, its casualties and its afterlife in colonial writing.

contested.note: Casualty figures are estimates. Colonial losses are reasonably documented from town and church records; Indigenous losses are not, and depend on pre-war population estimates that historians dispute.

events.title: The Stono Rebellion
events.summary: About twenty enslaved people, many of them Kongolese and Catholic, seized weapons at a store on the Stono River and marched south for Spanish Florida, which had promised freedom to anyone escaping British slavery. Roughly sixty more joined before the militia caught them.
events.significance: The largest slave rebellion in the mainland British colonies. It produced South Carolina's 1740 Negro Act, which banned teaching enslaved people to write, restricted their movement and taxed new imports for a decade, and it shows enslaved people using imperial rivalry as an escape route.

places.name: Stono River bridge, Rantowles
places.note: Where the rising began at Hutchenson's store.

places.name: St Augustine, Florida
places.note: Spain's free settlement at Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose was the rebels' destination.

people.name: William Bull
people.role: lieutenant-governor who happened on the marchers and raised the militia

toll.note: About 25 white colonists and between 40 and 50 Black rebels, killed in the fighting or executed afterwards. The figures come from the colony's own reports, which had reason to be precise about white deaths and less so about Black ones.

pedagogy.hook: The rebels marched south towards Florida beating drums and carrying a banner reading Liberty, thirty-seven years before anyone in Philadelphia wrote the word on parchment.

misconception.belief: Enslaved people rarely rebelled because rebellion was hopeless.
misconception.correction: They rebelled constantly, and they used the rivalries between empires to do it. Spain offered freedom in Florida to anyone who escaped British slavery and converted; the free Black town of Mose outside St Augustine was the result. Stono was one attempt among many, and the laws passed after it show how seriously the colony took the threat.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Stono links slavery, resistance and imperial rivalry in one march, and explains why Georgia was founded as a buffer and why Britain took Florida in 1763.

evidence.author: Peter H. Wood
evidence.work: Black Majority: Negroes in Colonial South Carolina from 1670 through the Stono Rebellion
evidence.supports: The rising, its Kongolese context and the 1740 Negro Act.

contested.note: Almost everything known about Stono comes from a handful of colonial accounts written by the men who suppressed it. The rebels' own aims are inferred, chiefly from the direction they marched and from the Kongolese and Catholic background of many participants.

events.title: The Expulsion of the Acadians
events.summary: The governor and council at Halifax decided to deport the whole Acadian population of Nova Scotia, burn their farms and scatter them among colonies that did not want them. About 10,000 people were removed over nine years and roughly a third died.
events.significance: The largest forced removal of a European population by a British government before the twentieth century, carried out by a colonial council without instructions from London. It emptied the best farmland in the Maritimes for New England settlers and created the Cajuns of Louisiana.

places.name: Grand-Pre
places.note: Where the men and boys were held in the church on 5 September 1755 and told they were being deported.

places.name: Fort Beausejour
places.note: Captured in June 1755; its fall removed the last French protection for the mainland Acadians.

people.name: Charles Lawrence
people.role: lieutenant-governor who ordered the deportation on his council's advice and without waiting for London

people.name: John Winslow
people.role: New England officer who carried out the removal at Grand-Pre and recorded his unease in his journal

people.name: Joseph Broussard (Beausoleil)
people.role: Acadian resistance leader who fought the deportation for years and led survivors to Louisiana in 1765

toll.note: About 10,000 to 12,000 Acadians were deported from Nova Scotia, Ile Saint-Jean and Ile Royale between 1755 and 1764. Deaths from shipwreck, smallpox and exposure are usually put at a third or more of those removed; the Duke William and the Violet alone sank with about 700 people in December 1758. Parish and shipping records are incomplete.

pedagogy.hook: The men of Grand-Pre were summoned to their own church to hear the order, and then held there while their farms were burned in front of them.

misconception.belief: The Acadians were deported because they were spies or rebels.
misconception.correction: They had lived under British rule for forty-five years and had repeatedly offered a qualified oath: loyalty to the king, but no obligation to bear arms against their Mi'kmaq neighbours and French relatives. Britain had accepted that arrangement for decades. In 1755, with war coming and their land wanted, the council decided the qualified oath was no longer enough.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case in North America of an empire removing an entire civilian population, done by a colonial council, and it shows how quickly a long-tolerated compromise can be revoked when land and war are in play.

evidence.author: John Mack Faragher
evidence.work: A Great and Noble Scheme: The Tragic Story of the Expulsion of the French Acadians from their American Homeland
evidence.supports: The decision, the operation and its human cost.

evidence.author: Naomi E. S. Griffiths
evidence.work: From Migrant to Acadian: A North American Border People, 1604-1755
evidence.supports: Acadian society and the long negotiation over the oath.

contested.note: Historians argue about whether the deportation should be described as ethnic cleansing or genocide, and about how far London was implicated. The numbers deported and the scale of mortality are also estimates from incomplete records. That it was ordered in Halifax, executed by New England troops, and killed thousands is not in dispute.

events.title: The Fall of Quebec
events.summary: After a summer of bombardment and the burning of the parishes below the town, Wolfe's army climbed the cliff at the Anse au Foulon overnight and beat Montcalm's on the Plains of Abraham in about twenty minutes. Both commanders died; Montreal capitulated a year later.
events.significance: It ended French North America and gave Britain a colony of 70,000 French-speaking Catholics it had no idea how to govern. Removing France also removed the ally Indigenous nations had played against Britain, which is a direct cause of Pontiac's War four years later.

places.name: Plains of Abraham, Quebec City
places.note: The battle lasted about twenty minutes on a field the French had not fortified.

places.name: Anse au Foulon
places.note: The cove where 4,500 men climbed a 50-metre cliff path in the dark.

people.name: James Wolfe
people.role: British commander, killed in the battle; had ordered the systematic burning of Canadian farms that summer

people.name: Louis-Joseph de Montcalm
people.role: French commander, mortally wounded; chose to fight rather than wait for reinforcements

people.name: Francois-Gaston de Levis
people.role: beat the British outside Quebec at Sainte-Foy in April 1760 and still lost the colony when the first ships up the river were British

people.name: Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil
people.role: Canadian-born governor general who negotiated the capitulation of Montreal and the terms for his people

toll.note: Killed and wounded on 13 September 1759, roughly 660 British and 640 French by the armies' own returns. Canadian civilian deaths from the bombardment of Quebec and the burning of about 1,400 farms were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: The battle that decided who would rule half a continent lasted about twenty minutes, and both generals were dead within a day of it.

misconception.belief: Britain conquered Canada in one battle.
misconception.correction: Quebec fell in September 1759; the French army beat the British outside the same town at Sainte-Foy in April 1760, and only the arrival of a British fleet rather than a French one decided the siege. Montreal held out until 8 September 1760, and the colony was formally ceded only in 1763.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The conquest created a British colony with a French Catholic majority, which forced the empire into the concessions of the Quebec Act and made Canada permanently bilingual.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The campaign, the battle and the capitulations.

events.title: The Peace of Paris, 1763
events.summary: France gave up Canada and everything east of the Mississippi; Spain gave up Florida to recover Havana; France secretly gave Louisiana to Spain. Britain became the only European power in eastern North America and doubled its debt doing it.
events.significance: The largest single transfer of territory in the empire's history to that date, and the cause of everything that followed: the Proclamation line, the taxes to pay for the garrison, Pontiac's War, and within thirteen years the American revolution.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where Britain, France and Spain signed on 10 February 1763.

places.name: Havana
places.note: Captured by Britain in 1762 and traded back to Spain for Florida.

people.name: John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute
people.role: British prime minister who made the peace and was burned in effigy for giving too much back

people.name: William Pitt the Elder
people.role: attacked the terms in Parliament for returning Guadeloupe, Martinique and Havana

people.name: Etienne-Francois, duc de Choiseul
people.role: French minister who chose to keep the sugar islands and let Canada go

pedagogy.hook: France was given a choice at the peace table and kept Guadeloupe and Martinique instead of Canada, because sugar was worth more than a continent of snow.

misconception.belief: Winning the Seven Years' War made Britain's empire secure.
misconception.correction: It nearly destroyed it. The war doubled the national debt to about £133 million, the new territories needed a standing army of 10,000 men in America, and the taxes raised to pay for that army — the Sugar Act, the Stamp Act, the Townshend duties — provoked the rebellion that lost thirteen colonies twenty years later.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: 1763 is the hinge of the whole first British Empire: the moment of greatest triumph and the start of the crisis that broke it.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The Scratch of a Pen: 1763 and the Transformation of North America
evidence.supports: The terms of the peace and their consequences across the continent.

evidence.author: Fred Anderson
evidence.work: Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America, 1754-1766
evidence.supports: The war, the debt and the imperial reorganisation that followed.

events.title: The Royal Proclamation of 1763
events.summary: George III set up governments for the new colonies of Quebec, East Florida and West Florida, and reserved all land west of the Appalachian watershed to the Indigenous nations, forbidding settlement there and allowing only the Crown to buy Indigenous land.
events.significance: It is the founding document of Aboriginal title in Canadian law, still cited in the courts and named in the Constitution Act 1982. It was also one of the first grievances of the American colonists, who read it as a wall built to keep them near the coast where they could be taxed.

places.name: Fort Pitt
places.note: The western limit of settlement the Proclamation was meant to enforce, and the place where smallpox blankets were handed to Lenape emissaries in June 1763.

people.name: Obwandiyag (Pontiac)
people.role: Odawa war leader whose coalition made a new western policy unavoidable

people.name: William Petty, Earl of Shelburne
people.role: president of the Board of Trade who began drafting the western policy

people.name: William Johnson
people.role: Superintendent of Indian Affairs who had to make the line work on the ground, and moved it west in 1768

pedagogy.hook: The same piece of paper is a founding charter of Indigenous rights in Canada and one of the reasons Americans rebelled. It depends which side of the line you were standing on.

misconception.belief: Britain protected Indigenous land out of principle.
misconception.correction: It did it after losing eight forts in a summer to Pontiac's coalition, and to control land speculation. The recognition of Indigenous title in the Proclamation is real, enforceable and still law in Canada; the motive was a war Britain could not win and a frontier it could not police.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: One document, two opposite legacies, and a lesson in reading motives and consequences separately.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The Scratch of a Pen: 1763 and the Transformation of North America
evidence.supports: The Proclamation's drafting, purpose and reception.

contested.note: Historians disagree about the balance of motives: protection of Indigenous nations after Pontiac's War, control of settlement so that colonists stayed governable and taxable, and Crown control of the profits of land purchase are all documented in ministers' correspondence.

events.title: Pontiac's War
events.summary: A coalition of Odawa, Anishinaabe, Wyandot, Lenape, Shawnee, Seneca and other nations, inspired partly by the Lenape prophet Neolin, took eight of the twelve British forts west of the Appalachians in a single summer and besieged Detroit for five months.
events.significance: It forced Britain to abandon Amherst's policy of treating Indigenous nations as conquered subjects, produced the Royal Proclamation, and showed that the interior could not be held by garrisons. It also produced one of the best-documented cases of deliberate biological warfare in the empire's history.

places.name: Fort Detroit
places.note: Besieged from 9 May to 31 October 1763.

places.name: Fort Pitt
places.note: Besieged from June 1763; blankets and a handkerchief from its smallpox hospital were given to Lenape emissaries on 24 June.

places.name: Bushy Run
places.note: Where Henry Bouquet's relief column fought its way through in August 1763.

people.name: Obwandiyag (Pontiac)
people.role: Odawa war leader at Detroit; made peace in 1766 and was killed by another Indigenous man in 1769

people.name: Neolin
people.role: Lenape prophet whose teaching of separation from European goods and alliances gave the rising its ideology

people.name: Guyasuta
people.role: Seneca leader who helped organise the western nations

people.name: Jeffery Amherst
people.role: British commander-in-chief who cut the customary presents and wrote approving the use of smallpox against the besiegers

people.name: Henry Bouquet
people.role: Swiss officer in British service who relieved Fort Pitt and to whom Amherst wrote about the blankets

toll.note: Roughly 400 British soldiers killed and perhaps 2,000 settlers killed or captured; Indigenous losses were never counted and the smallpox deaths cannot be separated from other outbreaks. All figures are estimates from military returns and settler petitions.

pedagogy.hook: In June 1763 British officers at Fort Pitt gave two blankets and a handkerchief from their smallpox hospital to Lenape emissaries, and wrote in the accounts that it was done to convey the disease.

misconception.belief: Smallpox blankets are a myth.
misconception.correction: For 1763 they are documented in three places: the fort's own account ledger, William Trent's journal, and an exchange between Amherst and Bouquet in which Amherst asks whether smallpox could be sent 'among the disaffected tribes of Indians' and Bouquet agrees to try. Whether that particular attempt caused the epidemic that followed is uncertain; that it was attempted and approved is not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Pontiac's War is the reason the Proclamation line exists, and it shows Indigenous nations as a military power that could force imperial policy to change.

evidence.author: Gregory Evans Dowd
evidence.work: War under Heaven: Pontiac, the Indian Nations, and the British Empire
evidence.supports: The rising, Neolin's teaching, Amherst's policy and the Fort Pitt blankets.

contested.note: The documents proving the attempt at Fort Pitt are not disputed. What is disputed is the epidemiological effect: smallpox was already circulating in the Ohio country, and historians differ on whether the blankets caused any of the deaths that followed.

events.title: The Stamp Act
events.summary: Parliament taxed every legal document, newspaper, pamphlet, licence and pack of playing cards in the American colonies to help pay for the 10,000 soldiers now stationed there. Colonists refused to buy the stamps, boycotted British goods, and Parliament repealed it in eleven months.
events.significance: The first direct internal tax Parliament ever levied on the colonies, and the moment the argument shifted from trade regulation to the right to tax. The repeal came with a Declaratory Act asserting Parliament's power to legislate for the colonies in all cases whatsoever, which conceded the money and kept the principle.

places.name: Boston
places.note: Where crowds destroyed the stamp distributor's house in August 1765 and forced his resignation.

places.name: New York City
places.note: The Stamp Act Congress of nine colonies met here in October 1765.

people.name: George Grenville
people.role: prime minister who devised the tax to make the colonies pay a third of the cost of their own garrison

people.name: Patrick Henry
people.role: moved the Virginia Resolves against the act in May 1765

people.name: Ebenezer Mackintosh
people.role: Boston shoemaker who led the crowds that made the act unenforceable

people.name: Benjamin Franklin
people.role: colonial agent whose examination before the Commons in February 1766 helped secure repeal

pedagogy.hook: The tax that started the American revolution was a stamp duty on paper, and it was repealed within a year because colonists simply refused to use paper that carried it.

misconception.belief: The colonies were taxed heavily by Britain.
misconception.correction: They were among the lightest-taxed people in the empire: British taxpayers paid roughly twenty-five times more per head. The argument was never about the amount. It was about who had the right to levy it, and about a standing army stationed in peacetime among people who had never had one.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows a constitutional argument, not an economic grievance, driving an empire apart, and it shows boycotts and crowds defeating an act of Parliament.

evidence.author: Edmund S. Morgan
evidence.work: The Stamp Act Crisis: Prologue to Revolution
evidence.supports: The act, the colonial resistance and the repeal.

events.title: The Quebec Act
events.summary: Parliament restored French civil law in Quebec, guaranteed the Catholic church its tithes, replaced the anti-Catholic Test oath so Catholics could hold office, and extended the province south-west to the Ohio and the Mississippi.
events.significance: It bought the loyalty of 70,000 French Canadians, who stayed out of the American revolution the following year. The thirteen colonies listed it among the Intolerable Acts because it gave Catholics rights and closed the west, and it is the legal root of Quebec's distinct civil law today.

places.name: Quebec City
places.note: Where an American army was beaten in a snowstorm on 31 December 1775.

people.name: Guy Carleton
people.role: governor who argued in London that Quebec must be governed through its own institutions, and later defended it against invasion

people.name: Jean-Olivier Briand
people.role: Bishop of Quebec, who urged Canadians to stay loyal in 1775

pedagogy.hook: Britain gave Catholics in Quebec the right to hold public office in 1774. Catholics in Britain and Ireland had to wait until 1829.

misconception.belief: The American revolution was a fight for liberty against tyranny.
misconception.correction: One of the Intolerable Acts the Continental Congress protested against was the Quebec Act, which extended religious toleration to Catholics and recognised Indigenous land west of the mountains. Liberty in 1774 meant different things to different colonists, and for many of them it included the freedom to expand west and to keep Catholics out of office.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why Canada exists: the empire kept the St Lawrence by conceding to the people who lived there what it refused to concede to the colonies that rebelled.

evidence.author: Hilda Neatby
evidence.work: Quebec: The Revolutionary Age, 1760-1791
evidence.supports: The act's drafting, its terms and its effect in 1775-76.

events.title: Dunmore's Proclamation
events.summary: Virginia's last royal governor, on a warship in the Chesapeake, declared martial law and offered freedom to any enslaved or indentured man belonging to a rebel who would join the king's forces. Several hundred reached him and formed the Ethiopian Regiment.
events.significance: It made the war a war about slavery three months before independence was declared. Britain repeated the offer in the Philipsburg Proclamation of 1779, tens of thousands of enslaved people fled to British lines, and about 3,000 were carried to Nova Scotia in 1783 as free people.

places.name: Norfolk, Virginia
places.note: Where the proclamation was printed and where Dunmore's fleet lay.

places.name: Gwynn's Island
places.note: Where smallpox killed much of the Ethiopian Regiment in the summer of 1776.

people.name: John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore
people.role: royal governor who issued the proclamation from HMS William

people.name: Titus (Colonel Tye)
people.role: escaped from New Jersey and led a loyalist raiding company for four years

people.name: Harry Washington
people.role: escaped from George Washington's Mount Vernon, served in the Black Pioneers, and went to Nova Scotia and then Sierra Leone

toll.note: Of the several hundred who reached Dunmore, most died of smallpox and camp fever within a year. Across the war perhaps 20,000 enslaved people reached British lines; a majority died of disease, some were re-enslaved by loyalist owners, and about 3,000 were evacuated as free people from New York in 1783.

pedagogy.hook: The first emancipation proclamation in American history was issued by a British earl on a warship, to win a war, three months before the Declaration of Independence.

misconception.belief: The American revolutionaries were on the side of freedom and the British on the side of oppression.
misconception.correction: For enslaved Americans the calculation ran the other way. Britain offered freedom to those who would fight for it, and about 20,000 took the offer; Washington and Jefferson both owned people who ran to British lines. Britain's motive was military, not moral, and it kept slavery in its Caribbean colonies for another sixty years. Both things are true at once.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It forces students to hold two facts together, which is what historical thinking is: an empire acting from self-interest can still be the better option for the people it offers freedom to.

evidence.author: Simon Schama
evidence.work: Rough Crossings: Britain, the Slaves and the American Revolution
evidence.supports: The proclamation, the Black Loyalists and the evacuation to Nova Scotia.

evidence.author: Cassandra Pybus
evidence.work: Epic Journeys of Freedom: Runaway Slaves of the American Revolution and their Global Quest for Liberty
evidence.supports: The numbers who escaped, where they went and what happened to them.

contested.note: How many enslaved people left their owners during the war is genuinely uncertain. Older estimates ran as high as 100,000; Cassandra Pybus's archival work argues for a figure closer to 20,000 reaching British lines, and the difference matters for how the war is understood.

events.title: The American War of Independence
events.summary: What began as a colonial rising over taxation and self-government became a world war when France joined in 1778, Spain in 1779 and the Dutch Republic in 1780. Britain fought in North America, the Caribbean, Gibraltar, the Gulf of Mexico and southern India, and lost thirteen colonies.
events.significance: The empire lost its largest settler population and gained a lesson it applied everywhere afterwards: give settler colonies self-government before they demand it. It also redirected Britain towards Asia, where its Indian empire grew faster in the twenty years after 1783 than in the fifty before.

places.name: Concord, Massachusetts
places.note: Where colonists turned back a British column on 19 April 1775.

places.name: Saratoga, New York
places.note: Burgoyne's surrender on 17 October 1777 brought France into the war.

places.name: Yorktown, Virginia
places.note: Cornwallis surrendered about 7,000 men on 19 October 1781 after a French fleet cut him off.

places.name: Gibraltar
places.note: Besieged by France and Spain from 1779 to 1783; Britain held it and gave up Florida and Menorca instead.

people.name: George Washington
people.role: commander of the Continental Army; kept it in the field for eight years, which was the strategy

people.name: Lord North
people.role: British prime minister for the whole war; resigned in March 1782 after Yorktown

people.name: Thayendanegea (Joseph Brant)
people.role: Mohawk leader who fought for the Crown and whose people lost their homeland at the peace

people.name: Bernardo de Galvez
people.role: Spanish governor of Louisiana who conquered British West Florida

people.name: Comte de Rochambeau
people.role: commanded the French army that made Yorktown possible

toll.note: No agreed figure exists. Roughly 25,000 American deaths from all causes, about 24,000 British and German, and unknown numbers of Indigenous people and of enslaved people who died of disease in British camps. Disease killed far more than combat on every side, and nobody counted civilians.

pedagogy.hook: Britain lost the war in America and won it everywhere else: it kept Gibraltar, Jamaica and India, and gave away the Floridas and Menorca to get the peace it wanted.

misconception.belief: 1776 ended the British Empire.
misconception.correction: Ask whether the empire was bigger in 1770 or 1820. It was bigger in 1820, and by a wide margin. Losing thirteen colonies cost Britain about 2.5 million subjects; the conquest of Bengal, Ceylon, the Cape, Trinidad, Malta and Mauritius over the same forty years gained it tens of millions. The empire did not end in 1783; it moved east.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the pivot between the first empire, Atlantic and settler, and the second, Asian and ruled, and it is the reason Canada, Australia and New Zealand were given self-government early.

evidence.author: Piers Mackesy
evidence.work: The War for America, 1775-1783
evidence.supports: The war as a global conflict fought by a British government with limited resources.

evidence.author: P. J. Marshall
evidence.work: The Making and Unmaking of Empires: Britain, India, and America c.1750-1783
evidence.supports: The simultaneous loss of America and expansion in India.

contested.note: Casualty totals for this war are unusually uncertain: army returns are incomplete, militia deaths were rarely recorded, and the deaths of enslaved people who fled to British lines were not counted at all. Estimates of total deaths range from about 30,000 to over 90,000 depending on what is included.

events.title: The Treaty of Paris, 1783
events.summary: Britain recognised the independence of the thirteen states and gave them everything east of the Mississippi between the Great Lakes and Florida. On the same day it signed separate treaties returning East and West Florida and Menorca to Spain and settling with France.
events.significance: It handed the United States a vast interior Britain had promised in 1763 to protect for Indigenous nations, none of whom were consulted or defeated. Britain kept its western forts until 1796 and armed its former allies from them, which fed thirty years of frontier war.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Signed at the Hotel d'York on the rue Jacob.

places.name: Fort Niagara
places.note: One of the western posts Britain held on American soil until 1796 in breach of the treaty.

people.name: Benjamin Franklin
people.role: American negotiator who opened separate talks with Britain behind France's back

people.name: John Jay
people.role: American negotiator who insisted on recognition of independence before substantive talks

people.name: Richard Oswald
people.role: British negotiator, a Scottish merchant who had made a fortune in the slave trade

people.name: Thayendanegea (Joseph Brant)
people.role: Mohawk leader who called the treaty a betrayal and organised the Western Confederacy in response

pedagogy.hook: Britain gave away the homelands of a dozen Indigenous nations in Article 2 of a treaty that never mentions them, and several of those nations had never lost a battle.

misconception.belief: Peace treaties settle wars between the sides that fought them.
misconception.correction: The 1783 treaty was signed by two parties and disposed of a third. The Haudenosaunee, Shawnee, Lenape, Miami and Creek had fought as Britain's allies, were undefeated in 1783, and were not represented at Paris. The Northwest Indian War that followed lasted twelve years and included the worst defeat a United States army ever suffered at Indigenous hands.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single example of the empire's habit of settling other people's futures in European rooms, and the same pattern recurs at Berlin in 1885 and at Paris in 1919.

evidence.author: Colin G. Calloway
evidence.work: The American Revolution in Indian Country: Crisis and Diversity in Native American Communities
evidence.supports: The treaty's effect on Britain's Indigenous allies.

evidence.author: Maya Jasanoff
evidence.work: Liberty's Exiles: American Loyalists in the Revolutionary World
evidence.supports: The peace settlement and the dispersal of loyalists that followed.

events.title: The Loyalist Exodus
events.summary: About 60,000 loyalists left the new United States, taking some 15,000 enslaved people with them, and roughly 3,000 free Black Loyalists sailed from New York under the protection of promises Britain had made them. Most went to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, the Bahamas and Britain.
events.significance: It doubled the English-speaking population of British North America in two years, created New Brunswick and Upper Canada, and produced the Black Loyalist community whose 1,196 members founded Freetown, Sierra Leone, in 1792 after Nova Scotia broke its promises to them.

places.name: New York City
places.note: The main evacuation port; the Book of Negroes was compiled here listing about 3,000 Black Loyalists by name.

places.name: Birchtown, Nova Scotia
places.note: The largest free Black settlement in North America in the 1780s, and the poorest.

places.name: Freetown, Sierra Leone
places.note: Founded in March 1792 by 1,196 Black Loyalists who sailed from Halifax.

people.name: Guy Carleton
people.role: British commander at New York who refused Washington's demand to hand back formerly enslaved people and had their names recorded instead

people.name: Thomas Peters
people.role: Black Loyalist sergeant who sailed to London to protest Nova Scotia's broken land promises and won the Sierra Leone expedition

people.name: David George
people.role: Baptist preacher, formerly enslaved, who founded churches in Nova Scotia and then in Freetown

people.name: Thayendanegea (Joseph Brant)
people.role: led Six Nations loyalists to the Grand River in Upper Canada

toll.note: About 60,000 loyalists left, plus roughly 15,000 enslaved people carried by them and some 3,000 free Black Loyalists. Figures come from British embarkation returns, claims commission records and the Book of Negroes, and are among the better-documented refugee counts of the eighteenth century.

pedagogy.hook: Britain kept a written list of the 3,000 formerly enslaved people it refused to hand back to their owners. The Book of Negroes gives their names and ages, and it is still the best record of these lives that exists.

misconception.belief: The loyalists were rich British officials who went home.
misconception.correction: Most were American-born farmers, artisans and soldiers, and about a tenth of those who reached the Maritimes were Black. They did not go home; they went to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Upper Canada and built new colonies. Canada's English-speaking population is largely descended from the losing side of the American revolution.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The exodus explains why Canada exists as a separate country, and the Black Loyalists' journey from Virginia to New York to Nova Scotia to Sierra Leone shows the empire as one connected system.

evidence.author: Maya Jasanoff
evidence.work: Liberty's Exiles: American Loyalists in the Revolutionary World
evidence.supports: The scale, destinations and experience of the loyalist diaspora.

evidence.author: Simon Schama
evidence.work: Rough Crossings: Britain, the Slaves and the American Revolution
evidence.supports: The Black Loyalists, Birchtown and the Sierra Leone expedition.

events.title: The War of 1812
events.summary: The United States invaded British North America expecting an easy conquest and failed. British, Canadian and Indigenous forces held the line; Britain burned Washington in August 1814; the peace restored every border exactly as it had been.
events.significance: It secured British North America and made a Canadian identity out of the defence of it. For Indigenous nations it was a catastrophe: Tecumseh's confederacy was destroyed with him at Moraviantown, and the peace abandoned the Indigenous buffer state Britain had promised.

places.name: Queenston Heights
places.note: British victory on 13 October 1812 in which General Isaac Brock was killed.

places.name: Moraviantown, Ontario
places.note: Where Tecumseh was killed on 5 October 1813 and his confederacy broke.

places.name: Washington, DC
places.note: Burned by British forces on 24 August 1814, in reprisal for the burning of York.

places.name: York (Toronto)
places.note: Burned by American forces on 27 April 1813.

people.name: Tecumseh
people.role: Shawnee leader who built a multi-national confederacy to hold the Ohio country and allied with Britain; killed at Moraviantown

people.name: Isaac Brock
people.role: British commander who took Detroit with Tecumseh's help in August 1812 and was killed at Queenston Heights

people.name: Laura Secord
people.role: walked thirty kilometres through American-held country in June 1813 to warn of an attack at Beaver Dams

people.name: Charles-Michel de Salaberry
people.role: commanded the Canadian Voltigeurs who turned back the American advance on Montreal at Chateauguay in October 1813

people.name: John Norton (Teyoninhokarawen)
people.role: Mohawk leader who commanded Six Nations warriors at Queenston Heights and Beaver Dams

toll.note: Roughly 15,000 American and 8,600 British and Canadian deaths from all causes, disease included, plus Indigenous losses that were never counted. Figures come from army returns and are incomplete on all sides.

pedagogy.hook: The war ended with every border exactly where it had started, and the United States and Britain have each claimed victory ever since. The people who unambiguously lost were Tecumseh's confederacy.

misconception.belief: The War of 1812 was a draw that changed nothing.
misconception.correction: It changed everything for Indigenous nations east of the Mississippi. Britain had promised a permanent Indigenous territory in the Ohio country and dropped the demand at Ghent in exchange for a return to the pre-war borders. Tecumseh was dead, the confederacy was broken, and American expansion into the interior became unstoppable within twenty years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment British North America stopped being a set of colonies waiting to be absorbed by the United States, and the moment Indigenous nations east of the Mississippi ran out of allies.

evidence.author: Alan Taylor
evidence.work: The Civil War of 1812: American Citizens, British Subjects, Irish Rebels, and Indian Allies
evidence.supports: The war as a civil conflict on a borderland, and the Indigenous alliance.

events.title: The Rebellions of 1837-38
events.summary: Reformers in Lower and Upper Canada took up arms after London rejected their demands for a government answerable to the elected assembly. The Patriotes fought several battles in the Richelieu valley; Mackenzie's Toronto rising collapsed in a day.
events.significance: The risings failed militarily and won politically: Britain sent Lord Durham to investigate, and his report of 1839 recommended responsible government, which arrived in Nova Scotia in 1848 and became the model for every settler colony in the empire.

places.name: Saint-Denis-sur-Richelieu
places.note: The Patriotes' only victory, on 23 November 1837.

places.name: Saint-Eustache
places.note: Where about seventy Patriotes died on 14 December 1837, many burned in the church.

places.name: Montgomery's Tavern, Toronto
places.note: Where Mackenzie's rising was scattered on 7 December 1837.

people.name: Louis-Joseph Papineau
people.role: leader of the Patriote party who wrote the Ninety-Two Resolutions and fled to the United States when fighting began

people.name: Wolfred Nelson
people.role: doctor who commanded at Saint-Denis, was transported to Bermuda and later became mayor of Montreal

people.name: William Lyon Mackenzie
people.role: Toronto newspaper editor and first mayor who led the Upper Canadian rising

people.name: Chevalier de Lorimier
people.role: notary hanged at Montreal on 15 February 1839; his last letter is a founding text of Quebec nationalism

people.name: John Colborne
people.role: British commander whose troops burned Saint-Eustache and Saint-Benoit

toll.note: About 325 people were killed, the great majority of them Patriotes in Lower Canada. Twelve Patriotes and two Upper Canadian rebels were hanged, and 58 Patriotes and about 90 Upper Canadians were transported to Australia. Figures come from court and military records.

pedagogy.hook: The rebels lost every battle that mattered and got what they had demanded within eleven years. Britain conceded responsible government because holding Canada by force looked more expensive than sharing power.

misconception.belief: Britain gave self-government to its settler colonies because it believed in liberty.
misconception.correction: It gave it after armed rebellion, and after calculating the cost. Durham's report of 1839 said plainly that the alternative was another 1776. Where London thought the calculation ran the other way, in India, Ireland, Kenya or Cyprus, it fought instead.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Responsible government is the empire's most exported constitutional idea, and it came out of a defeat: rebels who lost the fight and won the argument.

evidence.author: Allan Greer
evidence.work: The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada
evidence.supports: The Lower Canadian rising, its rural base and its suppression.

events.title: The Durham Report
events.summary: Sent to investigate the rebellions, Lord Durham recommended two things: give the Canadas a government answerable to their own assembly, and unite them so that French Canadians would be outnumbered and, he hoped, assimilated.
events.significance: Britain adopted both recommendations and got one result it wanted and one it did not. Responsible government became the constitutional model for Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa; the assimilation of French Canada failed completely and made Durham a hated name in Quebec.

places.name: Quebec City
places.note: Durham spent five months in Canada in 1838 before resigning and going home to write.

people.name: John Lambton, 1st Earl of Durham
people.role: governor general and high commissioner; resigned after five months and wrote the report that changed the empire

people.name: Charles Buller
people.role: Durham's secretary and, with Edward Gibbon Wakefield, a principal author of the report

people.name: Louis-Hippolyte Lafontaine
people.role: the French-Canadian leader who used the union Durham designed to destroy his assimilation plan, by allying with Baldwin

pedagogy.hook: Durham described French Canadians as a people with no history and no literature, and proposed to dissolve them into an English majority. Nine years later a French Canadian was co-premier of the province he designed.

misconception.belief: The empire's constitutional reforms were about extending rights.
misconception.correction: Durham's report proposed self-government and cultural assimilation in the same paragraph. Britain wanted colonies that governed themselves cheaply and thought like Britain. Where settlers were British the first half worked; the second half failed in Quebec, and the whole package was never offered to colonies whose populations were not white.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the origin of the two-track empire: self-government for settler colonies from the 1840s, and refusal of it elsewhere for another century, with race as the operative criterion.

evidence.author: Ged Martin
evidence.work: The Durham Report and British Policy: A Critical Essay
evidence.supports: The report's authorship, its reception in London and how much it actually changed.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how influential the report really was. Ged Martin argues that responsible government came from colonial pressure and Colonial Office pragmatism rather than from Durham's text, and that the report's later fame outran its immediate effect.

events.title: The Oregon Treaty
events.summary: Britain and the United States divided the jointly occupied Pacific Northwest along the 49th parallel, with a bend south to keep the whole of Vancouver Island British. Neither side fired a shot over a territory the size of France.
events.significance: It completed the longest land boundary in the world, made British Columbia possible, and is the empire's clearest example of a territory given up by calculation rather than defeat: 5,000 American farmers on the ground outweighed a fur company and a fleet.

places.name: Fort Vancouver
places.note: The Hudson's Bay Company headquarters that ended up on the American side of the line.

places.name: Fort Victoria
places.note: Built in 1843 in anticipation of losing the Columbia, and the reason Victoria is a city.

people.name: James K. Polk
people.role: US president elected on Fifty-four Forty or Fight who settled for the 49th parallel with a war against Mexico starting

people.name: Robert Peel
people.role: British prime minister who preferred a boundary to a second American war

people.name: George Simpson
people.role: Hudson's Bay Company governor who moved the company's Pacific base north to Vancouver Island before the treaty was signed

pedagogy.hook: Britain handed over a territory the size of France without a battle, because 5,000 American farmers had walked there and a few hundred British fur traders had not.

misconception.belief: Empires took territory whenever they had the power to.
misconception.correction: Britain had the navy to fight for Oregon in 1846 and chose not to. The beaver were trapped out, the settlers were American, the Royal Navy was needed elsewhere, and Peel's government was in the middle of repealing the corn laws. Empires make cost-benefit decisions, and this one shows the arithmetic in the open.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the counter-example to the idea that empires only grow, and it draws the border that made Canada a Pacific country.

evidence.author: Frederick Merk
evidence.work: The Oregon Question: Essays in Anglo-American Diplomacy and Politics
evidence.supports: The negotiations and the decision to settle at the 49th parallel.

events.title: The British North America Act
events.summary: Westminster united the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick into a federal dominion with its own parliament, effective 1 July 1867. The delegates had wanted to call it a kingdom; the Colonial Office thought that would irritate the Americans.
events.significance: The first federal dominion in the empire and the constitutional template later stretched to Australia in 1901 and South Africa in 1910. It also gave Ottawa authority over Indigenous peoples and their lands, out of which the Indian Act of 1876 was built.

places.name: Charlottetown
places.note: Where the first conference met in September 1864, gatecrashing a meeting about Maritime union.

places.name: Westminster, London
places.note: The act passed after about four days of parliamentary debate.

people.name: John A. Macdonald
people.role: chief architect and first prime minister

people.name: George-Etienne Cartier
people.role: delivered French Canada in exchange for a province with its own civil law and schools

people.name: Joseph Howe
people.role: led Nova Scotia's repeal campaign after the fact and was refused

people.name: Samuel Leonard Tilley
people.role: New Brunswick premier; proposed the word Dominion

pedagogy.hook: No one voted on Confederation. Not one of the three colonies held a referendum, and Nova Scotia elected eighteen anti-Confederation MPs out of nineteen ten weeks later and was told it could not leave.

misconception.belief: Canada became independent in 1867.
misconception.correction: It became self-governing. Britain still controlled Canadian foreign policy, still heard final appeals from Canadian courts until 1949, and still had to pass any amendment to the Canadian constitution until 1982. Confederation created a country; independence took another 115 years and three more statutes.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the model settler-colony constitution, the one Britain reused across the empire, and the one it refused to offer where the population was not white.

evidence.author: P. B. Waite
evidence.work: The Life and Times of Confederation, 1864-1867
evidence.supports: The conferences, the politics and the act's passage.

evidence.author: Phillip Buckner
evidence.work: Canada and the British Empire
evidence.supports: Confederation in its imperial context.

events.title: The Red River Resistance
events.summary: When Canada bought Rupert's Land without consulting anyone living there, the Metis of Red River stopped the survey, turned back the incoming lieutenant-governor, seized Fort Garry and formed a provisional government under Louis Riel that negotiated the province of Manitoba into being.
events.significance: It is the only case in the empire of a people about to be transferred between governments stopping the transfer and dictating terms. It produced the Manitoba Act, with guarantees for French, Catholic schools and 1.4 million acres of Metis land, and the execution of Thomas Scott that made Riel unpardonable in Ontario.

places.name: Upper Fort Garry, Winnipeg
places.note: Seized on 2 November 1869 and held until August 1870.

places.name: Saint-Norbert
places.note: Where the Metis National Committee was formed and the survey party was stopped on 11 October 1869.

people.name: Louis Riel
people.role: president of the provisional government; negotiated the Manitoba Act and then fled a Canadian army

people.name: John Bruce
people.role: first president of the Metis National Committee

people.name: Thomas Scott
people.role: Ontario Orangeman executed by the provisional government on 4 March 1870

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the 1,200 men sent from Ontario, whose arrival began months of reprisals against Metis families

people.name: Louis Schmidt
people.role: secretary of the provisional government and one of the negotiators sent to Ottawa

toll.note: Thomas Scott was executed in March 1870; at least two Metis men were killed after the Wolseley expedition arrived, and others were beaten and driven out. No one counted, and no one was prosecuted.

pedagogy.hook: Canada bought a territory the size of India and did not tell the 12,000 people living in it. They stopped the surveyors with their feet on the chain and made Canada negotiate.

misconception.belief: Riel was a rebel against lawful government.
misconception.correction: In October 1869 there was no lawful government to rebel against: Hudson's Bay Company authority had ended and Canada's had not begun, which Ottawa admitted by delaying the transfer. Riel's provisional government negotiated terms Parliament enacted as the Manitoba Act. Canada hanged him in 1885 for a second resistance; in 1992 the same Parliament called him a founder of Manitoba.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest demonstration that colonised people were political actors who could force an empire's successor state to bargain, and the clearest case of promises made in a treaty and broken afterwards.

evidence.author: J. M. Bumsted
evidence.work: The Red River Rebellion
evidence.supports: The course of the resistance and the negotiation of the Manitoba Act.

contested.note: Whether to call this a rebellion or a resistance is itself the argument, and Canadian usage has shifted from the first to the second over the last fifty years. The execution of Thomas Scott, and whether the provisional government had authority to order it, remains disputed.

events.title: The Numbered Treaties
events.summary: In eleven treaties between 1871 and 1921 Canada obtained the surrender of about 4 million square kilometres from Cree, Saulteaux, Blackfoot, Dene and other nations in exchange for reserves, small annuities, farm equipment, schools and hunting rights.
events.significance: They are the legal foundation of most of western and northern Canada and the source of the country's longest-running legal disputes, because the written English texts and the oral promises made at the negotiations differ, and Canadian courts have repeatedly held that the oral terms count.

places.name: Lower Fort Garry
places.note: Where Treaty 1 was signed on 3 August 1871.

places.name: Fort Carlton
places.note: Where Treaty 6 was signed in 1876 with the famine clause the Cree negotiators insisted on.

places.name: Blackfoot Crossing
places.note: Where Treaty 7 was signed in 1877; the Blackfoot understood it as a peace treaty, not a land surrender.

people.name: Mistawasis
people.role: Cree chief who argued for Treaty 6 as the only way to survive the loss of the bison

people.name: Mistahimaskwa (Big Bear)
people.role: held out against Treaty 6 for six years, seeking one large territory for all Cree bands instead of scattered reserves

people.name: Isapo-muxika (Crowfoot)
people.role: signed Treaty 7 for the Siksika; his people say he was told it was a peace agreement

people.name: Alexander Morris
people.role: lieutenant-governor and treaty commissioner for Treaties 3 to 6, whose published account is a main source

pedagogy.hook: Treaty 6 contains a promise of a medicine chest and of help in famine, put in at Cree insistence in 1876. Canada is still arguing in court about what those words meant.

misconception.belief: Treaties were imposed on people who did not understand them.
misconception.correction: The Cree negotiators at Fort Carlton in 1876 knew exactly what they were doing: they refused the first terms, demanded and won famine relief, medical care, farm instruction and a ban on liquor, and Big Bear held out for six years for something better. What they could not control was that the treaties were negotiated as the bison vanished, and that Canada wrote the English text.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The numbered treaties are living law. They are the reason Canadian courts have ordered governments to consult First Nations about pipelines and mines a century and a half later.

evidence.author: J. R. Miller
evidence.work: Compact, Contract, Covenant: Aboriginal Treaty-Making in Canada
evidence.supports: Treaty negotiation, the gap between oral and written terms, and their later legal force.

evidence.author: James Daschuk
evidence.work: Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life
evidence.supports: The conditions of hunger under which the prairie treaties were signed.

contested.note: What was agreed is genuinely disputed. The written English texts describe a surrender of land; Indigenous oral histories, supported by the commissioners' own transcripts, describe agreements to share it. Canadian courts have increasingly given weight to the oral record.

events.title: The North-West Resistance
events.summary: Metis at Batoche, who had moved west after losing their Red River land and whose petitions Ottawa ignored for years, formed a provisional government under Louis Riel and Gabriel Dumont. Canada moved 5,000 troops west on the unfinished railway and crushed them in seven weeks.
events.significance: It ended armed resistance in the Canadian west, justified the completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and produced the hanging of Riel and of eight Cree and Assiniboine men, the largest mass execution in Canadian history. It also split Canada along French and English lines for a generation.

places.name: Batoche
places.note: The Metis capital, taken after four days of fighting on 12 May 1885.

places.name: Duck Lake
places.note: Where Dumont's men beat a police column on 26 March 1885.

places.name: Battleford
places.note: Where eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together on 27 November 1885.

places.name: Regina
places.note: Where Riel was tried by a six-man jury and hanged on 16 November 1885.

people.name: Louis Riel
people.role: brought back from Montana to lead the Metis petition, then the provisional government; convicted of high treason and hanged

people.name: Gabriel Dumont
people.role: Metis military commander whose tactics won at Duck Lake and Fish Creek; escaped to the United States and joined Buffalo Bill's show

people.name: Pitikwahanapiwiyin (Poundmaker)
people.role: Cree chief who tried to keep his people out of the fighting, was convicted of treason-felony and died months after release; exonerated by Canada in 2019

people.name: Mistahimaskwa (Big Bear)
people.role: Cree chief whose band killed nine people at Frog Lake against his wishes; imprisoned and died within two years of release

people.name: Frederick Middleton
people.role: British general commanding the Canadian force

toll.note: Roughly 100 Metis, Cree and Dakota and about 60 Canadian soldiers and settlers were killed in the fighting, including nine at Frog Lake on 2 April. Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged at Battleford on 27 November and Riel at Regina on 16 November. Figures come from military returns and court records.

pedagogy.hook: Louis Riel was elected to the Canadian Parliament three times and never took his seat. In 1885 Canada tried him for treason and hanged him; in 1992 the same Parliament recognised him as a founder of Manitoba.

misconception.belief: 1885 was an Indian uprising joined by the Metis.
misconception.correction: It was a Metis political movement over land titles that a few Cree bands were drawn into and most refused to join. Poundmaker actively tried to keep his people out and was convicted anyway; Crowfoot kept the Blackfoot neutral. Canada used the fighting to prosecute chiefs it wanted out of the way, and set aside Poundmaker's conviction in 2019.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It closed the Canadian frontier by force, made the railway politically unstoppable, and left a hanging that still divides how Canadians tell their own story.

evidence.author: Blair Stonechild
evidence.work: Loyal till Death: Indians and the North-West Rebellion
evidence.supports: Cree involvement, the trials and the executions at Battleford.

evidence.author: George F. G. Stanley
evidence.work: The Birth of Western Canada: A History of the Riel Rebellions
evidence.supports: The military and political course of both resistances.

contested.note: Riel's trial is still argued over: he was tried under a statute of Edward III for high treason before a jury of six English-speaking Protestants, his lawyers pleaded insanity against his wishes, and the jury recommended mercy. Whether he was mentally ill, a political prisoner, or both, has never been settled.

events.title: The Klondike Gold Rush
events.summary: Skookum Jim, Dawson Charlie and George Carmack found gold on a Yukon creek in August 1896. When news reached Seattle in July 1897 about 100,000 people set out; some 30,000 to 40,000 arrived, and Dawson City grew from nothing to 30,000 people in two years.
events.significance: It made Yukon a separate Canadian territory in 1898, put the North-West Mounted Police on the passes to enforce Canadian sovereignty, and turned the vague Alaska boundary into an urgent dispute that Canada lost in 1903.

places.name: Bonanza Creek
places.note: Called Rabbit Creek until the gold was found in it.

places.name: Dawson City
places.note: Built on the Tr'ondek Hwech'in fishing camp at the mouth of the Klondike, whose people were moved downriver.

places.name: Chilkoot Pass
places.note: Where the Mounted Police turned back anyone without a year's supplies, about a tonne of goods carried up in relays.

people.name: Keish (Skookum Jim Mason)
people.role: Tagish man who found the gold; the claim was recorded under his brother-in-law's name

people.name: Kaa Goox (Dawson Charlie)
people.role: Tagish man in the discovery party

people.name: Shaaw Tlaa (Kate Carmack)
people.role: Tagish woman, Skookum Jim's sister, whose husband took the credit and later abandoned her

people.name: Sam Steele
people.role: Mounted Police superintendent who policed the passes and made the Canadian side orderly

people.name: Chief Isaac
people.role: Tr'ondek Hwech'in leader who moved his people from the Klondike mouth and sent their songs to relatives in Alaska for safekeeping

toll.note: No reliable death toll exists. Hundreds died on the trails, including at least 65 in an avalanche on the Chilkoot Pass on 3 April 1898, and epidemic disease spread through Han and Tutchone communities along the river. Nobody counted the second group.

pedagogy.hook: The Mounted Police let nobody over the Chilkoot Pass into Canada without a tonne of supplies. Men carried it up in thirty or forty loads, and that human chain on the ice is the most famous image of the rush.

misconception.belief: Gold rushes made prospectors rich.
misconception.correction: Of roughly 100,000 who set out for the Klondike, perhaps 30,000 to 40,000 arrived, about 4,000 found gold and a few hundred got rich. The people who made money reliably were the merchants in Seattle and Dawson. The people who lost most were the Tr'ondek Hwech'in, moved off their fishing camp so the city could be built on it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The rush is how the last blank space on the imperial map of North America was claimed, and it shows sovereignty being asserted by a police post and a customs charge rather than an army.

evidence.author: Kenneth Coates
evidence.work: Land of the Midnight Sun: A History of the Yukon
evidence.supports: The rush, its scale and its effect on Yukon First Nations.

contested.note: Who actually found the gold is disputed in the sources: Tagish oral tradition credits Skookum Jim, contemporary records credit George Carmack, and the two accounts have never been reconciled. Numbers of stampeders are estimates from shipping records and police counts at the passes.

events.title: The Alaska Boundary Tribunal
events.summary: A six-man tribunal of three Americans, two Canadians and one Briton decided where the Alaska panhandle boundary ran. The British member, Lord Alverstone, voted with the Americans; the two Canadians refused to sign, and Canada was left with no port on the northern Pacific.
events.significance: It is the moment many Canadians date their loss of faith in Britain as a protector of Canadian interests, and it pushed Canada towards running its own foreign policy. Britain wanted American goodwill in Europe more than it wanted a Canadian inlet.

places.name: Skagway
places.note: The port at the head of the Lynn Canal that Canada wanted and did not get.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the tribunal sat, in the Foreign Office.

people.name: Richard Webster, Lord Alverstone
people.role: Lord Chief Justice of England and the deciding vote; sided with the three American members

people.name: Wilfrid Laurier
people.role: Canadian prime minister, who said afterwards that Canada needed the power to protect its own interests

people.name: Theodore Roosevelt
people.role: US president who appointed three openly committed partisans as impartial jurists and let it be known he would take the territory by force if the tribunal failed

people.name: Allen Aylesworth
people.role: one of the two Canadian members who refused to sign the award

pedagogy.hook: Britain's judge voted with the Americans, and the two Canadian judges refused to sign the map. Canada learned that being inside the empire did not mean the empire was on your side.

misconception.belief: Dominions like Canada were content to let Britain handle their foreign relations.
misconception.correction: 1903 is why they stopped. Canada had no treaty-making power of its own, no representation in Washington and no vote on its own boundary. Laurier said afterwards that Canada needed the authority to protect its own interests; Canada opened a Department of External Affairs in 1909 and signed its first treaty alone in 1923.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the practical demonstration that imperial unity meant British interests came first, and it is one of the steps from dominion to independence that had no battle in it at all.

evidence.author: Norman Penlington
evidence.work: The Alaska Boundary Dispute: A Critical Reappraisal
evidence.supports: The tribunal, its composition and the political pressures on it.

contested.note: Historians differ on whether Canada's legal case was actually strong. Penlington and others argue the American reading of the 1825 Anglo-Russian convention was the better one and that Alverstone voted on the law; Canadian nationalist accounts treat the award as a sacrifice of Canadian interests to Anglo-American friendship.

events.title: Destroyers for Bases
events.summary: With Britain alone against Germany and short of escorts, Churchill gave the United States 99-year rent-free leases on base sites in Newfoundland, Bermuda, the Bahamas, Jamaica, Antigua, St Lucia, Trinidad and British Guiana, in exchange for fifty old American destroyers.
events.significance: It is the clearest single measure of how far the empire's power had fallen by 1940: territory in eight colonies traded for second-hand warships. Newfoundland and Bermuda were given outright as gifts, not even as part of the exchange, and none of the colonies was consulted.

places.name: Argentia, Newfoundland
places.note: A US naval base whose construction required the removal of an entire Newfoundland community.

places.name: Kindley Field, Bermuda
places.note: Built on land taken by the US Army in 1941; part of it is Bermuda's airport today.

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: British prime minister who made the deal and told Parliament afterwards

people.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
people.role: US president who did it by executive agreement to avoid a vote in Congress

people.name: Humphrey Walwyn
people.role: governor of Newfoundland, which was under British commission rule and had no government to object with

pedagogy.hook: In 1940 Britain paid for fifty second-hand destroyers with 99-year leases on land in eight colonies. Nobody asked the colonies.

misconception.belief: The empire ended because colonies demanded independence.
misconception.correction: It also ended because Britain could no longer afford it. In 1940 Britain traded imperial territory for warships; by 1945 it owed the United States and India enormous sums, and the decisions to leave India in 1947 and Palestine in 1948 were taken by a government that could not pay for either. Nationalist pressure and bankruptcy worked together.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It puts a price on imperial power at the exact moment it collapsed, and it is why American bases sat on British colonial soil for the rest of the century.

evidence.author: Peter Neary
evidence.work: Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1929-1949
evidence.supports: The Newfoundland bases, their construction and their political effect.

events.title: Newfoundland's Confederation Referendums
events.summary: Newfoundlanders voted twice in 1948 on whether to keep the British Commission of Government, return to responsible government, or join Canada. The second ballot chose Canada by 78,323 votes to 71,334, a margin of 52.3 per cent to 47.7.
events.significance: It is the only case of a British territory voting itself into another country rather than into independence, and it completed the map of Canada. It also ended the strange fifteen-year experiment in which a democracy asked Britain to govern it because it was bankrupt.

places.name: St John's
places.note: Where the responsible-government campaign was strongest and confederation lost.

places.name: Ottawa
places.note: Where the terms of union were negotiated in 1947 and signed on 11 December 1948.

people.name: Joseph Smallwood
people.role: broadcaster who ran the confederation campaign on family allowances and pensions and became premier for twenty-three years

people.name: Peter Cashin
people.role: led the responsible-government campaign and accused Britain and Canada of arranging the result

people.name: Chesley Crosbie
people.role: led the Economic Union party, which wanted closer ties with the United States and was kept off the ballot

pedagogy.hook: Newfoundland is the only place in the British Empire that voted to become part of another country instead of becoming a country. It won by 6,989 votes.

misconception.belief: Every colony wanted to be independent.
misconception.correction: Newfoundland had been independent, as a dominion from 1907, and it went bankrupt. In 1934 it asked Britain to take self-government back; in 1948, offered the choice of returning to it, it narrowly chose Canadian pensions and family allowances instead. Independence is not always what people vote for when they are asked.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the counter-case to every story about decolonisation, and it shows economic security weighing more heavily than sovereignty in a real vote.

evidence.author: Peter Neary
evidence.work: Newfoundland in the North Atlantic World, 1929-1949
evidence.supports: The referendums, the negotiations and the British and Canadian roles.

evidence.author: Sean T. Cadigan
evidence.work: Newfoundland and Labrador: A History
evidence.supports: The campaign, the vote and its long aftermath.

contested.note: Newfoundlanders still argue about whether the referendums were fair. The complaints are that Britain and Canada openly wanted confederation, that the Economic Union option was excluded from the ballot, and that Catholic districts voted heavily against. Historians who have worked the archives find pressure and partiality but no evidence of a falsified count.
